Diesnory of AIiDREW SNOT., For 53 years Incumbent of St. Diary's, Birkenhead, Died 12th October, 1881, Age 85. ga, being dead, yet Epeaketh."—xi: lieb. 4. v. Be has gone to the grave, but we will not deplore him," We'll cherish his memory long in the heart; The lessons of love through life that he taught us Will, now he has gene, consolation impart. Bo more will the widow and orphans behold him, For whom he long pleaded, and never in vain; Their sorrows he soothed by his own balm of kindness, Tlaeit burdens he lightened by sharing their pain.. Be lived as he taught ILI, and this is a bleeing ; The force of example abides with us long; Ile spoke as he felt, and the words that be uttreel Went straight to the hearts both of weak 9_ jid of Ile has fcught a good fight" in life's IVAtle jus*endad, And joined the great concourse of these gone before ; With the songs of the ransomed his lawn will be blended, Where sorrow and sighing are beard of no more. Ring's elougb, Birkenhead, J. O. B.

_ QUEEN'S WTIZATti ON THE PRUsIDENT'S BIER. Still westward thrOugh the night in silence sweeping, Wife of a hero watching by thy dead, On through a nation, silent, round thee weeping— That weepest not until thy task be sped. They meet thee still in city after city To honour and to mourn their dead and thine, With bared heads, kneeling, hushed in awe and pity, For crime inhuman met with grace Divine. Saluting always, with restrained emotion, One bier, arid on it laid one funeral wreath, Borne from the Mother-land beyond the ocean ; The hand of Love above the hand of Death. An hearts thus owning as with one pulse beating, Goodness and truth, the Eternal and unseen; 'the hearts bf two great kindred nations meeting Through the true heart of one true, widowed Queen. Oh, Queen I 'ti s not thy crown of empire only, Thy crown of sorrow hallows thee to this! And thou, last stricken, fear not to be lonely, Since of such woe is born earth's saving bliss. G..ce more "the N eil grows thin" the heavens effacing,. One triumph more through paths in anguish trod; Two nations through two women's hearts embracing, / One people bowing low before one God. * Alluding to President Gerfield's speech on adjourning Con- after President Lincoln's assassination. —Good Words.

OUT ALL NIGHT. Oh, Dolly, my Dolly, I did not know I left you under the tree, I But my cousins stayed till after dark, and as soon as nurse had , tea She called sod hurried me off to bed, and I wondered where you could be. The chilly white moon looked through the pane, and a cloud flew over the sky, There was nothing but moonlight in the room, and I almost, had to cry; But while I was wishing for you to hug, sweet sleep came by and by.' And all the while you were here in the grass, right under the big plum tree ! Where you scared' You don't look sad at all! I think you are smiling at me I Oh, Dolly„ do tell me how you felt out alone all night long to be ' Did the tree bend dowa and rustle its leaves? Did the daisies say anything? Did a bird come late, hopping through the grass, and stop at yoJr-feet toeing? Did little brown elves ko trooping by to get water fresh from the spring? Did you think you heard noses in the dark, or was it all cold and still ? There are no bears in our pad, I am sure; but when it grew late and chill Wasn't it dreary to lie and I is tr front the swamp-woods the . ? Maybe yolr didntlie still, after all; now, Dolly, child, tell me

true. Did the roses come dancing off the bush, and haves sweet romp with you? . . I delft know what happens in gardens et night, but Dolly, dear; von do ? Did the hollyhocks bend on their high stems? Did my lily lift her face ? Did those little vieletehy the stone go tripping out- of their place? And, oh (MI the flowers talk at night, and the glowworms light all space ? • Did the poppies enie and put you to Bleep! Oh, Dolly, . tell something to mei . Ton smile in My face, your cheeks are red, and your eyes are as bright as can be. Did you smile In the long dark night alone when I was not there to see ? —Leeds Afereary Wieldy.

_ "The only true way of assisting the poor," said Arch- bishop Sumner," is to make them agents in bettering their own condition." Queen Elizabeth onc3 said to a courtier," They pass best over the world who trip over it quickly; or it is but a bog; if we stop we sink." Tasso replied to a proposition that he should take yen- gence on a man who had injured him, "I do not wish to deprive him either of his goods, his honour, or his life. I wish only to deprive him of his ill-will." Eferodotns (the Greek historian) has written—" From the age of five years to that of twenty, the ancient Persians in- structed their children only in three things, viz., to manage a horse, to shoot dexterously with the bow, and to speak the MA." - • The linfortance of fiirming good habits cannot be over- estimated. .-" Remember," said Lord Colllngwood to a young man whom he greatly esteemed, and who was about to sm. bark-in We, before you are five.and-twenty you must estab- lish a character that will serve you all your life." David Wilkie (celebrated Scotch painter) was once told by Graham, trio coaster of the Trustees' Academy at Edin- burgh—" If you have genius, industry will improve it; if you have no genius, industry will supply its place." "So," said Wilkie, " I was determined to be very industrious, for I knew I had no genius."—" Reading the Will," " Distrain- ing for Rent," "The Penny Wedding," and other well- I known pictures, show how Wilie valued and appreciated the above advice. Dr. Johnson on one occasion was saying to a friend : " Accustom your children coustautly to tell the truth, with. out varying in any circumstance." A lady who Was present exclaimed, "Nay, this is too much; for a little variation in narrauve must happen a thousand timea a day if one is not perpetually watching." "Well, madame," replied the Doctor, and you ought to be perpetually watching. It is more from carelessuees. about truth than from intentional lying that thinitia, ea mach falsehood in the world." often forgot- ten Itgteß4elr,,P, Sicir.eopu,,-,l,Fisvtoo the ett of a canstahtly depressed mode of llte must be, where each day follows another with unbroken monotony of grinding work, just enough to keep body and soul together. Streets of poor people, all equally poor, all engaged in a hand-to-hand tussle against drink and pauper- ism. Into such lives there comes no golden ideal of pros- perimand. progress. no sweetening and raising of the,apirit by art of intellectual enjoyments, no lifting from the eter- nal dead level; when they are sick, they are tempted to "curie God ~nd die." How can such people have any brightening, cheering influences over their sick relatives, whca they sit huddled together in one small dirty attic, with fusty rags hanging on a line across the ceiling, and the sooty windows hermetically secured? Either discom- tort and noise, or perfect solitude are the conditions of the sufferer's existence. Now mark what happens with the advent of the nurse—the moral sunshine. She admits air, light, the necessary conditions of health ' • she institutes order, cleanlines., method, until patients have been known to declare they never knew what comfort was before. She chats brightly and merrily where it is desirable, she teaches the mother how to still the cries of the fractious baby, gives good advice to the drunken husband, has a word and a smile and a helping hand for all. Can these advantages be under- valued, advantages of prevention as well as cure ?—Good Words. THE VIKINGS AND THE VIKING SHIP.—The Vikings and their followers were for many a long day the special plague of Scotland. They had effected a settlement in Ireland, and having become acquainted with the Scotch ports, paid them several practical visits. They spread themselves over the Hebrides as early as 703, and during the next two centuries they appear to have emigrated to Orkney, Shetland, Skye, and the Isle of Man, all ofewhich places seem to have be- come Norwegian colonies. They associated and intermarried with the inhabitants, and to this day their descendants may be readily distinguished, both in physiognomy and tempera- ment, from these of Celtic origin. Many names of the clans as well as designations of places also bear testimony to the presence of the Vikings. During 870 a large and Powerful armament Failed from Dublin under Anlaf and Ivar, overran all North Britain, ravaging the country and pillaging its inhabitants, returning to Ireland gorged with blood and plunder. In 881 Constantine met his death whilst futilely fighting with them on the banks of the Forth. They still continued their descents on Scotland' daring the reign of Donald, who, however, signally de- feated them twice. During the last battle, which was fOnglit in 904 on the banks of the Tay, Donald himself was Wain., but, unlike Constantine, not until he had killed the Viking leader. . . . The struggle had been long and tediously protracted. From about 866 to 1014 it had con- tinued, but eventually the pluck and steady determination of the Scotch conquered, and they had the satisfaction, after struggling for some 148 years, of seeing the last of their foes. But the piratical descents of the Vikings were not confined to Scotland and Ireland. They seem to have made three descents upon England dur- ing the eighth century ;. but these do not appear to have c=u,-1 mulch alarm among the inhabitants. During the ev.,.of Egbert's reign, however, their invasions became more 11,e-10e0t and much more disastrous, and for the. next two unfired years they troubled the country more or less. 'Whether ths galley we are concerned with- did or did not Visit thia epuntry is a question which cannot now be deter- mined. We do not know the name of the Viking owner, or anything about his doings or by what np.rne he called his vessel. We can merely say that he lived at some time dur- ing the period from the end of the eighth to the middle of the eleventh century. and that when he died he was buried in his vessel, which was drawn up on land and had a mound Of earth thrown over.% which, luckily for posterity, pened to consist ,of blue clay. At any rate it was in - such as this one that the Vikings arrived on our sho 2herefore, nationally, if not arclueologically, we are int, 13 the discovery.—" ThP Viking Ship," in Good Words.

An alarm was raised, and tve master, rushing out of the house, shouted, "Let the cows out; let the cows out!" This, no doubt, saved 'the lives of the men, u the bull left them the moment the cows came'ln sight, and in a little time became placid, and was driven with them into the yard, and finally into his own shed, which he was never again permitted to leave alive— death having been the penalty awarded for his sins.— F. W. 8., in the Agricultural Gazette. MANIIRB MADE UNDER COVEE.—Of CORMS all the ad- vantage of making manure in covered yards may be secured by box feeding, with less outlay for roofing, since more space must be allowed for a given number of animals turned loose together than when confined in stalls; it is the tkotection from rain and sun, the abundant use of litter: and its thorough incorporation with the excrements, and the ex- clusion of air by compact treading, which go to make the superior manure; all these features of the method work against the loss of valuable plant food. Nor does box feed- ing and constant accumulation of the manure under the feet of the animals necessarily imply offensive stalls. Mr. Law- rence said that everybody noticed the general sweetness of his stalls; it is only essential that enough litter be used to absorb all liquids, and this absorption is more effectual if the straw is cut up. One method or the other, box feeding or covered yards, should be adopted by every farmer who lives where manure is worth saving, and who finds himself compelled to supplement his stable manure with commer- cial fertilisers. Stable manure must not be lost sight of in this increasing interest in these concentrated fertilisers, for we cannot produce our crops and have enough for ourselves and othera without its aid; and there is nothing in all the list of commercial mixtures which gives so good an average return for the money iravested in it as well-made stable manure.;--Professor Caldwell, in American Agriculturist for October. . TerLivortat IN DOGS.—Every one has heard of ,the gid , in sheep, known in different parts of the country as the " sturdy," " vertigo," " staggers," " tarnsidet " or the "whirls." - Well, if the brain of an animal that has died of this disease be opened, there will be found therein what are called hydatids, or cysts, little bladder-shaped objects. These are nothirg more or less than small colonies of the larvae of the very large tapeworm, called thg Tcenia ccenurns. We have seen this parasite nearly two yards long, and repeatedly over one yard. Each gid hydatid is loaded, so to speak, with hundreds of tapeworm heads, growing from a common centre, and every head, if introduced into the dog's body, is. capable of being developed into a tapeworm. The cbig often becomes infested with this parasite from eating sheeps' brains; and dogs thus afflicted, and allowed to roam at plea- sure over. fields and hills where sheep are fed, sow the seeds of gid in our flocks to any extent. We know too well the great use of Collie dogs to the shepherd or graziei to advise that dogs should note employed as assistants, but surely 'it would be to their owner's advantage to see that they were kept in a state of health and cleanliness. Says Cobbold : " The propagation of entozoa in general, and of tapeworms In particular, is intimately connected with, and absolutely depeudent upon, the promiscuous association of different kinds of animals; and as regards the production of parasit- ism amongst domesticated animals used as food, it is per- fectly certain that the tapeworrbs'of the dog play a most conspicuous part." Striking language this from so great an authority, and affording much food for thought.

1, Take hold, then, cheerfully of the tasks before you; put envy put of your hearts, and don't be discontented. , The largest half of the troubles of life are of our own making, and the rest will be borne the easier if we are cheerful and hopeful. The celebrated Dr. Carey, who had been brought up as a shoemaker—or cobbler. as be once deprecatingly remarked— has left the tenoning record as to the value of persever- ance :—" Whoever • gives me credit for anything e besides ibeing a plodder will do too much. *I can plod—l can per- ?severe in any difficult pursuit—and to that I owe every- :thing. Two .Irishmen Were poring over the news in one of our .. . city papers, and coming to the heading "Latest," and im- mediately following it, "Very Latest," one said to the 'other —" An' sure, Tim, will ye be afther explainin' what ;this mean" " Arrah, bedad," said Tim, "an' its myself ;that can :explain that to ye. Sure the latest is what comes in time to he printed, and the very 'latest is what Comes afther the paper is out." i EXAMINATIONS AND CRAMMING.—nt a meeting of the lAecham Society, Dr. Boyd Carpenter, in an address on ieducation, denounced the system of competitive examina- tions as overstraining the faculties and leading to failure in !after life. Mr. Fronde, who ,eoresided, expressed concur- rence in these views, and mentioned a case where a young ;man gained an appointment on account of his admirable answers in political economy, of which science he confessed lafterwards he knew nothing beyond the cramming he got from his "coach." Oh,l wonder we ever forget all his! I wonder we are net always tender of the old !—Rose .Porter.. If'l , ...,.,. . RIEUTE TO A. Often de I sigh in py etrngeeies with the hard, uncaring world for the sweet, Ideepitiecerity I felt when, of an evening, nestling in , her boson3,lL listened to some iiiiiet tale, suitable to my age, read srt.' her tender and untiring voice. Never can I forget her sweet glances cast upon me when I appeared asleep; +never her kiss .of peace at night. Years have passed away , since we laid her beside my father in the old churchyard; . yet still her voice whispers from the grave, and her eye watches over me as I visit spots long since hallowed to the .memory of my mother.—Lord Macaulay. : A DELIGHTFUL FLAVOUR. CULTIVATION OF FRUIT TREES. We give below a summary of an article by Mr. E. K. Kynasten on "Fruit Growing," in which he shows how, by treating separately the fruit fibres and the wood fibres of a tree's root—nourishing the one, and pruning the other—an iabundance of fruit maybe secured. He has had many years I experience, and hgs found that with his cultivation, fruit comes to his trees, even in his neighbours' bad years; and what is more, with careful storage, he manages to ripen it. Mr. Kynaston says :—ln the minter of 1879-80 I under- took the "restoration" of rather over 100 mixed fruit trees (apple, pear, and plum). The trees, mostly very old stan- dards, were all nearly "gone to wood," moss covered to the last degree non-bearing for long years, and altogether dilapidated in appearance. Matters climatic and otherwise looked on the whole hopelessly against me; but, neverthe- less, and knowing the extraordinary force possessed by "good cultivation," which means strict attention to the natural laws ordained for fruit trees, by which we are en- abled to apply the right force in the right direction, I had the said old standards wood-root pruned at proper distanees, manured, and otherwise attended to, the result being that in the spring following they one and all recommenced active life and usefidness by blooming moderately and throwing out samples of fruit—even the oldest and most decayed of the standards bore apples, and many of the plant trees yielded largely. This was a good and quick beginning, con- sidering that the previous cold and wet 1879 summer had failed to thoroughly ripenithe new wood and bnds of fruit trees generally, a circumstance which caused 1880 to be classed on the whole as a fruit-failing year. Also a large quantity of fruit bushes (currant and gooseberry), hitherto but poor at their best, on being similarly cultivated, cropped at ence unusually well. In the severe winter last past the now renovated trees required (save manuring) hardly any labour at all, as the judicious treatment which they had undergone had stopped on their part all superfluous wood growth, causing them to throw out instead an uniform and rich supply of fruit spurs and buds without which, of course, no fruit can be had. In the spring,notwithstanding it was characterised by late frosts of unusual severity, bitter, east winds and trying dryness, the trees bloomed splendidly, and, from their uniform vigorous appearance, looked as if under some unusual and powerful cultivation, and they could this August be seen covered with-a perfect wealth of fast-growing fruit. Some of the trees have gone altogether to excess in it—their way, perhaps, of showing their gratitude at being released from their late long and unfruitful bondage—and A few now cropping well have never before been known to bear, proof sufficient of the great searching force possessed by "good cultivation ;" for if fruit be in a tree it will to a certainty bring it out. Also the bush fruit, which was good last year, was a perfect mar- vel for quantity this. Perhaps some may say, "Al, but your restoration must have proved an expensive business." Not so by any means, for the work was done in the month of November and part of December, when other jobs wefe scarce, principally by one labouring man utterly ignorant of fruit culture, but who did as he was told, and the requisite manure would hardly have been missed from the farmyard heap, as a single load will suffice for a good many trees. The trees are all growing in the very heart of the Bala Moun- tains, where the weather—for climate it can hardly be called —is the reverse of picked, so much so that people about began to think it top precarious: for the growth of fruit. The secret of this result is that the whole force of the cul- tivation was thrown upon the fnaltf fibres of the trees, and so fruit followed as a natural and certain consequence. Ever since the discovery of that great natural law—that a fruit tree is divided as to its roots (wood roots, fruit fibres, and tap root)—with a clear, separate function for each division, I have had no difficulty whatever in yearly filling my gar- den mithihe finest kinds of outdoor .fruit, simply because the'natural law in question opened np to me the following four highly im i portant matters, which n combination make up what most justly may be termed "good cultivation":- 1. That there exists in every fruit tree two natural but strongly antagonistic, forces, the one the wood root, the other the fruit fibre. Now, if in a tree the former or wood root force be in the ascendant, as in trees imperfectly culti- vated, the tree goes to excess in wood ; but if fruit fibre force be uppermost, as in trees perfectly cultivated, the tree goes to excess in fruit—that is to say, a tree will throw out more fruit than it can as a rule fairly maintain unless the fruit fibres be extra well nourished. •(The pamphlet, "Out- door Fruit for the Million," fully explains all this.) 2. The true scientific distance for wood root pruning my trees, viz., jest outside the circle of their fruit fibres. This knowledge I find to be invaluable, because it enables me not only to leave the exact amount of wood root naturally required for the fair and profitable extension of the tree, but also to extract from the fruit fibre force its fullest power. 3. The extreme necessity that exists for nourishing well and prezerving intact a tree's fruit fibres, because -on their vigour and well-being depend not only the fruit, but also the life of the tree itself. 4. The true use designed for the tap-root, viz., to give due stability to the tree and nothing else. It is, therefore, plainly enough the main object of "good -cultivation" always to have the fruit fibre force well upper- most, a matter managed easily enough by timely and judi- cious wood root pruning, and manuring liberally, both in spring time as well as autumn. A tree's fruit fibres, which apparentlY for that purpose are always conveniently massed around Its Stem. It also ought to be remembered that "good cultivation" is by no means a matter of money but of management, because any labouring man, by gathering a few barrow loads of manure from off a highway, would be able, with. the addition of a little lime, to fill the. treeirin his cottage garden as fall of fruit as I myself could, if onlji; he knew how.

How vain is the pride of ancestry, when we are all de- scended from a penniless, houseless, unclad working gar- dener'. • Christian character is .not an act, but a process; not a sudden creation, but a development. It grows and bears fruit like a tree, and like a tree it requires patient and un- wearied attention. NATURAL slot ARTIFICIAL LANT.—No human laws are of any validity if contrary to tile law of nature; and such of them as are valid derive all their authority, mediately or immediately, from this original.—Blackstons SCHOLARSHIP AND INTELLECT.—High litergy culture and great literary facility are compatible with great feeble- ness of intellectual grasp. _Scholarship in itself is as warranty of sound thinking4Ponock's Life of Spinoza. To do little things for the Ldrd's sake ifione of the sweetest fruits and highest evidences of the divine life in the soul. And the. Master's estimate of them is "Because thou hest been faithful in a very little, have thou authority," dm It Is the "very little things" that make the pivots on which the great issues of bodily and spiritual life are found to tarn !—.Recorder and Covenant. Doetopeoldsmith once stepped into a coffee-house and desired a cup of,coffee, which, on being set before him, was scarcely half full. Wishing to give the master of the house some pointed renroof, he asked hist if he had not been bred a printer. "No," said he, "but I know something of books." "I imagined so," rejoined the doctor, "because I never met , with a handsomer margin to a coffee cup in my life." LETTER FROM BOSTON, U.S. Boston is at the present time expecting the visits of pro- minent men from England. Next Monday Mr. Edward A. Freeman, the eminent historian, is to deliver the first of a series of lectures on "The English People in their Three Homes." These homes are Germany,England, and America. Mr. Freeman is one of those-who ‘will not listen for one, , • moment to thetheory that we English have a great deal of Celtic blood in our veins. He believes that we are the pure and unadulterated descendants of those Teutonic barbarians described by Tacitukand Cesar, whose early home was in tie depths of the forests of North Germany. While I can- not go altogether with Mr. Grant Allen and others who have taken up the cudgels for the Celts and have attempted to prove that we are as much Celtics as Teuton, I think Mr. Freeman's view ,of our almost exclusive Teutonic origin, would be difficult to maintain in the face of numerous facts. This is, I believe, true as regards England herself, but much 1 more as rwrds this newer and greater England of the I ' Western continent. It is wonderful what numbers of nationalities are to be found here, and what new shoots are being grafted on the parent stem. America is becoming_ less and less English in the strict sense of the term, every year. New York ranks next to Berlin and Vienna as the third German city of the world. Here in Boston there are tens of thousands of Irish. The pity government is con- trolled by the Irish vote. That vote is always cast in favour of the Democratic party, who rule Boston though the state of Massachusetts is Republican, and the Mayor of Boston, whose acquaintance I have been fortunate enough to make, owes his position to the support of his Celtic fellow-citizens. How strong is this Irish vote may be inferred from the fact that one of the large and fine steam-ferries which convey passengers and vehicles from East Boston to the city proper is named "D. D. Kelly," after a prominent local Irish poli- tician, the other ferries being named after such illustrious Bostonians as Winthrop and Franklin. D. D. Kelly is, I \have no doubt, a worthy man, but he is, to say the least of it, a curious companion for the illustrious patriot who snatched the lightning from heaven and the sceptre from the tyrants. The mixture of populations and blending of peoples may be seen still more strongly by anyone who should take a minute's walk from where I now sit, He Will find a street tilled with negroes, or "coloured people," as they are most usually called here. All down the long and some- what dirty data which leads from Boston out to Cambridge are the "coloured people" found. This district, curiously enough,ls ,united for municipal and state purposes with a rich and aristocratic section; and the custom is to send al- ternatively to the Massachusetts Legislature a "gentleman" from Beacon-street, and a poor man from the humbler por- tion of the district. I hope this compromise is acceptable to both parties concerned. In the same region in which the negroes live) the Chinese are also to be found. They "run" the laundry business, and are in much request in that way. Besides these, I have met here English, Scotch, Germans, French, and Norwegians; and yet perhaps Boston is less cosmopolitan than any of the great American cities. But I have wandered far from Mr. Freeman and his intense Tea- tonism, having placed All these facts before your readers in order to show how largely the structure and composition of the American nationality is being modified. The English language, and English sentiment, political and still more, religious, will always prevail here, but it is more than doubt- ful whether, a century hence, some future Mr. Freeman will be able to speak of this countryaas the home of the English race. • If he can, it will only he in the sense that that race is dominant. Mr. Freeman is likely to have a warm wel- come, though not of the enthusiastic and popular kind that greeted Thackeray, Dickens, Professors Huxley and Tyndall, and Dean Stanley. ,He is better known to scholars thawto the general public; but Boston is full of culture and learn- ing, and knows hbw to appreciate such a scholar as Free- man. Mr. Freerhan will also lecture at Newhaven, Connec- ticut, the seat of Yale College. The inevitable "interviewer" met him .on landing at New York, and discovered that he had suffered but little, from mat de mer, that he was going', to se his son in Virginia and to visit the West, and that he- looked like a stout, honest, farmer. It is several years since I Saw and heard Freeman, but I recognise this description as approximately true. . Another visitor is Mr: James Bryce, M.P., who is also tic;: appear on the lecture-platform. He has been staying at one of the sea-side resorts not far from Boston with some Amerit can friends, and I hope has gained strength after the severe and trying session of Parliament. Mr. Bryce, as English- men know, is not only an accomplished scholar and his- torian„but also a graceful and polithecl ,speaker. He has made his mark in politics said literature, and will doubtless , secure the attention of the dainty Boston people. Another.l . visitor is Mr. T.P. O'Connor, who comes to secure help for the Land League. He will find much support and a great deal of sympathy, even from native-born Americans as well as from the Irish. Great interest in the Irish question is felt here; and on the whole what I regard 'ai a very just ' view is taken amongst well-informed citizens. A coercive policy, is generally condemned, while on the other hand Americans feel that the union between England and Ireland ought to be maintained, since its violation would be detri- mental to both Countries. They think that Ireland should ' espy equal laws as to suffrage with England, and that the frith should be permitted to manage their own affairs to as large an extent as is consittent with union. This is a just and humane view, the importance of which I wish were more clearly seen by the English Liberal leaders. Nothing lass can possibly Battle the Irish question; and this is getter-. ally felt by Americans. Mr. Parnell was not thought very highly of in Boston, I am tohl. Perhaps my friend Mr.. O'Connor may do better; he is much more fitted to awaken -I ,ontliiisissm and to interest an audience. InconnectiOn with. this I„ must say that among Aniericans, the greatest enthu- slain:l4or Mr;Gladstone existenniversally, and people are ;ever tired of hearing about him; they regard his premier- ship as a fortunate thing for England at the present time, and admire the industry, eloquence. and statemanehip which. he displays at his advanced age. There is a strong wish that both Gladstone and Bright would visit this Country. They would meet with such a reception as has been -ex- tended to no foreigner since Kossuth pleaded here thirty fears ago for the cause of Hungarian freedom. ' ',spent the other evening some very interesting hours With the wince of American orators, Wendell Phillips, whomn Johialidght described, Inntteen years ago, as "the greatest crater' who -speaks the gttlish ,tottgue." Mr:Phillips is loolting well; and seems active both in body and mind, thorigil nearlY seventy years of age. He told me he was growing Old and must cease work. But there are few signs af age beyond white hair. A more truly lovable, genial, and altogether beautiful man I never saw. The flame of his genius burns as brightly as when, forty-six years ago, he Made his first great anti-slavery Speech in Fennell HalL He is simille and happy as a child, brim-full of mirthful anecdote, in private life the most fascinating and charming Of companions. And he is—always perfectly serene, even When launching the thunderbolts of oratory against despot- am and injustice of all Vide. It la something to have grasped the hand of this grand champion of humanity who in old age bas not toigntten the aspirations of his youth. i I have bald an Interesting visit to two of the Massachu- setts cotton-towns; but must reserve a description to a future letter.

THE POSSIBILITY OF SECURING FINE WEATHER ON BANK HOLIDAYS.—It has been noticed, I believe, that almost every great battle has been followed by a shower of rain; and the phenomenon is attributed to atmospheric con- cussions produced by the amount of gunpowder exploded. A mock bombardment of London from a circle of fifty miles would perhaps be too great a price to pay for clearing the air of rain in preparation for the " Derby ;" but processes are cheapened by the progress of discovery, and perhapsthe same thing may be effected hereafter at a lower figure. What may not be expected, for instance, from this new-born power of electricity which we have just succeeded in bottling up like the Arab story-teller's Afrite for use whenever re- quired? If we can catch the wandering forces of winds and tides and streams, and imprison them in electric cells, to be set to work where they are wanted, the smoke of Lon- don and our big towns will become a wanton atrocity, to be blown away for ever by the breath of public indignation. With smoke will go fog, and with fog an immense deal of bronchitis and bad temper. But that is not all. Rain, as well as other elements of weather, is largely dependent on the electric condition of the atmosphere, as indeed is shown by thunder showers. Now, if we can convert every moving force of nature into stored-up electricity, we may accumu- late any conceivable amount of it. And if so, who shall set a limit to the extent of our power to adjust the balance of electric currents between earth and air and clouds? It was thought a wonderful achievement of Dr. Franklin to draw down lightning out of the sky. But it will be a still greater thing to put it back again; yet surely by no means impos- sible. At any rate, be. that as it may, hi our growing con- trot of the immeasurable force of electricity, there is cer- tainly the "promise and potency" of human dominion over the air as well as over the sea and land. Artificial thunder- shocks may so shake the atmosphere that it will deposit its rain at our bidding, and so vve—in the persons of our great- great-grandchildren—may at least be able to secure one fine day at our discretion. The clerk of the weather office will no longer be a myth. Or like many another myth, he will turn out to be a proof of the deep prophetic instinct buried under human ignorance. Like the seven-league boots realised in railways, like Puck's girdle round the earth, now almost achieved by the electric telegraph, he toe will be embodied—and I do not envy him his post.— ," Weather and Morals," ' Good Words. -- - The new Dean of Westminster was on Tuesday instal/ed in his office. • Reports as to the weather of Tuesday show that snow fell over all parts of the country. An unmarried lady, whose parents occupy a respectable position among the dile of Ironbridge, in Shropshire, has eloped with a publican. The Court of Review at Montreal has ordered a Mr. Duckett to pay 675,000 for sitting and voting in the Quebec Legislature without being legally qualified. At a conference on Monday night between Oldham clergy- men and nonconformists it was agreed to reduce the burial fees from 255. to 215., and in case of non-parishioners from 50s. to 21s. Mr. F. North, Q.C., of the Inner Temple, has been ap- pointed to the judgeship vacant in the High Court of Justice by the elevation of Mr. Justice Lindley to the Court of Appeal. At a Liberal meeting at Merthyr Tydvil, on Monday, a resolution was adopted deploring the necessity for coercion in Ireland, end recognising in the Land Act a wise, conspre- hensive, and beneficial measure. An engine-driver named John Edwards got off his engine at Coleham station on Monday, when he was knocked down by a passing train and decapitated. It is supposed he slipped as the train was passing. At Glyneeath, Monmouth, a man named Daniel has been arrested, charged with threatening to murder his wife, who had just tried to kill her child and attempted to commit suicide. Whilst in a dying condition she confessed having been unfaithful, and Daniel at once became furious. A razor was found on him. The Exchequer accounts from the Ist April to the 29th October are as follow :--Revenue, £44,805,277 ; expenditure, £49,595,964; balances, £2,017,351. Last year: Revenue, £43,440,620; eipenditure,£4B,2l7,B3B; balances, £2,202,613. At a meeting of the Durham Federation Board, on Tues- day, resolutions were passed expressing sorrow at the death] of Mr. Macdonald M.P. Deraitations of miners, enginemen,l mechanics, and Bokemen will attend the funeral, and the Miners' National Association will also be represented. A meeting was held at Margate, on Tuesday, to raise a fund for the relief of the widows and orphans of the fisher- men lost in the late gales. It was reported that six Rams- gate boats with their crews have not been heard of since the 14th ult., while about 100 casualties of various degrees of severity occurred. A painful feeling has been created in Glasgow by the discovery of extensive frauds by Mr. Tames Thomson, city registrar, and clerk to the Bonbon School Board. He has absconded with £l7OO, and a warrant has been issued for his apprehension. Mr. Thomson is the son of a well-known Presbyterian minister. The earliest volume of the Manchester Court Leet Records, which has been "missing" for quite twenty years has now been returned to the custody of the Corporation from an anonymous source. It is a volume of much interest, com- mencing in 1552 and extending to 1586, and a reward had been offered for its recovery. This, however, has not yet ' been claimed. According to a statement of the Oldham Master Cotton Spinners' Association the town of Oldham now consumes 4nore than one-fourth of the entire qaantitv of raw cotton used in Great Britain, and considerably more than one-fifth 'of the cotton imported. The weight of cotton conveyed to Oldham and its district is stated to reach nearly 160,000 ions per annum, and the annual amount paid for freightage and cartage is nearly £lOO,OOO a year. , Sir Wm. Harcourt, speaking at • the opening of Cocker- mouth Industrial School, on Saturday, entered at length Into the subject of juvenile crime. He thought magistrates should have power to deal with mischievous boys by whip- ping them or giving them 24 hours' confinement, that offenders should be sent to reformatories without previous imprisonment, and that parents might be bound over for the good behaviour of their children. AN Litmus Pita.—At the Rotherham police court on Monday, a case in which a father and two sons, all colliers, had been charged with a savage assault on another collier was called on. The two sons were brought up in custody, but not their father: and the solicitor for the prosecution stated that when the sons were apprehended the father wished God might strike him dead if his sons had done anything. Within 12 hours his impious prayer was granted, and the man was a corpse. bEATH OF MR. ALEXANDER MACDONALD, M.P.—Mr. Alexander Macdonald, M.P., died on Monday afternoon, of heart disease, at his residence, Welthall, near Hamilton, in his 61st year. He was elected in 1874 for Stafford, which 'he has since represented. ,He was secretary to the Miners' Association for Scotland, and chairman of the Miners' 'National Association. When young he wrought in a mine, but for thirty years he had devoted nearly all his attention to promoting the interests of miners. For some years past •he has been in infirm health. Ile addressed a tninerte meet- ing in Hamilton a month ago, after which he never left his house. He was never married. On Monday morning he was able to dictate several letters, one of which related to the death of his brother James, in America, on the 16th October. At a large meeting of working men of Plymouth, on Mon- day, after an address from Mr. Broadhurst, M.P., tetelutions were passed in favour of the principle of labour representa- tion, expressing approval of the Land Act, and confidence 'in the Government. Towards the close of the proceedings, ' a telegram was received announcing the death of Mr. Mac- donald, the working men's member for Stafford, Mr. Broad- hurst, rising, said they could not receive such news without being somewhat unnerved, for Mr. Macdonald had in early life worked in a mine, but by his own energy he became to a great extent in educated man. He was always fighting the battle of labour, especially in connection with the mining population. Ide (Mr. Broadhurst) was proud of having been the means of introducing Mr. Macdonald to ,Stafford. The meeting passed a resolution expressing its sense of. the great loss the country has suetained. • • NATIONAL LAND.. I,IIAGEFE OF GREAT BRITAIN, MICHAEL Deanrr Bnearen.—At the usual weekly meeting of this branch km Sunday, the following resolution was proposed by Dr. Dixon, seconded by Mr. Waters', and carried with accla- mation :—That in the opinion of this meeting it is impera- tively necessary to the interests of the industrial classes of this country that the question 'of the land tax should receive the promp attention 4:sf the Legislature, and that with this object it is expedient that the House of Commons be peti- tioned to appoint a committee next session to inquire into the causes which have resulted in the shameful evasion of the Act passed in the fourth year If the reign of William and Mary, imposing a tax of four, shillings in the pound on the annual rentals of landholders; and to obtain a repeal of the Act 9 William 111., c. 10, whereby the said tax is made a fixed annuity instead of increasing with the value of the land, as justice requires it should do. Tun LATE MR. THOMAS BAINES.—On Monday morning, Mr. Thomas Baines one of the best known of local histo- rians died very suddenly at the age of 75 years. He was third' son of the late Mr. Edward Baines, who represented Leeds in several Parliaments, and brother of the present Sir Edward Baines, proprietor of the Leeds Mercury. Mr. Thomas Baines was the editor of the Liverpool Times, one of the old papers which expired under the pressure of the cheap dailies. He was the author of "History of Liver- pool," "Lancashire and Cheshire; Past and Present," and Yorkshire ; Past and Present." About thirty years ago he removed to London, where, in 1858, he established the Liverpool Office, the affairs of which he continued to direct until his death, which took place quite suddenly at the residence of his son-in-law, Mr. E. K. Muspratt, Seaforth Hall, Lancashire. Mr. A. B. Forwood was also a son-in-law of the deceased, having married his second daughter. THE SICK Rscrort earn HIS Cu.—Au extraordinary story was told by the Rev. A. Langdon at the Exeter Diocesan Conference. The rector of a living worth £l,OOO a year was very ill, and as he was assured he would not live 48 hours, he was anxious to arrange his worldly affairs. A lawyer was summoned, and there was dfhcovered a client anxious to get hold of the advowson and next presentation to the living. This client being informed that the rector could not live forty-eight hours longer, agreed to give £lO,OOO for the next presentation. No sooner were matters settled than the sick man felt a great weight lifted from his breast, and he at once had a great desire for chicken broth, mutton chops, and so on, and gradually got well, living for 25 years in the enjoyment of his benefice. If the rector had retired on getting well, and allowed the purchaser to at once make the next presentation, it would have been simony. The speaker moved—" That this Cqnference is of opinion that immediate steps should be taken to remove the scandals attending the present system of the sale and purchase of Church patronage." The Earl of Devon seconded the motion, and hi the discussion which followed the traffic in livings was strongly condemned. The motion was carried, and a rider adopted to the effect that Mr. Stanhope's bill was a step in the right direction. THE SHROPSHIRE MYSTERY EXPLAINED.—This extraor- dinary story has now assumed another phase. It will be remembered that, in consequence of a man having alleged that he saw the apparition of a woman, named Sarah Duckett. near the Copper Hole shaft, near Church Stretton, the popular idea was that the woman who was said to have mysteriously disappeared a few years since from the village, after returning from Australia, had been murdered and her, remains cast into the disesed shaft, which had since been filled up. It was, therefore, about a month back determined to reopen the shaft. After many days' labour, the bottom of the shaft was reached, but no remains found. About that time a lettenwas received by a tradesman, purporting. to be from London, and was as fellows :—" You will fail to find the body of Sarah Duckett in the Copper Hole; look in the cellar of the Toll Bar, examine the part nearest the road, in the left-hand corner. One who knows." Public attention pburo was then directed to the Toll Bar, and there was a strikingly ceeixc tdispositioneaentea t efotlolowanthaebraudpvticeteorfmitnhaetiownrittery, t notuhne another letter being received stating that Duckett was alive, and was residing at Martley, in Worcestershire, where she was living happily with her husband. The letter purported to be written by the veritable Sarah Duckett herself, but from f subsequent events it would appear that this epistle emanated rom some persons desirous of hoaxing the villagers, for last week the following letter was received in Worcester :—" St. Faith's Rectory, Eaton-under-Heywood, near Church Stret- ton.—Sarah Duckett, the missing wornan.—The relatives of the above have reason to believe that she died in Worcester in 1876. Will you kindly look over your registers for the last seven months in 1876, to ascertain if you can find the oteath entry ?—Yours truly, Holland Sandford."—Mr, Jeffery handed the letter to the superintendent-registrar, and after an investigation of the register of the year mentioned, there has been found an entry of the death of Sarah Duckett, aged 45, and she was described as being a domestic servant, and as having dieirat the Worcester Infirmary.

The preceding articles have dealt with our Land System as it is, showing the evils resulting from Primogeniture and Entail, and the obstacles and impediments in the way of "Free Land" or "Free Trade in Land," i.e., the power to sell or buy any piece of land in the United Kingdom ac- cording to the free arrangements of seller and buyer, or in the words of Mr. John Bright, spoken many years ago, Free Land means:—" The abolition of the Law of Primogeniture, and the limitation of the system of Entails and Settlement, so that 'life interests' may be for the most part got rid of, and a real ownership substituted for them. It means also that it shall be as easy to buy or sell land as to buy or sell a ship, or at least as easy as it is in Australia, and in many or in all the States of the American Union. It means that no legal encouragement shall be given to great estates and great farms, and that the natural forces of accumulation and dispersion shall have free play, as they have in regard to ships, and shares, and machinery, and stock-in-trade, and money. It means, too, that while the lawyer shall be well paid for his work, unnecessary work shall not be made for him, involving an enormous tax on all transactions in con- nection with the purchase and sale of lands and houses. A thorough reform in this matter would complete, with re- gard to land, the great work accomplished by the Anti- Corn Law League in 1846." Surely there is nothing very shocking or revolutionary, or communistic in all that. No man in the United Kingdom can have land without he honestly pays for it, nor can, any man be deprived of his land except for some distinctly public good, such as for instance the formation of a railway in which case Parliament confers compulsory powers of purchase on the railway company. We will, however, consider in detail the various points of Mr. Bright's definition, dealing only in this article with the abolition of Primogeniture, and the limitation or abolitiOn of Entail by Settlement or Will. It seems strange when we come te amine the question, that there is such a peculiar we felt by many people re. I spading any interference with "land." Some tell us, that to,meddle with the Land Laws or our present Land System, we shall endanger the constitution, the House of Lords, and the welfare of the country generally. But as Lord Carring- toe said to his tenants, "Is it possible to deny how much good has been done by the gradual reforms that have been brought about in the present reign? Is it not better that questions of this importance should be properly and reason- ably discussed on their merits, than that strong opposition should be offered to their very mention, that all the power of intellect, position, and wealth, should be brought against the idea that such laws may be improved ?" Why should land be regarded differently to any other kind of property? Why should the eldest son or other heir at law, take all the landed property of an intestate, but only be entitled to his proportionate share of personal or move- table property? The absurdity of this is easily illustrated. If a man takes a piece of ground on a lease for 10,000 years, it is leasehold property, and therefore in the event of his dying without leaving a will, would belong in the usual proportiots to his family or next of kin like cash or rail- way shares or any other kind of moveable estate. But if that land had been freehold, i.e., belonged "to him and his heirs for ever,", it would go to his heir at law absolutely. How much difference is there between a term of "10,000 years" and "for ever." Well might Oliver Cromwell 200 years ago describe the laws of England as "a tortuous and ungodly jumble." Land Law Reformers desire that on the death of a land- owner without a will, his real estate shou!cl belong, or the proceeds of it if sold, should go to hie family or next of kin, exactly as if it were the same value in money. As Mr. Bright said on another occasion, they do not want to enact the system of France by which a division of property is compelled. To force the division of property by law is just as contrary to sound principles and natural rights as to pre- vent a division, which is done by the English law. If a man choose to act the unnatural and absurd part of leaving the whole of his property to one child, we should not cer- tainly look with respect upon his memory, but we would not interfere to prevent the free exercise of his will. If, however, a man die by chance without a will, then it is the duty of the Government to set a high moral example, and Ito divide the property equally among the children of the former owner, or among those who may be said to be his I heirs, among those, in fact, who would fairly participate in his personal estate. The great objection of many to the Abolition of the Law of Primogeniture in cases of Intestacy is, that it would, as in America, gradually lead to the abolition of the Custom of Primogeniture as effected by entails and life estates. The United States Congress, so far back as 1787, abolished Primogeniture as a law in that country, and the result has been that it has never been observed there even as a custom with regard to landed property. This brings us to the second point in the programme of Free Land—the limitation or abolition of the system of life estates, found: only in this country. To go into the details of various schemes would involve too much technicality, so we will take the simple definitions of eminent men who have given the subject much study. Mr. Shaw Lefevre, M.P., explained a Bill of his as follows :—" I have aimed at prohibiting the entail or settlement of land or other pro- perty upon an eldest unborn son, or any particular unborn child of a living person, in such a way as to prevent the parent having the full power of dividing the property among his children in such proportions as he may think fit. The effect of such a restriction will not not be wholly to prevent settlements, but to compel them to take the form of the ordinary settlements of personalty, viz., to a person for life, with remainder to his children as he shall appoint; in lieu of the present form in the case of land to a person for life, with remainder to his eldest unborn son in tail," rim. Mr. Kay says:—" The best and soundest plan, however, is to give the proprietor power to leave his land to whomsoever he will, but to de- prive him at the same time of all power of preventing his successor from selling any portion of the land, and of leaving his successors any other than the whole estate in the land devised to them." In fict, the object of abolishing entail is to make every "nominal" owner a "real" owner, able to sell, lease, or do what he likes with the land, instead of, as is generally the case at prosent, tied hand and foot, neither able to make the best of the land, nor sell it to someone else,who can. - The evils resulting from limited ownerships have been re- cognised by such a staunch Tory as Lord Cairns' who, in February, 1880, introluced into the House of Lords the Settled Estates Bill, entitled "A Bill for facilitating sales, leases, and other dispositions of settled land, and for pro- moting the execution of improvements thereon," which pro- fessed to deal with the question as affecting national in- terests. It therefore burported to make sweeping changes, and to give to the tenant for life very considerable power, without the tedious and costly proceedings now necessary to obtain the consent of the Court of Chancery. But this Bill and two supplementary Bills (all since dropped by his Lordship) were like the Tory " Agricultural Holdings Act," designed to have a big gonna but little practical effect, for, in the words of Mr. Brodrick, "They would do nothing, and were deliberately framed to do nothing, towards curtailing the right of settling. The power of crippling ownership would be maintained, though artificial limbs would be amply provided to aid the life tenant in moving. The grasp of the Dead Hand would be as powerful as ever for the pur- pose of regulating the relative interests of the unborn, and the living head of the family as powerless as ever, except for the purpose of improving the family property, Of which he would remain a mere life tenant." To make the "nominal" owner the " real " owner seems reasonable enough. But it is argued that it is part of the political and social system of this country to preserve landed estates in families, that the House of Lords is principally based upon the possession of property in families, and that the law of entail and settlement is intended for that pur- pose; and it is feared that if the laws by which big estates are kept together are relaxed, the result in the long run will be the breaking up of many of the big estates, whose holders now sit in the House of Peers. But if circumstances require it, let them be broken up. Yes, but a Peer without landed property would be an anomaly. Then let him be so. There are countries in Europe where a seat in the Second Chamber requires a certain amount of wealth on the part of an here- ditary legislator, and on his not being able to comply with the requirement 'he loses his claim to a seat. Then let it be So here. If it is necessary for the continuance of our pre- sent House of Lords that the evils pointed out in previous articles as flowing from Entail should exist, then we pay too high a price for our hereditary Chamber, however much we may respect it, and its continued existence in its present form must be considered of secondary importance to the in- creased welfare of the country as a whole by improved cul- -1 tivation, and the consequent greater productiveness of the I Soil. Those are misguided and over zealous supporters of the House of Lords who identify it with the evils of our present Land System, by contending that the continuance of the latter is necessary for the preservation of the Peers, although it involves the locking up of 52,000,000 acres in a condition "of ownerless sterilising disability." It by no means fol- lows that a reform of the Land Laws would lead to the termination of our House of Lords. An hereditary Peerage is kept up in different Continental countries by having cer- tain landed property attached to the title so as to descend with it, but there is no reason whatever why such an immense proportion of the soil of the country should be so locked up, with which the Peers are in no way connected. There is nothing in "Free Land" which necessitates the breaking up of large estates, unless natural causes and spe- cial circumstances absolutely require it, in which latter cases the law should not step in to prevent it. 1 But how could Entails and Life Estates be abolished I without doing injury to vested interests? Simply enough, for there is no occasion to do it by a stroke of the pen. An Act of Parliament might be passed, and infect will be passed at no distant date, giving to every limited owner the power to sell his land out and out, subject only to two conditions; first, that the sale be an honest one; and secondly, that the purchase money be secured and applied for the benefit of all persons interested in the land itself ' • and providing that on and after a certain date, to be named in the Act, no new Entail or Settlement of land shall be legal, with the excep- tion, of course, of trusts for the widow or infant children (until they attain majority) of a testator. Mr. Gladstone has said that be is in favour of the disap- proves of the law of entail and settlement, of which he May sape- proves on economical, social, and moral grounds. behe live the live to bring about its abolition, which crowning triumph of his long life o woachievements.ebj eeobject the Primogenitnre and entail have or Wily should the law accu- mulate onlygreat keeping of land in great estates. tenant farmers, mutate land in great masses in few hands, and make it almost impossible for persons of small means, andto become possessors of land? DILLON.—At the Waterford Town Council on Tues- day, it was resolved, by a majority of 23 votes to four, that the freedom of the city be conferred on John Dillon, M.P., for services to the Irish nation. ILLerss or MR. PARNELL.—Mr. Parnell is stated to have been suddenly seized with illness while sitting in his room in Kilmainham Gaol with other suspects on Sunday even- ing. He endured much suffering for several hours from violent spasms. THE MURDER OF A DUBLIN POLICEMAN: SENTENCE OF DEATH.—At the Dublin Commission Court, on Tuesday, the trial of Peter Duff for the murder of Police-constable Daly last month was continued. Baron Dowse summed up, and the jury, after consideration, found a verdict of guilty, and sentence of death was passed. The case excited great interest. THE RANK ROBBERY IN Dninis.—On Tuesday, at the head offices of the National Bank, College Green Dublin, was received a large brown paper parcel bearing the London postmark and containing one-half of the notes and the bank post bills, stolen with the cash box from the General Post Office some days ago. The cheques, it is expected, will also be returned, being crossed "National Bank" and of no use to anyone. ANOTHER BISHOP DF,NOUNCES THE "No RENT" MANI- FESTO.—After Mass at Team Cathedral, the Archbishop delivered a most impressive sermon', in which in unsparing language he condemned the teachings of the new doctrine of "No rent" as being contrary to every principle of reli- gion, every dictate of morality, and a breach of that law which saYs "Thou shalt not steal." It was simply telling the people to be thieves and rogues. Further arrests are reported. Mr. J. M. Wall, acting editor of the Roscommon Herald, was arrested on Tuesday at Doyle; Mr. J. T. Heffernan at Kildare; Mr. Cantwell, secretary of this Attey Land League; Mr. Heart, secretary of the Castledemiett branch; two men named Gannon and Reynolds, at Cleone, county Leitrim; David Leonard and Dennis O'Connor, farmers, Janus M'Carthy, cooper, and Daniel O'Connell, tailor, at Milford. A party of over 500 men, provided with carts, assembled at Carrick-on-Shannon neighbourhood, and conveyed away the crops and other effects of a tenant and Land League piesident, which were about to be seized for non-payment of four years' rent. A local ,band paraded the neighbourhood, and when the operations were completed the tenant volun- tarily left the house. A meeting was afterwards held, when the landlord was denounced, and resolutions passed express- ing determination not to pay any rent, and to Boycott all those who do so. SERIOUS RIOTS: THREE KILLED, MANY INJURED.—A Swineford correspondent telegraphs that alarming rumours have reached there respecting the rioting at Belmullett. The people having made an attack on the barracks, the con- stabulary were ordered to fire and doing so they are reported to have killed two and injured 20 persons. Thirty arrests have been made, and military have left Ballina to quell the disturbances.—A later telegram says: A woman named McDonough, wounded during the riots at Belmallet has died of her injuries. Several others are not expected to recover. There are thus three killed and 20 wounded. Mr. John Dillon, M.P., who writes from Kilmainham Gaol, and Mr. Joseph Cowen, M.P., have each sent a con- tribution of £lO towards the testimonial to Dr. Kenny. Mr. Dillon says in his note that his present position renders it impossible for him to give public expression to his views on the action of the Government in this matter. Mr. Cowen says that amongst the many means and arbitrary acts com- mitted by the Government in the enforcement of their hate- ful coercion edicts there is nene.more mean and vindictive than their attempt, not only to punish, but to ruin Dr. Kenny. He is glad that Dr. Kenny's countrymen have re- solved to mark their appreciation of his generous and un- grudging public labours in a substantial manner. It is said that four deaths have resulted from an en- counter between the police and the people at Belmullet. Tax FIRST DECISION LIND= TEE LAND 'ACT—The Land Sub-Commissioners decided the first case under the new Land Act on Tuesday, and reduced the tenant's rent on a farm of 10 acres and odd from £8 les to six guineas. Each party was to pay bis own costs, as,the landlord had not been asked to reduce the rent Wore the original-notice was served. The effect of the decision practically amounts to fixing fair rent at £1 2s less than Poor-law valuation. The decision will induce many tenants to go into Court, and a large number of applications are expected in Castleblaney district. The decision is regarded as all the more important because two of the Commissioners are land agents and thoroughly inspected the farm. Not only was the farm generally inspected, but holes were made in different fields and the nature and quality of the sub-soil thoroughly tested. All the other cases listed to be heard here were Land League test cases, and have fallen through. The Commissioners go on to Armagh, where there are seven cases down for hearing. It is understood that Mr. Bond, the landlord in the case on Tuesday, will appeal.

An important point in the administration of the Land Act, which has occasioned much controversy, was decided on Tuesday by the Sub-Commission in Belfast. Objection was raised on behalf of the landlord that because a covenant in the lease under which the tenant formerly held, directing that certairt buildings and improvements should be kept in proper repair, these improvements were shown to be the property of the landlord, and should be considered in deter- mining the judicial rent. On the tenant's behalf, it was contended that, there being no evidence to show the im- provements had been effected by the landlord, the word of the Act, "improvements made by the tenant or his predecessors," should override any covenant a landlord might introduce into a lease. The Commissioners, after deliberation decided that the tenant was entitled to the benefit of improvements unless definite evidence was forthcoming be show that they had been made by the land- lord or his predecessors. The decision was received with loud applause.

TEE MiemoxErrs.—Of all the common plants, the life. term of which may be contracted or prolonged at pleasure, the most interesting, perhaps, Is the mignonette. As usually treated it is an annual; but we'have had Immense mignon- ette trees that have lived fifteen years, and become quite woody and venerable, the one secret of keeping them so long being the systematic prevention of seeding. Allow them to swell a fair crop of seeds, and away they go. Do not allow a single seed-pod to swell, and in all probability a mignonette plant would live as long as its owner, and then become an "heir-loom," or more likely a "white elephant," to another possessor.-11rom "Familiar Garden Flowers' for November.

--- - - TRIPE STEWED WITH BACON.—Take two pounds cf fresh white tripe, half a pound of bacon, and a calf's foot. Cut the tripe into pieces three inches square, and scald these in boiling water for five minutes. Bone the foot, scald it for ten minutes, and cut it into six or eight pieces. Divide the bacon also into pieces convenient for serving. Put the meat into a stewpan with a large bunch of parsley, a sprig of thyme, two bay-leaves, three large onions, two cloves, and a little pepper and salt, and pour in an Much broth as will cover the whole. A glassful of brandy may be added or not. Cover the saucepan closely, let its contents boil, then draw it to the side, and let them simmer very gently until the meat is done enough. Take out the herbs, skim the sauce carefully, and serve the stewed meat in a ' tureen with the sauce poured over it. Send it to the table as hot as possible. Time to stew, three hours. Probable cost, 35. 6d., exclusive of the brandy. Sufficient for five or six persons.—M-om " Cassell's Cookery" for November. Mr. Sadler appeared for the plaintiffs, who are auctionev at Uphol- I land, and on the 30th August last they were selling for Mr. Henry Forshaw, of Skelmersdale, and amongst other lots they had to sell was a field of growing oats, estimated to be i about an acre. The conditions of. sale were read by the I auctioneer (Mr. Wilcock), one of them being to the effect 'Oat if anyone made default in paying for a lot, the lot When t' ethae fimertost tphuercfihaelsdersomf adoaetsrelspie ownasilbkleed. won. 3,..ards into the corn and told them he was selling ceuthe,lalwotfober k nTohc ke e cid e fde no wd ann ti ns at hi de tfihrastt There appeared to have been some dispute 4,::ereupon Mr. Culthaw withdrew his aaa sbb about thea2°ll bidding,acre . instance to Mr. did not pay for the oats, but he made the last bid, bid, and Mr. Kerfoot said h.' would give the £9. For some reason or other the defendant . he believed the defence would be that Mr. Kerfoot thought he had bougbt another field, which rei;.lly belonged to a Mr. Valentine. As he did not pay for them the oats were re-sold on the 10th September for £7 55., and the difference between the two amounts and expenses made the amount £4 les 4d, which amount they sought to recover from the defendant, George Wilcock said he was an auctioneer carrying on business at Uphelland. On the 30th August he conducted a sale for Mr. Henry Forshaw. There were over 100 lots, and lot 55 was a field of yellow' oats. When he came to this lot he went about 20 yards into the field and said he had got a field of yellow oats of about an acre. Ultimately the. oats were knocked down to Mr. Culshaw for £9. When he gave out the purchaser's name the defendant said that gs was his bid. Culshaw then withdrew his bid, and the defendant stood to his bid and became the purchaser. They afterwards received a letter from the defendant saying he I found that a portion of the oats he had bought belonged to another man, and that the oats put down te him Were only worth £3 10s. They advertised the re-sale of the oats as a Idefaulter's lot, which was the usual course, and on the 10th I September they were sold for XI ss. By defendant: He did I not say there was a Cheshire acre and a quarter. The ditch dividing the two fields was plain to be seen, and he did not say he was selling all the oats they could see, as there were several fields besides within sight. John Makinson said he saw the defendant with respect to the payment of the account,`and defendant said they could put him in the county court as soon as they liked. By defendant: You knew very well that the next field belonged to Valentine, and that there was a ditch between the two fields. Mr. Wilcock was re-called, and in reply to His Honour as to why a deposit was not paid by the defendant, he said it was not customary to get a deposit froth people whom they knew. Richard Valentine, farmer, Skelmersdale, said he was at the sale and heard the lot put up. The auctioneer walked 20 yards on the headland and described it as a field of yellow oats, of about an acre. Between the two plots of oats was a distance of 18 feet, with a ditch two yards wide. By defendant: Wilcock did not say it was a Cheshire acre and over. Thomas Wainwright, farmer, Skelmersdale, said the auctioneer intimated that it was a field of yellew oats, about an acre, but did not say anything about a Cheshire acre. John Valentine, Philip Forshaw, and Mark Baldwin also said they were present at the sale, and that the auctioneer put the oats down as about an acre. The two fields together would have been worth from £lB to £2O. Henry Forshaw said he was the owner of these oats in question, and in reply to the defendant he denied having said the following day that he was glad that Kerfoot had been taken in, as it would pay for the drink. He should think that the oats bought by Kerfoot were well worth £9.—This being the plaintiff's case the defendant said the oats were worth £4 or £4 10s. at the out- side. When the auctioneer went into the field he said there was a Ch‘shire acre and a quarter to be sold. Culshaw , asked him if he were selling all the oats he could see and Wileock replied that he was. He went a few days after the sale and found that the two closes mentioned by the auc- tioneer were only a Cheshire acre. :ffe wrote to Mr. Makin- son, asking him to come to some agreement, and he would pay for the oats that were not cut. Mr. Makinson came on the following day and demanded the money, and witness said to him that he had never had a bill, and that he wanted a Cheshire acre. When he bad got that he would pay for them.—By Mr. Sadler: He did not know that the other field belonged to Valentine; he did not know that Valentine had land adjoining. He had no notice from Mr. Makinson that they intended to put up the lot as a "defaulter's" lot, and he did not know about it until the oats were sold.—John Culshaw, innkeeper, Skelmersdale, said he was at the sale in question. There was no ditch that he could see; all ap- peared to be level. He asked the auctioneer if the oats were in one lot, and he replied that they were, and that there was over a Cheshire acre, in fact, that there was nearera Cheshire acre and a quarter than anything else. On this assurance, he commenced bidding at the oats, and the bidding went on up to £9. None of the persons present could see that there was a division in the oats; in fact, he felt Certain that Wil- cock himself did not know there was a ditch when be was selling them.—By.Mr. Sadler: If he had known that Wil- cock was only selling one field he should not have offered more than £3 or £4 for the oats. Every witness who had been in the box bld foresworn himself with regard to what the auctioneer said when he was selling the oats.—John Rigby said he was a farmer, and was present at the sale in question, The auctioneer, when he commenced, said there was a Cheshire acre and a quarter, and afterwards that there was over a Cheshire acre.—By Mr. Sadler: He was not aware there were two fields at the time of the sale, for the auc- tioneer said he was selling all that could be seen in a straight line. Yellow oats this year had sold at £1.3 per Cheshire acre.—By his Honour :—He was under the impression that the auctioneer was selling all that could he seen, and that there was no fence whatever. It was not a low price for the two fields, considering the quality, for they were moss oats. —James Critchley and two other witnesses swore to the auctioneer stating there was over a Cheshire acre of oats in the lot to be sold.—George Wilcock was then re-called, and said, in reply to his Honour, that he knew perfectly well about the ditch, for he went over the fields with Mr. For- shaw when he took the inventory. He also went over the land on the morning of the sale and pegged out each lot and each field with a peg and number upon it. Ile never men- tioned anything about a Cheshire acre. He simply said be had got a field of yellow oats, of about an acre, and asked for a bid. Culshaw did not put any question to him that he was aware of, and he did not ask him if he were selling the whole lot. Culshaw said he would withdraw his bid and would have nothing more to do with them.—By the defen- dant: He had not told any one that he was ignorant of the land, for he knew the land quite well. He could not say whether land was taken by the Cheshire acre in this part of the country.—His Honour said the real question appeared to be whether there was a proper description of the quantity of oats sold by the auctioneer. It seemed to him that be must hold that there was a proper description; the auctioneer pointed out what he was selling, there being a boundary between the field and another. Although the boundary could not be seen, he thought it was the duty of the buyer to ascertain whether there was a boundary or not. The evi- dence was very contradictory as to whether a boundary was mentioned or not, but without finding anything upon that point it seemed to him that a buyer must take care of him- self, he must see for himself what he was buying; he should take trouble to ascertain that information. It seemed very unlikely that Mr. Wilcock should offer all the oats in sight, because it appeared there were oats in sight which were not adjoining. He must hold that the description was a suffi- cient description, and that Mr. Kerfoot should have taken care not to be deceived as to the quantity. He should, there- fore, give a verdict for the plaintiff, with costs.
