THE NOXIOUS VAPOURS QUESTION. The CLERK read a letter from Mr. Thorieley, secretary of the Liverpool Association for controlling the escape of noxious vapours from manufactories, calling the attention of the Board to the sections of the Alkali, tee., Works Regula- tion Act, which related to the appointment, powers and duties of the inspectors of works in which noxious gases Were produced. It was understood that separate inspectors Would be appointed for each of suchl arge centres of chemical manufactures as St. Helens and Widnes. It appeared to the committee of the association and they had repeatedly pressed their views upon the Local Government Board, that no inspection could be satisfactory unless the inspector resided within range of the vapours, and within easy reach of the works to be inspected—say at a distance not exceeding two miles from them. The Executive Committee of the Asso- ciation thought that the sanitary boards of the district round Liverpool affected by the noxious vapours from Widnes and St. Helens should lose no time in urging the appointment of separate inspectors for Widnes and St. Helens chemical works, and that each inspector should reside at a distace not exceeding two miles from the works to be inspected. The committee wished to impress upon the Board the necessity of immediate action.—The Caen:maw remarked that the question was one which was well worth the consideration of the Board, but he did not think they were prepared to go into it that night, beyond acknowledging the receipt of the letter and the Act. In the meantime the members should perwe the Act and consider the matter. The Act gave them authority as it were to have these in- spectors appointed ; and if they resided within a radius of two miles of the works, it would be about approaching what ehould have been done years ago.—lt was understood that the chairman's suggestion would be adopted. PROPOSED IMPROVEMENT ON THE SEWAGE FARM. A special meeting of the Highway Committee was held on the 31st October. Mr. W. Goldsworth's report advising the Board as to the drainage of the sewage farm and the purification of the sewage, having been read, it was resolved that the report should be carried out belts entirety. On being put to the vote Messrs. Jowett, Ashton, Dobell, and Pinning. ton voted in favour of the motion ; Messrs. Burnyeat, Ihler, and Rogers did not vote. A diecussion ensued as to the fund from which the money required for carrying out the work was to be raised, when Mr. Joweerr moved, and Mr. BURNYEAT seconded, that the money come out of the rates, and this was agreed to. The Clerk was instructed to write to Colonel Wyatt, Lord Sefton's agent, informing him of the Board's intention with reference to the farm, and ask him if be would under the circumstances give the necessary tiles for the purpose.—At the request of two or three members who were not on the Highway Committee, the CLERK again read Mr. Goldsworth's report. The following is Mr. Golds- worth's estimate of the col of carrying out the various im- provements :—Draining, including tiles, £lB4 140; new bye- pass, sewer, £2O; filling up holes, pits, cutting new carriers, &c.,£15 125.; boundary fences. £3O 75.; cutting new watercourse and putting down wire fences between farm and Mr. Scot- son's land, £26 15s. 6(.1 • cutting down trees and removing cross fence, £5 155.; total, £383 is. 6d.—Mr. JOWETT moved that the minutes of the committ ebe confirmed. When the sewage farm was let to the present tenant, he (Mr. Jowett) told them he would never be able to work it. Time had proved that they were not able, and never had been able, to run all the sewage on to the land as it ought to have been to avoid a nuisance. Mr. Jump had complained to the Board three or four times about sewage going into the brooks un- filtered, and he thought the improvements as shown in Mr. Goldsworth's report should be carried out. There were three or four reasons why the report should be adopted.— Mr. BURNYEAT : And what about the money ?—Mr JOWETT thought that a secondary consideration. The first considera- tion was to put the farm into such a state as it would filter and purify the sewage as it came. That was the most im- portant thing the Board had had to consider since the farm was made.—The CHAIRMAN said there was no doubt the report had been very fairly drawn up, and it was absolutely necessary something should be done to put the farm into a proper condition. The tenant had either given up, or was about to give up, possession, and it was for the Board to decide what they were going to do. The farm could net be left in its present state nor without someone to attend to it. There was no doubt the estimated cost was rather more than they expected, but it was evident from the different opinions of practical members that the improvements would have to be done. In fact, the work should have been done before. The Board would have to face it, and face it at once. It appeared the present system of irrigation was not quite sufficient, and Mr. Goldsworth's report on the point was very fair and clear.—Mr. LEvENTON observed that £383 Is. 61. was a large amount to spend upon 25 acres of land, not the property of the Hoard. It came to nearly £l6 per acre. He considered the report too good. There was ono point on which he entirely disagreed with Mr. Goldsworth, and that was that they should take the farm into their own hands. He thought it would be a very serious matter.—Mr. ,Townyx remarked that Messrs. Dobell, Ashton, and Pinnington, three of the largest farmers in the neighbourhood, had considered the report, and were of opinion that it ought tobe carried ont.—Mr. PINNINGTON seconded the motion, contending that the farm would never do any good if the improvements were not made.—ln the course of further discussion, Mr. Roouns moved that the recommendation of the committee be referred back for further consideration. Ho did not object to Mr. golds- worth's report, but he objected to the money being taken out of the rates. He considered it ought to be borrowed and the payment spread over a number of years. He, however, subsequentlg withdrew his motion.—On being put to the meeting, Messrs. Cooper, Jowett, Pinnington, and Burn- yeat voted in favour of the minutes being passed; Messrs. Rogers and Eccles voted against; and Mr. Leventon did not vote.

PRESCOT LOCAL BOARD. The monthly meeting of this Board was held on Wednes- day, Mr. Henry Fogg presiding. There were also present Messrs. A. T. Galloway, T. S. Preston, and T. Bennett ; with Mr. H. Cross (clerk), and Mr. W. Goldsworth (surveyor).

GENERAL PERPOSFS CONNIT4TEE. A meeting of this committee was held on the 31st October, when the Assist int Surveyor reported that Mr. Jas. Beesley bad received instructions from the Liverpool Corporation to put in the eater to the Hill-street and Stome-street houses without a supply, but that the work had not yet been done.—The Surveyor had written to Mr. James Ranson, surveyor for the township of Eccleston, as to the complaint of the Rev. Father Brindle, suggesting a meeting, but had received no reply.—The Assistant Surveyor reported that the cellar boavd to house in High-street had been repaired, and the °vend served with notices to take down and repair four different dangerous buildings bad complied therewith. —The minutes were confirmed.

div.head: COST OF CHESHIRE HIGHWAYS,
div.p: COST OF CHESHIRE HIGHWAYS,

The Local Government Board have issued an abstract of the receipts and expenditures on account of the highways for the year ending March, 1880, from which it appears that there are in Cheshire highway parishes 441, with a rateable value of £1,409,045; and with 288 miles seven furlongs of main roads, and 1,853 ' miles two furlongs of the ordinary highways. The receipts arnonnted to £45,218; and the expenditure to £38,893; the outstanding loans at the end of the year being £Bl7, at 4! per cent. interest. The receipts comprised £41,831 (contributions from 'parishes; £2,440 ditto county authority; £43 ditto expired turnpike trusts; £147 on account of extraordinary traffic; and .£757 from other sources. The expenditure included £8,904 for repairs of main roads; £25,321 ditto of ordinary highway roads; £l5O ditto existing turnpike roads; £1,840 for im- provements ; £420 for law charges; £2,700 for salaries; £222 for repayments of loans; £64 for interest on loans; and £482 for other expenses.

DATEESBERY district comprises 23 highway parishes, of the rateable value of £138,440; and with 11 miles 2 fur- longs of main roads, and 139 miles 7 furlchlgs of ordinary highways. The receipts were £2,811, and the expenditure £2,146. The former comprised £2,702 contributions from parishes; £2B ditto county authority; and £Bl from other sources. The expenditure included £226 for repairs of main roads; £1,408 ditto ordinary highways; £305 for im- provements; £3 for law charges; £165 for salaries; and £39 for other expenses. EAST EDDISIIVEY district comprises 20 highway parishes, of the rateable value of £55,192; and with 19 miles 5 fur- longs of main roads, and 84 miles 3 furlongs of ordinary highways. The receipts amounted to £1,705, and the ex- penditure to £1,347. The former comprised M,550 contri- butions from parishes- £134 ditto authority; 43 on account of extraordinary traffic; and £Bl from other sources. The expenditure included £364 for repairs of main roads; £778 ditto ordinary highways; £165 for salaries; and £4O other expenses. ' WEST EDDISBERT district comprises 39 highway parishes of the rateable value of £114,900; and with 9 mile:3 2 fur- longs of main roads, and 158 miles 2 furlongs of ordinary highways. The receipts amounted to £4,379, and the ex- penditure to £4,020. The former comprised 4,182 contribu- tions from parishes; £lB2 ditto county authority; and £l5 from other sources. The expenditure included £436 for repairs :of main roads; £2,849 ditto ordinary highways; £333 for improvements; £l2B for salaries; £lB9 for repay- ments of loans; £35 interest on loans; and £5O other ex- penses. div.head: SPECIAL REPORTS OF TEE HOSPITAL COTT/LIME.
div.p: SPECIAL REPORTS OF TEE HOSPITAL COTT/LIME.

At a meeting of the committee for making provision for temporary hospital, held on the 11th October, the Medical Officer and Surveyor reported on what had been done by them, and it was resolved that Chorley-house be engaged at a weekly rent of 55., and fitted up to receive patients.—A deputation, consistingof Messrs. Case and Hewitt, attended with a memorial, to which 168 persons had appended their signatures or marks against the expense of a hospital as unnecessary and against the site selected, and after explana- tion from the chairman, medical officer, and surveyor, they were unable to give any satisfactory reasons in favour of the memorial, and retired.—lt was ordered that the head nurse, recommended by the medical officer, be employed at £1 is. a week, travelling expenses, board, and lodging, and 15s. for disinfection of clothes. If engaged for more than 13 weeks, at £2 2s. per week at the expiration of the 13 weeks. That the nurse and her husband lately employed by the Ashton Local Board be employed—the former at 10s. per week, and the latter at 20s. per week, and their board and lodging. That the medical professional men of the town be written to afford every facility to the Board and its officers in their exertionf to stamp out the epidemic.—At another meeting of the committe, on the 14th October, the Surveyor re- ported that the Ashton Local Board nurse and her husband were unable to accept the post, and the Medical Officer re- ported that he was making efforts to secure some one in their place.—ln answer to the Chairman, the SURVEYOR stated that there were no patients in the kospital as yet. The nurse had been engaged in visiting the houses infected with the fever, and giving the occupants information as to the best mode of disinfecting and washing clothes. REGISTRAR'S REPORT.—DEATHS FROM SCARLET FEVER. The REGISTRAR'S report showed that during the month of October there had been 17 births in the district as compared with 29 in the corresponding period of last year. The deaths numbered 20 as against 13 in the corresponding month of last year. Death-rate per thousand, 3739 ; last year, 26.04. Ten deaths had occurred from scarlet fever. Thirteen of the deaths were those of children under five years of age.—The reporters werce requested to notice the fact that the fatal cases of scarlet fever were confined to children entirely. There was not a single death of an aclulf 11 person from the disease.

div.head: PROTEST AGAINST THE PROVISION OF A FEVER HOSPITAL.
div.p: PROTEST AGAINST THE PROVISION OF A FEVER HOSPITAL.

The CLERK read a letter which he had received from Mr. James Hewitt, enclosing copy of resolutions passed at a public meeting of the ratepayers of Prescot, protesting against the action of the Local Board in taking Chorley- house to be used as a fever hospital as being entirely un- necessary, and condemning the house as being totally unfit for the purpose.—ln reply to a remark by the Chairman, Mr. PRESTON said he did not see the Board could do anything respecting the resolutions passed at the public meeting. The meeting should have been held before the Board took action in the matter. The Board could not undo their work now.— After some conversation the further consideration of the matter was adjourned to a meeting to be held to•night (Friday).

div.head: ALTERLTIONS TO THE SVZILN INN.
div.p: ALTERLTIONS TO THE SVZILN INN.
- The SURVEYOR submitted plan of alterations to the Swan Inn, Derby-street, add the same was approved subject to the drainage being carried out to the satisfaction of the Surveyor.

div.head: MARKETS.
div.p: MARKETS.

LIVERPOOL CORN, THURSDAY.—The market for wheat and flour was steady to-day, and a moderate huffiness was done at late rates. Indian corn was firmly held; sellers asked 5s 10fd per cental for new mixed American. Beans were un- changed. Peas and oats quiet. Oatmeal in moderate request at late prices. LIVERPOOL PROVISIONS, THURSDAY.—Beef slow of sale at the quotations. Pork dull, and easier in value. flacon: Demand for home moderate. Hams dull of sale. Shoulders date at late prises. Lard easier with lower advices from America. Cheese: Fine sells steadily. Butter dull of sale. Tallow remains with- out botable alteration. MANCHESTER COTTON, THURSDAY.—The business seems to have been done, as the phrase runs here, and buyers and sellers are alike indifferent to further transactions of more than retail magnitude; prices are, therefore, very evenly balanced and the indications given by cotton figures and forecasts are too vague and conflicting to have any definite effect upon this market.

LIVERPOOL COTTON. TEURSDAY.—Spot: There is a better Inquiry than yesterday, and a good business is concluded. Prices of American are firm. The quotations for Brazila are raised 1-16 d. Other growths are unchanged. Sales 12,00 bales, including 1,000 on speculation or for export. In pot since ThursdAy 54,202 bales, including 42,415 American. Futures opened firmly at 1-32 d advance, but there are now sellers at the advance. CORK BUTTER,sTHUBSDAY.—Ordinary: Firsts. 117 i; seconds. 1093 ; thirds, lu0s; fourths, 98s; fifths 765. Superfine, 116 s ; fine mild, 127 s ; mild, 115 s. Salt Kegs Firsts, 120 s ; seconds IOSS ; thirds, 1023; fourths, Ms. Number of firkins in the market, 12,188.

' gamble: mn a you ng I 'ARE GALLANT YOUNG 31A24.--JOUlt I man, was charged with committing a b.'sath of tb4 Y fighting with a man whose name was unium wv.—lt ten ?eared from the evidence of a police con that t atahlo t en o'clock on Saturday night defendant, wit2lout lv"l.re- ceived any provocation, struck a roan on the treas.. w"." atick.—A. young married woman stepped into the a,,,x' and eck said that a young man placed his arm around her 1, when defendant interfered, and protected her. She did L. ID' see the defendant strike at all, but he might have done without being seen by her.—Defendant having endeavoured to protect the woman, the case was dismissed. HAWKING WITHOUT CERTIFICATES.--JAK Burgess was charged with hawking his labour without a license on Tuesday afternoon. An old license, dated November, 1879, was found upon him. Defendant said he had a wile and seven children, and had been sick for nine mcnths, and that his family, who lived at Widnes, did not know where he was. He was fined Is. and costa, altogether 3s. 6d.—Frank Mellan, of Earlestown, was fined Is. and costs for hawking clothes props on Wednesday in Parr. FRIGHTENING A GAMEKEEPER.—Tbornas Richards was charged with having, on the 23rd Marlast year, threatened to beat and illtreat James Pimbley, a gamekeeper, at Rijn- hill and Bickerataffe, in the service of Lord Derby.—The gamekeeper and a watchman were on land in Rainford about four o'clock on the morning in question, when tney saw defendant, who had a gun in bighead. The gamekeeper accosted the defendant, saying that he was "early enouAh for thee, Tom, this morning." Defendant said that if the gamekeeper touched him or came near to him he would "shoot his entrails oat." The gamekeeper and watcher, whose name is Roughley, were afraid to approach, lest defendant should carry out his threats, and the defendant walked away. Defendant disappeared from this part of the country, and a suminons was taken out against him for poaching, and he was convicted in a heavy penalty. De- fendant recently visited this district, and the money having been paid he was apprehended under a warrant on the pre- sent charge.—Prisoner denied that he cocked the gun at the gamekeeper, and said that if he intended to do any harm to him he should not have run out of the country.—Colonel Gamble said they had a little difficulty in dealing with the case, because seventeen months had elapsed since the threats were alleged to have been made. There could be no question that the prisoner did threaten the gamekeeper, but as seventeen months had gone by the magistrates could not bind him ever.—The case was dismissed.

MONDAY.—Before Messrs. W. Blinkborn ana R. Pen- nington, jun. ASSAULT UPON THE POLlCE.—Timothy Fynn, of Parr, was charged with being drank and disorderly, and assaulting P.C. James Malenry.—Complainant said that at a quarter- past eleven on Saturday night prisoner was drunk, shouting and swearing in Liverpool-road. A large crowd assembled round him, and he refused to go away. Witness took him into custody, and whilst on the way to the Town Hall pri- soner kicked him severely several times on the legs.—, Prisoner had been convicted 43 times previously, and this was the sth time this year.—Prisoner, who pleaded guilty to being drunk and disorderly, and expressed his ignorance of committing the assault, was sent to gaol for a month with hard labour on the first charge, and one month with hard labour for, the assault, one sentence to take effect after the other.

THE OAKES CASE—Mr. Swift, jun., said tbat John Oakes, husband of Mary Oakes, of the Rifle Corps Inn, Duke-at., was some time ago charged with committing an assault upon his wife, but the case was then adjourned, as it was evident the defendant was not in his right mind. He had been taken to an asylum, and the case bad been adjourned several times to see what tarn events might take. The condition of Oake's mind had not improved, but had gone worse; and Mr. Swift asked that the summons might be withdrawn, andlhe license transferred to his wife, Mary Oakes.—This was done.

A VIOLENT MAN.—Henry Brogan, Peter-street, was charged with assaulting P.C. Mitchell on Saturday night, and assaulting his wife Elizabeth Brogan.—P.C. Mitchell said that he was sent for by a person to go to prisoner, who was ill-using his wife. He went, and found prisoner's wife crying very bitterly, and prisoner was using very filthy language to her. Witness told him that if he continued to abuse her he should have to report him. Wit- ness then left, but he had, not proceeded far when ahoy ran after him and said that his father was killing his mother in the house. Witness went back, and saw the prisoner tearing his wife's hair. Witness pulled prisoner off his wife and took him to the Town Hall. On the way prisoner was very violent, and knocked witness and kicked him two or three times. Witness called for assistance, which soon came, and the prisoner was taken to the police station and locked up. —Elizabeth Brogan stated that her husband entered the house and said that his mother had told him to leave his wife and six children. Witness retorted by saying, " Yes, and a nice mother she is to want thee to leave me with six children." Prisoner thereupon flew into a rage and com- menced to abuse witness both with hands and tongue, and was only stopped short .in his violent occupation by the timely appearance of the pliceman. She had been married to the 'prisoner "twelve years come this Christmas."— Prisoner on the first charge was fined 103 and costs or 14 days, and on the other charge £1 and costs or one month's imprisonment.

THE WEIGHTS AND MEASURES ACT.—Michael McGee,! Liverpool-street, was charged with having a measure in his I shop that was not stamped, and also with having measures I that were Lot of the denomination of the Board of Trade standard.—Superintendent Johnston said that on Tuesday, the 25th ult., he visited the shop of defendant, who was a provision dealer and seller of milk and beer. When witness went to the beer department he asked defendant to show him his measures, and the jugs produced were exhibited to him as pint measures. Superintendent Johnston produced a pint measure, which was very old and corroded, and which defendant had shown to him. He could not say that it was used for trade purposes. Defendant might have avoided that prosecution, because on the 29th September he (Supt. Johnston) visited the house, and when defendant showed him the jugs he cautionea him, and told him to provide himself with proper measures.—Defendant said it was not a common thing to measure beer with standard measures.— Superintendent Johnston said that defendant had been con- victed of selling drink during prohibited hours.—Mr. Blinkhorn : We see no excuse, considering that you have had fair warning, for your not providing yourself with pro- per measures; and you will be fined £1 and costs (13s), ti e first summons to be withdrawn.—Bridget Costello was summoned for having an unjust scale in her shop.—Supt. Johnston said defendant was a poor woman and kept a coal yard. The sheet of iron produced was found in the scale On the customers' side, and was, no doubt, intended to make up for some hole. It was, however, three-quarters of a pound against the purchaser.—Fined 2s 6d and costs. DESERTING HIS FaiktiLr.—A man named Greenall was charged with running away from his wife and family, thereby leaving them chargeable to the common fund of the Prescch Union.—Mr. S. H. Hartley. clerk to the Prescot Board of Guardians, said he was instructed to ask their worships to inflict the fullest penalty—three months' im- prisonment. The cases of neglect and desertion of family were on the increase in the Prescot Union, and they wished to make an example of offenders. Defendant was formerly a pattern maker and could earn 355. a week at Messrs. Pil- kington's, but from his intemperate habits he was obliged to leave, and he took his tools with him. They had had very great difficulty in ascertaining his whereabouts, but they at last found out that he was residing about five miles from Glasgow.—Frederick Augustus Harrison, relieving officer, said that the prisoner was the husband of Ellen Greenall, 'who was in receipt of relief. He apprehended prisoner at a place five miles from Glasgow, where he was working as a labourer at an ironworks. He brought him back to St. Helens. Prisoner would leave this district not later than the 22nd August, as the wife then got relief, and had con- tinusd. in receipt of relief from that time.—Prisoner said that his wife kaew where he had gone to, and she was aware of his intention nine or ten tlays before he went.—Mr. Hartley said prisoner's wife did not' know where prisoner had gone to.—Mr. Spencely said Mr. Hartley should not say that, as he could not prove it.—Prisoner was sent to prison for a month.

Tiarr.—Fanny Wareing was charged with stealing an ulster coat from a shop in Church-street, the property of Mr. Martin, draper.—Francis Beresford, assistant to Mr. Martin, said he saw the ulster safe in the shop on the 26th tilt. It Was worth fis. He missed it at 20 minutes to six the same evening. Prisoner did not buy the ulster, neither did he sell it to anybody.—Emma Jones, wife of James Jones, Liverpool-street, said the prisoner lodged at the same house as she and her husband. About nine o'clock on the evening of the 28th, prisoner said to the "Mrs. of the house" that she had an ulster which she should like to sell. The "Mrs. fearing to get into trouble advised the prisoner to give the ulster up, and she did give it up to a Prisoner, who who pleaded guilty, was tined £1 and costs, or one month's imprisonment.

A NEGLECTED Grnr..—Hannah Waterworth (13), a very dull and uncared-for looking girl, was charged with stealing two buns and three cakes, the property of James LYon, grocer and provision dealer, Glover-street.—Mrs. Lyon mid that on Friday evening she found the prisoner behind ho shop counter with a bag in her hand. She asked the girl what she was doing there, and the prisoner .replied "Nothing," but subsequently said that she had becm In lying some bread. She searched the bag, and found if I two buns and three cakes, which belonged to her, a. some bread which she 'did not recognise as belonging t.. Supt. Johnston said the girl had been two days in prison for ,stealing bread before. The girl appeared to be badly cared for.—The father of the girl said he looked after her as much as he could but lie could not be responsible for her when she was out of doors.—Mr. Blinkhorn: But she would not steal bread if she was not told to do it.—The father said the ' girl had always been caught before she had got the bread home. He would be thankful if they would sent her to a reformatory.—Mr. Johnston: Ah, that's what he wants.- -Mr. Blinkhorn: You have evidently neglected her at home, and the best thing will be to send her too reformatory for fire years where she will better cared for. You will understand that yeti will have to contribute towards her support.
THURSDIT.—Before his worship the Mayor (Alderman

Harrison). ALLEGED ROEI3E/IL—Ann Barns was charged with steal- ing three pairs of boots from the shop door of Henry Alle*, in the Market-place, on the 28th Octoker.—Remanded.-4- William Winrow, alias John Spellman was charged with bnrglarionsly entering the shop of William Browd,

Exchange-street, and stealing therefrom 11Ibs. weight Of beef. —The lock was forced from its place, and the shop entered.—P.C. Groarke apprehended the prisoner, and a large iron file was found upon him. P.C. Groarke said the file mied have been used in forcing open the lock.—Prisoner %aid he did not use the file at all; he "punched" the door tpen.—He was committed to take his trial at the Sessions. A DRUNKEN Pim—John and Sarah Dunn, husband and wife were charged with being drank.—After the husband had wife, locked up, his wife went to the station, said she would have her husband out or be locked up herself, and threatened to smash the windows of the ,Town Hall. She was then locked np.—The man was fined ss. and costs, or seven days; and the woman was diQcharged on promising to 'nye the town.
sr. LTTE,LENS LITEIi:ARY & SCIENTIFIC ASSOCIATION. FLORAL DEFENCES

ing the members of the above associat. ion- On Tues eve.. 'nteresting and instructive lecture on day t were treated to an to.. ” s Rev. H. H. Higgins, of Itinhill "Floral Defences by M. . 'mit of the association OW. R.. In the absence of the presto, -lied the chair: There waif a Pilkington) Dr. Ricketts octalpresent,several latlies.—The good company present, incluelh.,74.•at a market gardener LECTURER commenced by saying ta, . wishing to improve his strain of cum-an:era, frequently pro.,a ceeds to select a flower from a cucumbe." Plant in s pollen _from the new ne' points finer than his own, and to place. flower on the stigma of a flower belonging to the plant already in his frame. The flower matures, yle2ding a cucumber apparently of the old sort. He, however/ ours the seed from this cucumber, and from them he expects; to grow plants bearing better cucumbers. He is often succesc- tut : be finds that pollen from the new flower has done its work, and the gardener forhis pains now has finer cucumbers for seed and for the market. This was called cross-fertilise- don. The lecturer said that what the gardener does for his cucumbers, nature does for many of her flowers. She takes the pollen from a distant flower, and hringit it home to the stigma of a flower of the same kind, but ust growing on the same plant, with the result that the seeds*getstronger than they would have been if the flower hadMlertilief by pollen from another flower on the samerstettr..a-Mr. Theiia proceeded to stato that nature carri ed poll en frotrikdistan v thewind, and mentioned the fact thht from a branch of halel bearing catkins a cloud of yellow dust would be carried away by the wind. Some of this pollen would fall on the'rlay crimson flowers borne on the twigs of hazel bushes faraway, and the twigs would produce fine clusters of ripe nuts when the proper time arrived. All catkin bearing and cone-bearing trees, together with grasses and sedges, were fertilised chiefly by the wind. Tennyson referred to the profusion of pollen dust thrown off by the yew tree in his Holy Grail near the commencement of the poem :- 6. 0 brother. I have seen this yew tree smoke. Spring after spring for half a hundred years."

After speaking of pollen being conveyed by Water, be went on to say that pollen was most frequently conveyed by insects. A humble bee banded with black and gold, with his muzzle deep down amongst the purple florets of a large thistle head, had•been seen by most people. The bee was helping himself and the plant at the same time—himself to the nectar which he loved, and the plant to tha pollen of another like flower previously visited, thereby dusting his limbs and coat with life germs of priceless value to the thistle on which he was feeding. Not all insects were alike suited to fertilise every kind of flower. Some plants would invite a butterfly, others a night flying moth, whilst not a few were willing to be "at home" to a variety of flying visitors, the only stipulation being that they must be of suitable size, shape, and habits to bring with them pollen of the right kind, and to leave it in the right place. Woodlice, ants, plant lice, and earwigs loved honey besides butterflys and bees, and were always hungry. They were unfitted in many ways to fertilise most flowers, and no pollen would be brought, consequently the floral life of the flower would have been spent in vain. Hence there was the necessity sfor flowers to have guards suitable for keeping away unwelcome visitors,—in other words "Floral defenzes. The lecturer said that a creeping thing would find great difficulty in getting down the slender neck of the flower, and. in crossing the incurved edges of the three white outer seg- ments of the perianth of the snowdrop. It would then have to surmount the green-tipped segments at the base of which on the inner side, the honey was. A bee had no such diffi- culty. Dr. Whewell had spoken of the pensile position of the snowdrop flower as conducing to its advantage. The nodding of the flower was occasioned by the force of gravity overcoming the elasticity of the flower stalk. This was very true, very beautiful, and very sacred. (Applause.) Science told them how it was that such a position was good for the flower. It kept away enemies and prometed cross-fertilisa- tion. "One of the most simple kinds of floral defence," the lecturer said, "is used when the nectar, pollen, and pistil of a flower are shut up in a box with a spring lid, too strong to be raised by little impertinent wanderers, but easily lifted by a friend. Such a box you have often seen in the Bawer of the garden Snap-dragon Antirrhinum majus. No ant or other small insect can raise the lid, but when a lusty bee comes, be shoves his head under the lid and shortly, almost his whole body disappears. Having finished to his satisfac- tion the little business on which he came, he backs out, his legs and body dusted with the yellow pollen from the arthers ready to be carried to another flower." (Applause.) The reason why an ant was unwelcome was because its polished armdur was not suited for carrying pollen, and then what a journey it would have to take before it could reach a snap- dragon on the other aide of the garden or on another flower bed. The lecturer gave several other instances of floral de- fence, such as glandular hairs, circlets of hair within the tube of the flower, the stiff hairs in the lower lobe of the fox-glove, and went on to say that the history of flowers pointed to a theory of development which had been charged with robbing our love of flowers of all its poetry, and of half its capacity for affording delight. Surely it had afforded new resources within:the reach of every willing observer. The chairman mentioned that the name of the fox-glove arose from the fact that the flowers had been considered to be in some way connected with the fairies or "good folks "as they were called; hence the name folksglove which had been corrupted into fox-glove. Speaking of evolution, Mr. Hig- gins said that although the flowers were not conscious of the extraordinary part they took in the economy of nature, and were not endowed with mind and reason still there was in- telligence and reason, and must be some where at the back of the plant. (Applause.) Darwinism did not rob us of the love for flowers and of the poetry of that love. The CHAIRMAN said he had been very much edified by the lecture; his admiration of nature was more intensified, and he would be able to study flowers in future with greater enthusiasm than he bad done before. Dr. Menem.. said the lecture seemed to him to be above criticism, and it would be like an attempt to paint the lily to try to add something to the lecture. The lecturer seemed to approach science in a very beautiful way; and the admirable admixture of scientific facts with a poetic grace gave a charm to it; which, of course, without imgina- tion and fancy it could not give. The lecture was most clear and picturesque, and it seemed to him (Dr. McNicoll) that under the able treatment of the lecturer the flowers were in- vested with a peculiar charm, and that they lived the lives of fairies, or were the abode of fairies. M long as Mr. Hig- gins gave them his annual visit, and he became their guide through the regions of Nature, he would have a large and appreciative audience. He moved that the best thanks of the meeting be git•en to Mr. Higgins for his instructive paper. (Applause ). The Rev. R. J. Wenn said he could only echo what had had been said by Dr. McNicall in his characteristic fashion. For the lecture to which they bad just listened they were greatly indebted to Mr. Higgins, and also to his family for the handsome diagrams with which the lecture had been illustrated. (Applause.) A thought struck him whilst Mr. Higgins was speaking that those insects of which they had heard, showed them clearly that "nothing moves with aimless feet," but that everything has its purpose. If the facts were looked into they would se‘. that nothing was without a purpose; and there were still many things that were not yet fully revealed to them. (Applause). Mr. WHITE said it had been his privilege to attend one or two botanical lectures in Manchester, but he might say without exaggeration that the lecture they bad just listened to combined fertility of expression with poetical illustration more than any lecture Ile had listened to. The facts had been most distinctly and clearly set before them, and had been free from many technicalities, which had puzzled him greatly in thee sort of lectures. They had ' not had jaw- breaking and Latinised names, but the case had been clearly put before them. He was extremely pleased to listen to one remark which had reference to the theory of evolution not being incompatible with the idea of a mind working be- hind. (Hear, hear.) Whether they had accepted or re- jected the theory of evolution, still there mast be a first cause. Whether they believed in the evolution theory Or in instantaneous creation, there was a first cause behind either. He seconded with the greatest pleasure the vote of thanks. Mr. W. GAMBLE supported the motion, and in doing ea. he could not help feeling that in a botanical point of view the audience was not vary appreciative. Of course, St. Helens was not a town well suited for the study of botany. (Laughter). lie took a delight in pretty flowers, tot he hardly knew the names of more than about twenty plants. He had received great pleasure from the lecture, and_ he most heartily supported the motion. Mr. Higgins having replied, the meeting terminated.

div.head: YEESOOT HIGHWAY BOARD.
div.p: YEESOOT HIGHWAY BOARD.

• The usual monthly meeting of the Prescot HighwitY Board ivas held at the Board-roern, Derby-street, en Tues- day, Mr. W. L. Evans, 32., presiding. There were also present Messrs. R. Tvrer (Knowsley), M. Lowe (Rainhilb, and T. Whitfield (Bola), with Mr. H. Cross (clerk), and Mr. W. Goldsworth. (surveyor.) _

FINANCIAL.—THE S'URVEYOR'S EXPENDITURE. It appeared that there was due to the treasurer in respect of over-draught on the bank and unpaid cheques the sum of £556 14s. 3d. Resolved, that the clerk to the overseers of the various townships to pay up the calls last made, and that the waywardens should see them and urge immediate pay- ment of the respective amounts.—The Surveyor snbmitted his statement of expenditure for four weeks, from September 29th to October 27th, which was as follows:—Bold, £lO les ; Knowsley, £7 2s. 4d.; Rainhill, £2O 7s. Ad.; Whiston, £l3 13s, ed.; team labour, £27 16s. Btd. new materials. £36 178, ; incidentals, £3 2s. 11d.; total, £ll9 17s. 04-d., for which a cheque was signed in favour or the Surveyor.—A long discussion took place respecting .the em- ployment of old men at full wages and the providing of cottages for labourers, but nothing was done in the matter.

3RD ANNUAL SALE FOR THE ARTlSTS.—Organised in their be- half by the Secretary in London to the Belgian Commission of the International Exhibitions bf 1871 to 1874. A collection of PICTURES and WATER-COLOUR DRAWINGS exceed- ing in excellence and variety the well-known collections of the two past years, and composed exclusively of the contri- butions of artists whose works are regularly admitted and sought after at the Royal Academy, the Paris Salon, and the leading exhibitions of England and the continent. The pictures and drawings are of the highest standard of excel- lence, and many of the choicest and most remarkable works which have been seen in recent exhibitions are comprised In this collection. English artists are largely represented, and particular interest will be attracted to the great number of works in this section by men of rising fame, The conti- nental portion presents a rich variety, and many of the best known artists in Europe have contributed to it. The works in most instances are from the walls of important ex- hibitions, many being diploma pictures, which have either been honourably mentioned or have procured medals or other distinctions for their authors when exhibited in the Paris Salon, Berlin Academy, Belgian Government Exhibitions of Brussels and .Antwerp, the German Academics of Munich and Dusseldorf, Milan Exhibition, Ac.—By MESSRS. BRANCH AND LEETE, on WEDNESDAY, THURSDAY, and FRIDAY, the 16th, 17th, and 18th inst., at One o'clock each day, in the HANOVER ART GALLERIES, PICTURES and WATER-COLOUR DRAWINGS, forming a most beautiful, interesting, and varied collection of over 400 works. The range of subject to be found in the collection is almost unlimited. A large proportion consists of very fine figure pictures of historical, classical, military, and other subjects ; exquisitely painted interiors ; little gems of genre painting in domestic and humourous subjects ; street scenes of present and past interest; landscapes of the most varied subjects, and representing favourite views in many of the most interesting spots in Europe. The following are some of the principal pictures : P. C. Gilardi's humourous work, 'The Bachelors"; Coessin's admirable picture from the Paris Salon, "A Pleasure Party in 1795 " ; a beautiful poetical landscape by Henri Pie ron. " Morn- ' ing Mists at Hurley-on-Thames "; W. Kreling's important figure-subject, "The Love Token"; one of Carl Rodeck's grand forest sunsets: a fine lake scene by A. Norman. "The Roms- daffiord, Norway ;" two excellent specimens of still life by Falchetti ; "Episodes of the Franco-German War," by Chr. Sell; a grand work by J. Bauck, "A Moonlight Solitude ;" L. Kratke's important picture, "The Heir to the Throne ;" a highly interesting work by A. Brain), and many equally im- portant pictures by the following well known artists : M. Ten Kate J Caraud F. THE SHOCKING ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.—On Satur- day, Anthony Brannon, 9, Caroline-street, died from injuries he met with on the 15th ult., through falling into the fire at his own home. It appears that deceased was a chemical labourer' but, owing to illness, he had not for some time attended his work regularly. On the 15th ult., whilst alone in the front room of his own house he fell into the fire, and was very badly burnt. He was attended by Dr. Cooper up to the day of his death. ST. PATRICK'S AMATEURS AT WIDNES.—The local dramatic company known as St. Patrick's Amateurs gave a performance in the Drill Hall, Widnes, on Monday evening. The company, as its name indicates, is one that has been formed among the Catholics of Widnes ; atkil the performance was held on behalf of the new schools in Newtown, a description of which has already appeared in The Examiner The schools are built to accommodate 600 pupils, and the. cost of their erection at £t,300. Something has already been done towards meeting this expenditure, but there still remains a deficiency. The pieces chosen were the popular drama "The Octoroon; or, Life in Louisiana," and the farce "The Goose with the Golden Eggs." Both of the pieces were creditably performed and well received, the exciting situations of the drama and the broad inn of the farce seeming to be equally appreciated by the audience, which was a numerous one. ST. JOHN'S PRESBYPERIAN CHURCH, WARRINGTON.— The Rev. James Lees, of Manchester, preached the anniver- sary sermons in aid of the Sanday school connected with the above church on Sunday last. There was a large con- gregation in the evening, and the collections for the day realised £lO. ST. Ewes RAND OF HOPE SOCIETY gave an enter- tainment consisting of glees and recitations in the Heath- side Infant schoolroom, on Monday evening. Favourable progress is being made by this branch of the Church of England Temperance Society, upwards of 400 members having joined the Band of Hope. LOYAL ORANGE INSTITUTION FUNERAL FUND WAR - RINGTON.—The quarterly meeting of No. 2 district, group 10, of the Orange Order, was held on Saturday evening. I3ro. M. Woodward, senior, occupiedthe chair, and Bro. John Cox the vice-chair. The officers of the funeral fund, pro- posed and seconded at a previous meeting, were duly installed for the ensuing twelve months. An interesting account of the working of the society was given by the secretary (Bro. Croley), who stated that after paying all demands since its formation in 1871 the society had at the presmt time cash in the bank and in the treasurer's hands amounting to i'7o. Other members of the brotherhood took part in the very pleasant meeting. BISHOP RYLE AND THE NEW BURIAL Ac.—Bisbop Ryle deserves credit for the sensible advice which he has given to his clergy in regard to the new Burial Act. He always thought the grievance to be imaginary; but the law has been altered, "by the almost universal demand of the laity, and it is childish and ungracious t 9 Waste ttic” in use- less complaint." So he reconnnends willing obediena on the part of all loyal clergymen, for the sake of peace and charity. He counselled them to allow the Act to work as pleasantly as possible, and to avoid all friction and collision. He advised them to "nicks no difficulties about the use of the parish bier, or the tolling of the bell," and even to per- mit the burial of non-parishioners in accordance with the Act. We should be glad if this good advice were adopted 'by the clergy, not only in the diocese of Liverpool, but everywhere; but, unfortunately, we almost every week re- ceive information, which shows that some of the clergy are still showing their soreness at the passing of the Act by , ill-natured and almost spiteful acts, of which they ought to be ashamed.—The Liberator. SUPPOSED INCENDIARY FIRE IN WARRINGTON.—About two o'clock on Thursday morning, P.C. Rowbottom observed a fire in Wharf-street, and proceeding there discovered the storage shed of Mr. Spann, wheelwright, to be on fire. He at once aroused the inmates of the house adjoining, and the 'Deputy Superintendent of the Fire Brigade (P.S. Johnson) accompanied by Inspector Singleton and P.S. Spinks were quickly on the spot with, the new reel from the police station and one from the engine station. It was found impossible, however, to save the shed, and the window frames and the doer of the house adjoining were burnt away. The furniture was fortunately removed from the rooms. In the shed were two new coaches, and the damage is stated to be about £lOO. Only the shed is insured. The tire is believed to be the woik of an incendiary.
LOC AL NOTES.

The distribution of prizes to the children attending Holy Trinity Day Schools, Runcorn, passed off remarkably well: Tho Public Hall was well filled, and Mr. Clarke Aspinall, of Liverpool, presented the prizes and certificates in a manner which won the hearts of all, and especially of the fair sex. He had an apt word for eight out of every ten of the large

number of little ones who presented themselves before him. During the course of an interesting speech, Mr. Aspinall sketched the rapid growth of the schools since 1879, when Mr. Annet took charge. At that time 155 boys were in attendance, against 215 at the present time, and the fees had risen from £75 to about £l5O. The Government grant had • also advanced from £77 lls. to £175 in the present year. .Under such favourable conditions, Mr. Aspinall evidently considered himself quite justified in speaking in terms of very high praise of the schoolmaster, who will no doubt prove quite alive to the fact that his very BUCCB3S in Runcorn may constitute a danger in itself. Mr. Annett has been so successful in regard to the number of children he has lately passed at the examination by Her Majesty's Inspector that it would not surprise me to hear of some of his competitors in the scholastic field liccoming a little jealous when the Book of Books says " Who is able to stood before envy r

The number of street loafers in Widnes at night time has become a sonsce of considerable nuisance to respectable fcot passengers, to some of whom time is money; and it is gratifying to see that Superintendent Barker is determined to summons all who in future are found obstructing the footpath. It is a pity that some of the rich men of our religion denominations cannot devise some means which would prove a counter attraction to the public-house and the street corners for the scores of loungers in a town like Widnes, who appear to be utterly at a loss know where to go. I also often wonder what the temperance people are think- ing about that they do not provide speakers who could address numbers of these men, who seem to have no object in life save that of diving as far down as possible into the mysterious depths of their large trousers' pockets, and passing the time as b9st they can in sucking short pipes. The field in Widnes Is certainly ripe for the temperance harvest, and there are hundreds of homes] amongst the lower classes of the town which are rendered miserable by the devotion of the husbands to drink. There is, however, no Father Matthew, who is determined to devote all his energies to the work of trying to win some of these men to the paths of wisdom, whose ways are pleasantness.
I baveoften been amusedwhen attendingtbe annual meet-

ting of the Runcorn branch of the British and Poreign Bible Society, in the ante-room of the Public Hall, to sees notice in large letters •' No smoking alloyed." Are the Public Hall Company members of the Anti-Tobacco Society, or are they suspicous that some of ". the white-tie gentlemen who attend this gathering will be inclined to take a whiff, to save them- selves from that effect of the rather prosy speeches ? I should advise that either the notice be reprinted, and made to look presentable, or removed to the lumber room.

The proposal to erect a theatre in Widnes appears, for the present at least, to have ,fallon through. Though the proposal to establish a Free Library in Widnes was received so favourably at the large meeting held a few weeks ago in the Public Hall, I hear oLnothing being done with the object of getting Major .Cross to call 11 meeting on the subject.

Some , tinie agO ari h —l"lll6elnent appeared in your columns to the effect that the Liberals of Runcorn and Widnes were making preparations to hold a banquet at as early date, wad were also arranging for lectures during the coming season. It appears to me that the Liberal organi- sation in the town needs a little life putting into it,'for it is only about twice a year that one is made aware there is such a society in existenc The Conservatives are quite as Laodicean in anything they do with the object of stemming that Radical wave which is said to be "sweeping over the land." RUNNLNG DOWN OF A RUNCORN SCHOONER.-011 Mdnday night, the Lady Stewart, which was the property of several people living at Runcorn, was run into by the schooner William Howard whilst lying at anchor at Holy- head, and sunk in a few minutes. The crew were saved. HALTON MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOOIETY.-011 Mon- day evening, the Rev. George Hack, of Runcorn, delivered a lecture in the Wesleyan schoolroom, under the auspices of this society, the subject being "George Whitfield, the eloquent and successful preacher." Mr. A. E. Davies, one of the vice-presidents of the society, occupied the chair; and at the close a collection was made an behalf of the society.

DEICE-STREET AND FRIARS GREER BAND OF HOPE SOCIETY—The third entertainment of the season in eonnec- tion with the above society was held in Brick-street school- room, on Tuesday last. There was a good attendance with a fair number of actults. The chair was taken by the presi- dent of the society, Mr. Peter Taylor, who made a very appropriate% address, showing the interest he took in the temperance cause as a Sunday school teacher. He directed his remarks chiefly to the children, showing that the errors of the drunkard were not confined to himself but that his children had but too frequently to suffer with him. He urged them to keep their pledge which, he assured them, was their best safeguard against temptation. The programme, which was both instructive and amusing, was gone through in a creditable manner by the children. VICTIMISING A WARRINGTON TRA_DESMAN—MP. R. Jones, draper, Market-street, was made the victim of an im- pudent imposition on Tuesday afternoon. Whilst only the shop boy was in attendance a woman entered the shoo, and asked for two shirts, which she stated had been purchased by her father on the previous day. The boy desired her to call again, when Mr. Jones could attend to tier, but she was imperative, saying, "I want them now, father is wanting to put one of them on." .Still the boy protested, but on being told that if he informed Mr. Jones that she was Mr. Maloney's daughter it wOuld be all right, he gave her the articles. The woman placed them in her basket, and walked from the shop, succeeding, at the same time, in purloining a mad from the counter. The police are in receipt of the information, but have, as yet, no trace of the thief. WARRINGTON PARISH CHURCH. —Four new stops having been added to tire, splendid organ at the above church, to celebrate the completion of the instrument special services were held in the edifice on Sunday last. The sermon in the morning was preached by the Rev. Morley Stevenson, 8.A., that in the afternoon by the Rev. F. W. Cory, 8.A., and in the evening the Rector (the Rev. W. Quekett) occupied the pulpit. The musical portion of the services was admirably' rendered by the choir, assisted by several friends. In the morning the anthem "Behold how good and joyful" was given; and in the evening " 0 praise God in His holiness ;" the solos being taken by Miss Grindley, of Manchester, and Mr. P. C. Price. Mr. C. E. Rowley, the able organist, played the following pieces, the evening selection being listened to with much.interest by the crowded congregation which had assembled :—Morning: Invocation (Guilmaut) ; grand chorus (Guilmaut.) Even- ing: Organ sonato No. 1 iii F minor (Mendelssohn) ; marche funebre and chant seraphique (Guilmaut) ; Caril- lons de Dunkerque (Turpin); toccata and fugue in D minor (Bach.) DEATH OF A WARRINGTON MAN FROM YELLOW FEVER.—We regret exceedingly to have to announce the death of Mr. Frank H. Stubbs, M.A., who was for some time mathematical master at Huddersfield College. The follow- ing is taken from the Dewerara Argosy, of September 24th, 1881. The closing observations of the paragraph will be warmly endorsed by many in Huddersfield who knew Mr. Stubbs :—" In the obituary of the week we have to record with regret the death from yellow fever, after three days' illness, of Mr. Frank H. Stubbs, second master of Queen's College. Mr. Stubbs was the only son of the Rev. Richard Stubbs, of Warrington, Lancashire, and was educated at Christ's Hospital, where, in addition to many minor dis- tinctions, be achieved the honour of being elected Mathe- matical Gold Medallist and Exhibitioner of his year. He afterwards gained a scholarship at St. John's College, Cam- bridge, and graduated from there in mathematical honours in the tripos of 1874. On leaving the University he devoted himself to scholastic work, and held mathematical appoint- ments at Tunbridge and Huddersfield, and in December, 1879, he was seh cted for the second mastership of the Queens College of British Guiara, from a large number of candidates, and arrived in the colony on the 2nd February, 1880. It was evident from the first that the selection of the Secretary of State had been a most happy one. • Mr. Stubbs threw himself into his work at once with an earnestness and energy that never flagged to the last; he liked his work, and liked his pupils, and they in return recognised in him a friend as well as a teacher, whose discipline, though firm, was always just and kindly. His death leaves a vacancy in the staff of the college, and it is impossible in the immediate Present, and will be difficult in the future to fill it so ably and with so much promise. In his private life, though he had been so short a time in the Colony, the genial and sterling manlinesss of the character of Mr. Stubbs bad already endeared him, not only to his colleagues, but to an intimate circle of other friends, who feel his loss keenly ; and all who knew him will warmly sympathise with his young widow and her little son in their unlooked-for and untimely bereayement."—Huddersfield Examiner,

ELLESMERE-STREET MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS, RUN- * cOnw.-=—At the usual meeting of the above class,, held on Monday evening last, an essay on "Iron and Steel" was read by Mr. Richard Moore. The essayist gave an interest- ing desmiption of the character and composition of the metals under notice, and the way in which they were pre- pared for the menet. A discussion ensued, in which the Rev. J. Billington, Mr. Jones, Mr. T. Moore, Mr. Cordon, and the esgayist took part. Mr. J. Rolford, the president, occupied the chair, and there was a very large attendance.

DRAWING EXAMINATION AT THE RUNCORN NATIONAL Scwom.—The drawing examination at this school took place on Monday, when nearly 400 papers were forwarded to the Science and Art Department, South Kensington. The results of the examinations in March last are as follows: Boys' school-74 certificates, 17 prizes, and 4 second grade certificates, besides which 179 papers were marked "Fair." Girls' department-29 certificates and four prizes, and 91 papers marked "Fair." The total number of certificates obtained was 103, being 58 for freehand, 40 for geometry, and 5 for model. 270 exercises were marked "Fair." The teachers are much to be congratulated upon these very encouraging results. -

- SUNBEAM JIIVENILE TEMPLE, WIDNES.--This temple held its annual session on Wednesday evening, and as it was the commencement of a fresh quarter, newly elected set of officers were, accoiding to a custom, installed by Lrother Holton, S.I.T. The names of the newly installed officers Were as follows :—C.T., Bro. T. Hewitt; V.T., Sister Cooke; C., Sister Stanley; R.S., Bro. J. Thompson; F.S., Sister Bradbury; treasurer, Bro. W. Cooke; M., Sister E. Wright; D.M., Sister Anderson; T.G., Bro. IVoolstencroft ; S., Bro. Thomas Cooke; A.R.S., Bro. J. Atherton. It may be men- tiod that the temple has initiated during the past quarter 27 new members, coking a total of 92 members.

111.mcomv Sr. LLTRIL'S SABBATH SCHOOL.—On Sun- day three sermons were preached in aid of these schools, in the morning and evening, at Bethesda chapel, by the Rev. J. Yonge, ot Warrington., and in the afternoon at St. Luke's chapel by the Rev. J. McCordy Davis, of Liverpool, in the unavoidable absence of Mr. Carver, of Widnes. The col- lections realized £8 75., being in advance of those of last year. Mr. Yonge is a great favourite amongst the Congre- gationalists of Runcorn and the district. The two discourses were marked by the pulpit power for which the reverend gentleman is so well known. His complete want of affecta- tion, his vigour of thought, and his rich flow of ideas, with a very attractive delivery, at once win the attention of a congregation, and hold them until the close.

THE RuNcoRN FOUNTAIN WATER.—An analysis of the water at the Runcorn Fountain was made on October the 24th by Mr. P. Smith, chemist, with the following results In every gallon of water 85 grains of total solids, of chlorine 21.1, of sodium chloride 341, total hardness 21.7, reaction, alkaline, sulphate prevalent. In Mr. Smith's opinion the water was contaminated with organic matter sufficient to warrant a minute quantities analysis. The chlorine and solids were inordinate, and from his cursory examination he could not recommend the water for dietary or culinary pur- poses. Upon this result the fountain was closed, and an analysis of the water made on Oct. 27 by Dr. Carter Bell, the county analyst, with the following results: Total solids 84 grains per gallon, chlorine 20.8, oxygen for one gallon .154, free ammonia .03, albumenoids .12, poisonous metal nil. Dr. Bell did not consider the water first-class. The solid matter was very much too high, and the organic matter was double that found in good water. Presuming that the water was put into a clean bottle be should call it of doubtful Purity, Acting upon the result of the first analysis, the Medical Officer ordered the fountain to be closed. Many houses in the vicinity were consequently thrown without the water which they had been accustomed to receive with such plentitude, awl were compelled to make arrangements for supplies from the Waterworks Co. The Commissioners have had the matter under consideration, and it is postponed for further enquiry into the cause of the contamination. DEATH OF MR. EDWARD GRUNDY, OF LYMIL—Mr. E. S. Grundy died on Tuesday morning, after a short illness, at his residence, Reddish. The deceased gentleman was well known and highly respected, and his death is much re- gretted.

FOOT AND MOUTH Dirmsnm—On Saturday a case of foot and mouth disease was reported from Garstang, on the farm of Mr. James Kay, Ashes, Whittingham. One cow has been affected out of 17. The number of farina now affected in the County is 190, of which 168 are in Blackburn hun- dred, 20 in Amounderness hundred, and two in West Derby hundred. •

WARRINGTON ASSESSMENT Connyrrne.—At the monthly meeting, which took place at the Workhouse, yesterday, there were present Messrs. John Rylands (chairman), J. Harrison, W. Derbyshire, C. H. Cartwright, G. Blackburst, R. Garnett, E. C. Cooper, W. Balharry, W. Winstan ley, J. C. Sutton (clerk), W. WARRINGTON COUNTY' PETTY SESSIONS. These sessions were held on Wednesday beim e Messrs. Greeige Artingstall and Peter Stubs.—Mr. Hobson, school atten-

dance officer, summoned the following persons for neglecting to send their children regularly to school :—William Gos- ling, Warburton-street, Winwick-road ; Thomas Dirge, forge- man ; James Parsonage of Rixton ; John Yearsley, William Naylor, Jehn Leonard, Fisher.—Birge, Naylor, and Fisher were each fined 55.; the other cases were dismissed. Richard Kenwright was charged under a warrant, with being drunk and disorderly at Penketh, on the 11th September, and also with stealing a quantity of apples, of the value of 55., the property of Thomas Standish. P.C. Rogers stated that he saw the prisoner lying asleep on theground in Ferry lane, Penketh, on Sunday the 11th September. He went up to him, and found that he had a quantity of 'apples. concealed under his shirt. On the other side of the hedge , another man was laid with a quantity of apples by his side. This man had been dealt with, but the prisoner absconded.— For being drunk and disorderly, the prisouer was fined ss. and costs, and 20s. and costs for the theft.—William Barry, a labourer, was charged with stealing 521bs. of potatoes from the field of Hannah Parsonage, Great Sankey.—Tomas Fahey, farm labourer, said that about six o'clock on the evening o$ the 28th ult., he went into the field to cover some potatoes in a cart. He saw on one side of the cart a white bag containing potatoes, and •the prisoner was putting potatoes into another smaller bag. He detained the prisoner who said he saw them as he Was walking through the field and took them.—Prisoner was fined 20s. and costs or a month's imprisonment with hard labour.

• EXTELORDINAIIY CIIIMOrt SCIAITALL IN MANC/lESTER. —An extraordinary case was •heard before Mr. Headtam, at the Manchester City Police Court, on Wednesday. A young man named Richard Kirby was charged with hating been guilty of indecent behaviour in the churchyard of St. Luke'a, Chorlton-on-Medlock. It appeared that on §unday, the 23rd October, he attended the early communion service at St. Luke's. Me did not behave quite iu the ordinary fashion, and was suspected to be an emissary of the Church Association. After communion he went into the church- yard, and asked a young lady there if that place of worship was not a place of Rome? It seemed that he had not eaten the consecrated bread, for he showed a piece to the young lady, and said, "De you call that bread?" The rector of the church, the Rev. J. Cater, said the bread was made of flour and,water, and was pure wheat bread. He had not been threatened with proceedings by the Church Association on account of the ceremonial practised at his church. The defendant, speaking to Miss Cater, had said that he could not distinguish between the services of St. Luke's and those at a Roman Catholic church, and had shown her the conse- crated bread which he had taken from the church, without partaking of it. For the defence, the above facts were nht denied, but it was contended that they did not constitute an indecency. Mr. Headlam said that for a person to ex- hibit communion bread in a churchyard to a person who had just partaken of the communion with a great deal of rever- ence was certainly an indecent act within the meaning of the Act of Parliament. The defendant was fined Qs. and cots, but notice ef appeal was given. . Ms. Lots, OP Dittairr AimllEWsirr IttoXWOREs, ox Smoxs.—On Saturday night, an adjourned meeting of the South Staffordshire Mill and Forge Managers' Associa- don was held at Dudley. Mr. R. Edwards presided; and there was a large attendance. After the formal business, M. Morris, of ballam and Bewsey Ironworks, Warrington read a paper on "Smoke." He said the most persistent ex- periments on amoke affirmed that there was not a grain of :arhon in 'a ciliate foot of smoke. To get rid of the black smoklP all sorts of experiments had been tried, and when they had succeeded the proprietor had lost the use of great heat, and the air: had been charged with deleterious gases, instead of an honest disinfectant. Smoke with all its virtues had but one vice, and that was blackness. It was altogether a mistake to suppose that the emission of such smoke was wasted power, and doctors who had studied the question aaid smoke helped to decompose and destroy the malaria in the atmoaphere. If smoke was once formed it could not be con- sumed, but it could be diluted with air. The reader then cited many instances of failure on the part of so-called snke-consumers, but praised Dr. Siemens' gas furnace. Mr. Morris concluded hia paper with corns remarks on London fogs.—ln the discussion which followed, Mr. Farnworth said he was not quite convinced that it was not wasted power which escaped from the tops of the chimneys. At the same time, he did not believe that the escape of smoke was so dangerous as sanitary officials would have thrall believe. (Hear, hear.)—Several members complimented the writer of the paper oil its contents.—Mr. Yeomans believed that if air in proper proportion could be admitted into the grate they might prevent much of the smoke, for combustion would he more perfect.—Mr. Rigway was of opinion that complete combustion might mean complete oxidation—After some further discussion, the Chairman held that they dare not admit ' air by rule of thumb, but by v..lves easily governed.—A vote of thanks was given to Mr. Morris for his paper.

SAD SUICIDE AT BURTONWOOD.—The county cproner, Mr. C. E. Driffield, held an inquest at the Ship Inn, Win- wick Quay, on Saturday, on the body of a young man named John Bridge Hatton, who committed suicide last week under the following circumstances:—James Hatton, father of the deceased, said: I am a farmer, and live at Dallam Farm, Burtonwood. Mv son John lived and worked with me on the tarn, and was 23 years of age. A cousin of the deceased's, named Maria Yates, had also lived with tis for several years. The deceas?d and this girl were very friendly, but nothing wrsng, was suspected until a few days ago. On Tunday I spoke to the deceased about the matte,. saying that it was very unfortunate, 'but that we should have to get over it in some way. He did not say anything, but seemed much troubled. On Wednesday morning I went into the kitchen before going to Warrington. Maria Yates asked me for a quarter's wages, saying that she wanted to get some article of clothing. I did not give her any money. When I returned from Warrington,a few hours afterwards she had gone. My wife said she must have thrown her clothes through the upstairs window and gone through the front door, as she had left unobserved. I sent for deceased, who was in bed, to come to speak to me. I told him Maria had gone without her money. Deceased said she came up- stairs and asked him for a sovereign, which he gays her. I said that he ought to have gone and looked for her. He cried bitterly, and said he did not know where she could have gone. He then went to bed. About five o'clock on Thursday morning my, wife heard deceased go downstairs and pass the window. Shortly afterwards she heard a gun go off. She said to me, "Jump up, there is something amiss; I heard a gun shot." We went out immediately, and after searching for about ten minutes found the deceased in a potato pit, where he had been working the previous even- ing. He was in a sitting posture, with the gun between his legs and pointing upwards towards his head, which, was ter- ribly shattered. He was quite dead. I went for my son James and some men to help me to carry him to the house, and then gave information to the police. For the last week or two I observed that the deceased did not take his meals as usual, and as much as possible avoided conversation with me. He evidently had something on his mind, as previously he was of a cheerful disposition. When I spoke to him about his connection with Maria Yates I did so in a kindly manner. I did not say anything to him which I have cause to-regret. —Mary Hatton, wife of last witness, said : The deceased is my son. Last Monday I heard that there had been a dispute between Maria Yates and the deceased. When I spoke to him about it I did not scold him. The gun with which deceased shot himself was kept in the kitchen over the mantel-shelf. It was not usual for him to keep it loaded. He was fond of shooting, but he could not have gone out for that purpose on Thursday morning, at the time he did, as it was then quite dark.—James Hatton, a brother of the deceased, gave corroborative evidence, and the jury returned a verdict "That the deceased committed suicide whilst in a state of temporary insanity."
