THE PUDDLERS' STRIKE.

Dear Sir,—l have no doubt you have heard a great deal about the puddler's strike. Ido not know so much about it but I think the men cannot be wrong, for after reading the letter of "A "and of "One of them " in your contempo- rary, I think their case is clearly made out. But, sir, I have been acquainted for a number of years past with a number of ironworkers, and in my interviews with them relative to the strike, I think that the conduct of the em- ployers is haughty and arrogant in the extreme. The very fact speaks for itself, as no rebellious conduct on the part of the men has ever taken place, inasmuch that they have always agreen to what their employers have proposed until! it has become impossible to stand it longer. You know, Mr. Editor, that there is a strong difference between a man with a sovereign in his pocket and a man holding the position of the general managership of a firm like the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co. But lam glad to see that the men are alive to these impositions and are determined to resist them, and the committee,l believe, is composed of men who will do all in their power to aid add assist all who are out, and are holding concerts, and have also gained two nights at the theatre during next week. I think, sir, this is evidence enough to prove that the men are right. Let us hope they will win in the end—_l am, yours, &C., BENJAMIN DARBY.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday. The Rev. Canon Barclay presided, and there were also present, the Rev. W. Fen:l6llY, Messrs. John Simpson, James Pritchard, Thomas Norman, Richard Lea, and F. Rigby (clerk). A HINT TO CARRY-E-kg PARENTS.

Mr. RIGBY remarked that Mr. Bowyer, the attendance officer, desired to know if he must ask the Bench to enforce the immediate payment of a fine in the case of a person who had been convicted for sending his child to school irregu- larly. If any time was allowed for payment of the money the chances were that it would never be paid, and all the expenses would have to be borne by the Board. He thought iC would be well to have a standing order that all fines should be immediately paid. Of course, it was open for them to take out a distress warrant, and proceed against the parents for the recovery of the 55., but if it cost 10s. to do so it was obviously a bad bargain.—Mr. NoameN said that in many cases parents preferred going to prison rather than paying the fine.—The CHAIRMAN : So much for legislation. People go to prison rather than pay the fine, and there is never any improvement made, in the attendance of their children.—After some further conversation, it was unani- mously resolved that the attendance officer should press for the fine being paid at the time of the conviction.—The CHAIRMAN :—The clerk to the magistrates (Mr. Ashton) told me the other day that it was just as easy to get the fine at the time as not The persons fined, as a rule, always found the money. (Laughter.) EHUCATIONAL RETURNS.

Mr. BOWYER presented the following statistics :—Returns from the public elementary schools for October.—Certified Government accommodation, 2,289. Approximate atCen- dance : Number on the rolls, 2,758; ditto average attendance, 1,9991; average attendance for October, 1880, 1,9409; average attendance for the year 1874, 1,252; accomrnoda- tfon in exn.ss ef avenge attendance, 289.7; number on the it!;l6 of aetl,l.l.tniciox;, 469..- These tigures show' an increase in the arer.ige ;tutu:lance, as compared with the corresponding pe,10,1 ‘,l met,,year of 58.6, and an increase, as compared wli 1574, the year precztling the formation of the Board, of 7473. The toial ninkber in attendance at private adVent uto schools under ninepeoce per week is 63. THE RUNCORN RELIEVING OFFICER AND TIIE BOARD.

Mr. .NORMAN said tout Father Fennelly had mentioned to him an instance where the Guardians had objected to pay the school fees, although the case was a deserving one.— The Rev. W. FENNELLY observed that the case in point was one of the hardest in the town. The father only received 12s. per week, and had to maintain a large family and pay rent and rates out of it. The wife had been, twice before the guardians, and had been told that the fees had not to be paid.—The CHAIRMAN said •he had personally examined into the matter, and found that the Guardians had ordered the fees to be paid, and it was entirely the woman's own fault that any trouble had arisen owing to her not having made applicatiou for the ticket. —Rev. W. FENNELLY ob- served that the woman had told him she had been twice to the relieving officer, Mr. Wright, and he had told her the fees had not been g,ranteda—Mr. PRITCHARD remarked that the system now followed in the paym,nt of fees was very unsatisfactory. It appeared that the reason why the pay- ment of fees had been stopped in a number of Cases was that the parents receiving them ought to make a fresh ap- plication at the mid of three months, but no one had taken the trouble to inform them of this fact. He was surprised Chat Mr. Wright was so reticent with the parents, several of whom had been called upon to walk to Dutton Workhouse —which was a very considerable distance from Runcorn— unnecessarily.—The CHAIRMAN: Wright's fault is that he won't explain to the people.—Mr. PRITCHARD: Yes, I fancy that is the cause.—The CHAIRMAN: We Guardians of the poor have had many rows with him. If we were to deal with him as he deals with men, hb would come very badly off.—The woman referred to, whose name is Griffin,attended , before the Board and maintained that Mr. Wright had never said a word to her about the Guardians having .agreed to pay her fees—lt was agreed that the Chairman should send the relieving officer a note by Mr..Ronryer, and shortly after he entered the room and was confronted with the woman.— The CHAIRMAN said the Board were sorry to have to disturb Mr. Wright, and to request his attendance, but they had done so in order that ho might set himself right with the public.—Mr. WRIGHT stated he did not know that he had seen Griffin since the fees were alleived about a month ago. He invariably told such applicants when the Board day was' and afterwards what the Guardians had done. If she had called upon him, it was when he had been out of the office. —Mrs. GrRIFFIN persisted in her ,stattolent that when she went to Mr. Wright he told her there was nothing for her.— The CHAIRMAN: Here is the position—we bring Griffin up owing to her children not attending school, and she replies that they cannot attend because though they have applied to the Guardians to allow the fees, they will not do sc.' Now, the fact is that the Guardians have granted them, and how is she to know this 2—Mr. WRIGHT : She has not been near me since the fees were granted. I invariably tell them, after they make application, what has been done for them. \ If they don't come, I take no further notice of the matter, as I suppose they are doing without the fees.—Mr. PRITCHARD (to Mr. Wright) : I think it would he as well ifivou were to tell them that they are required to make a second application at the end of three months, if they wilt the payment of the fees to be, continued.— Mr. Warta.= : When I give them a ticket to go to school, loveriably;tell them,how .Jong,a period, ikoovers.—The Wears much obliged term Soi• coming, 'Mr. Wr ht.:—Pktra...Gairnw (to the oificer)t I ,was in your office four or live times, and my husband was also there about the granting of these fees.—Mr. Watouv : I don't dispute that, but that was before they were granted.—Mrs. Griffin having retired, the CHAIRMAN said : I can easily imagine that it is perfectly true, as such women have no notion of time or date.—Mt. SIMPSON : As I understand, j the Guardians are now quite willing to leave the decision in the matter of granting ,fees to the Runcorn section.—Tbe CHAIRMAN: I believe so.—Mr. SIMPSON : I think that will remove a good deal of the difficulty we have had.

div.head: MIL SIMPSON ON THE NEGLECTED BOAT CHILDREN.
div.p: MIL SIMPSON ON THE NEGLECTED BOAT CHILDREN.

Mr. SIMPSON observed that there were now scores of boat children who were growing up without education: He cer- tainly considered it was the duty of the Board to see that these received the benefit of education.—The CHAIRMAN : Perfectly true.—Mr. SIMPSON considered that they ought to take into consideration whether the Board were justified in the course they were adopting in regard to the boat children, and if they were doing their duty to the public under the Elementary Education Ad.—The CHAIRMAN : There is not much good in looking after them, when there is; no place for them to go to !—Mr. SIMPSON remarked that he quite agreed it was quite probable that if the School Board looked after the class of children referred to, they would, in the end, be onlig,ed to provide accommodation. He did not, however, think they were justified in neglecting their duties because of the fact that they would have to provide further accommodation.—Mr. NORMAN did not think the Board I would be able to provide for all the children connected with I the boats which had been registered in Runcorn, as they included vessels belonging to Manchester, Northwich, and Winsford.—The CHAIRMAN (humorously) : That is owing to the short-sightedness of the commissioners; who have only put the ratepayers to the expense of providing an additional school.—Mr. SIMPSON. remarked that if the children belonging to the Winsford boat people whose vessels were registered at Runcorn, Were attending school at Winsford, or somewhere else, that would satisfy the School Board. However, as the boats were registered at Runcorn, it was the duty of the Board to ace that the children living upon them attended school, and he did not think they ought to shirk the work. It was a very sad thing indeed tluit these children should be allowed to grow up in the way they were doing. No doubt the difficulties in the way of getting such youngsters to school were very great, but lie considered they ought to face them. He had again and again regretted that the Board had not looked at this matter fairly and allowed such a length of time to pass since the Act came into operation without making any special effort to see that the children attended school.—The Cwatnarax : Bowyer has pulled up some of the worst cases.—Mr. SIMPSON: Yes, where they have houses in Runcorn; I think that he attends to the cases of all the parents who have houses in the town.—The CnninmAN: There cannot I be many on boats, as the Act will not allow above a certain I number to live on each ves;el.—A MEMBER: So the Act I says. (Laughter.)--Another MEMBER : And who looks after the Act P—The CHAIRMAN : • The inspectors appointed by the Commissioners, and of course they cannot do any- thing wrong ! (Laughter.)—Mr. NORMAN remarked that he had heard of cases where boat people, in order to avoid the inspector, had told their children to join the vessel just outside the boundaries of Runcorn township. (Laughter.) —The CHAIRMAN : How would it be if, as an initiative with regard to doing something in the way of dealing with the boat children, Bower were to take steps to ascertain, as far as possible, what is the number of boats registered in Runcorn where the people do not live in this town, and the number of such children who ought to be in attendance at schools. But if the parents have no houses in Runcorn how can they get their children to school P—Mr. SIMPSON: The Act awe "must."—The CHAIRMAN : Then we must have a special school for them, and take them in one day in the week.— Mr. SIMPSON : Probably if the Act were carried out, it would lead to a number of them getting houses.—A. MEm- BElt: But it is not our place to attend to that.—Mr. SIMPSON: But it is our place to see that their children do attend school: and after the parents have been brought up before the magistrates a number of times, they will find that they must take steps to bring about such a result. It is for the parents to find the means whereby this is to be done. He thought the object of the Act was to make the boat people provide houses but there was no doubt that its prictical working would press very hardly upon some of the parents. —lt was resolved that Mr. Bowyer should ascertain.the number of boats reeistered at Runcorn ; the number of peo- ple living upon thew, and how many of them had houses in the town.

div.head: SCHOOL FEES QUESTION.
div.p: THE SCHOOL FEES QUESTION.

The Chair man and Mr. Thomas Norman were appointed a committee to meet the Relief Supervision Committee of the Runcorn Board of Guardians, for the purpose of taking into consideration all applications for the payment of fees coming before the School Board.

SUDDEN DEATH OF A CHILD AT PEESOOT. —On Mon- day, Mr. F. Smith, coroner for the Manor of Prescot, held an inquest at the King's Arms Hotel, on the body of a female child, three months old, daughter of a labourer named Richard Denton, who resides at 50. High-street. From the evidence it appeared that the deceased had evidently died in a fit, on the previous Saturday night, and a verdict of "death from natural cause" was returned.

MR. MAWSON, FORMERLY OF RUN- CORN, ON MUNICIPAL MAT lERS AT WIGAN. A few evenings ago a meeting was held in the Wigan Conservative Working Men's Club for the purpose of pre- senting Mr. J. Y. Mawson (formerly of Runcorn) with a requisition asking him to become a candidate for the repre- sentation of All Saints' Ward in the Town Council.—Mr. J. Preston presided.—Mr. G. Mather said he was present to represent the opinions of a vast number of the inhabitants of All Saints' Ward. In the course of a three hours' canvas on the previous day he had had the pleasure of obtaining upwards of 200 • signatures to a requisition inviting Mr. Mawson to stand as a candidate for the ward—(applause)— and of this number 8.0 were voters. He felt fully justified in making V:e assertion that if he had had time and oppor- tunity to canvas the whole of the ward he would have got at least two-thilds of the inhabitants of the ward to sign the equisition. Lvcu if Mr. Mawson did not stand on the present occasion he hoped the ti.oe was not far distant when be would do so, events having proved that he would make a capable and able rePresentative of the ward. (Hear, hear.) Much had been si,t about two good men retiring, but if Mr. Mawson contested the t do there would be three good men to pick from. (Hear, bear.) lie was of opinion that if their Radical opponents could not properly conduct the affairs of this great nation—and everyone saw that their policy not only in regard to foreign affairs but with respect to the sister country of Ireland was a miserable failure—they could not manage matters any better in the Council Chamber. He had great pleasure in presenting Mr. Mawson with the requisition, which, although small in point of numbers, expressed the hearty wishes of the whole of those who had signed it for his success. (Applause.)—After some remarks from Mr. Robert Johnson and another member of the club, expressive of distaste with which the Conservative voters contemplated the idea of a compromise with the Liberals, Mr. J. Y. Mawson, who was received with applause, said that words could not express the deep delight with which Le received the honour the meeting had bestowed on him. He fully endorsed the remarks made by Mr. Mather as to the desirability under ordinary circumstances of contesting the ward. He could assure him and the meeting that if it were only a matter of pounds, shillings, and pence he would fight the election in ,the face of every difficulty and every opposition. It had been truly said by one of the wisest politicians of ancient or modern..times that one of the greatest accomplishments of political craft and wisdom was to say "no." Until three hours , previously to that meeting he had been determined to say "yes" to this requision, and had he done so nothing would have turned him back. (Hear, hear). To give the reasons why he bad altered his mind was to tread upon very delicate ground. He felt he should be best serving the interests of the Conservative party in the borough by refraining at the present time from waging the battle of political sections. It was hard to say this. When one had determined on a certain line of action it was hard to throw oneself over and to sacrifice not only one's political feelings but those of his friends. (Hear, hear. This address was not the only token he had received of the feeling of the ward. Reference had been made to the capacity and ability of the two retiring members. That was ground upon which he must not touch, but when he said he had been solicited by tne Liberals themselves to place himself in opposition to the retiring member, the meeting might be sure it was doubly hard to give way at the last moment. (Hear, hear). But he felt certain it was for the best that he should do so. (Hear, hear.) He hated compromise. The essence of poli- tical economy was the greatest good to the greatest number, and it seemed to him that they now had the selfishness of the few against the rights of the many. (Hear, hear). Still He felt bound to give way. He was glad to think that at some future time, should occasion offer, those gentlemen would be prepared to support him as a candidate in an election for the ward. On the first opportunity that pre- sented itself he would stand, and would fight to the end. (Applause). There was one consideration which would have interfered materially with his candidature, apart from political considerations. He had received communications which would cause him to go to London, and he felt the re- sults of his visit to the metropolis would be more benficial to the borough than his presence in the Council Chamber. (Applanse.)—The Chairman moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Mawson for placing himself at the service of the Conserva- tive party.—Mr. J. Hodson seconded, and the motion was unanimously agreed to.—A motion, pledging those present to anpport Mr. Mawson at the next election, if he came for- ward as a candidate, was also agreed to.
OPENING OF THE FOURTH COCOA HOUSE IN WARRINGTON.

In no town, perhaps, in comparison to its size, has the Cocoa House movement, which has spread so rapidly throughout the country, been more successful than in War- rington. That the establishment of these houses in town has met a public want is evident from the fact that, al- though it is only about three years since the first house of this character was opened, the directors of the Warrington Pritish Workman Public House Company were engaged* on Thursday evening in the ceremony of opening the fourth place under their charge. With the house now under notice, the company have ;hive establishments, -itii,ked in the main thoroughfares true: r, tt/i7e. ruws s Commencing mse,rtioc,iin tou;.,,eirztri:isn eel! tenthal to Iffid,le-et.eot, where a house was opened near Brioge Foot. Then turning their attention to the market, the directors next opened premises in Market-street, at' which business was carried on every day until recently, when an alteration was made, and the house opened only on market days. Of the financial success of the undertakinT, it may be interesting to state that the directors have paid a dividend of five per cent. to the shareholders, whil a similar amount has been devoted tO the reduction of the capital account; and it is anticipated that the next financial statement will be of an equally satisfactory character. The house opened on Thursday evening is situated in Irlam- street, opposite the Police Station, and the premises have undergone complete transformation, having been previously occupied by a draper. Mr. Thomas Morris, the chairman of the directors, performed the opening ceremony, and amongst these present were Messrs. C. Broadbent, N. Legge, E. Place, Brown R. Siddall, H. Roberts (sec.), W. Boberts, &c. Mr. 71.11011 AS MORRIS sail bethought they would all agree that there could not be a more pleasant duty to perform than the one he had to perform that night, for, of all insti- tutions, cocoa houses were about the most effective, morally, physically, and he Must confess pecuniarily—for so far as the company were concerned, they had been very successful. The wonder to him had been how in was these institutions were not established years sooner than they were. Work- ingmen's clubs and the like seemed to fall into insignificance before the good and moral effect of these institutions. Al- though their tariff was low—very low indeed; perhaps the lowest tariff any company could offer to their customers— still they could afford to givetbe people little luxuries lathe shape of newspapers and fires. No one could beat them, especially when they compared the price to what they gave by way of comfort and convenience, food and drink. And yet, as he had said before, they secured a dividend for the shareholders. The directors of the company had always had their eye upon the. locality knowing it to be a densely populated neighbourhood and much traversed by work- people, male and female, passing te and from their various duties; and he would only express the hope that the people would take advantage of the boon the company were offering to them,:b7 opening that house in their immediate locality. He concluded by expressing the willingness of the company to do all they possibly could to promote the comfort of the people la that neighbourhood, and then for- mally declared the house open by drinking the first cup of coffee. • Mr. C. BROADBENT, at the invitation of Mr. Morris, said it was not a very large meeting, but he considered it a very important occasion. This was the fourth cocoa house opened by the company, and the public might rest assured they would not have been able to open the fourth unless they had done well with the other three. (Hear, hear.) They all believed that these cocoa houses had supplied a want that was much felt in Warrington. (Hear, hear.) They did not profess it to be a charitable institution or anything of that kind. It was a business undertaking, and although the leadingl motive originally was to do good in the town, they established the movement clearly and distinctly on a business footing. They wished to supply the public with what they wanted—a pleasant place for rest and refreshment without being subjected to the temptations of strong drink. (Hear, hear.) Some people said "Surely you don't want more cocoa houses ? " but he said, "Why should not we have more cocoa houses than public houses in Warrington if there is a demand and the public require them?" (Hear, hear.) He was sure they all felt indebted to the directors, especially those who took the most active part, for the care and assiduous attention that they had j give to the business of these insti- tutions. It was owing to their assiduity that the success had been so great as it had, for in this. as in all other busi- ness undertakings, success depended upon good manage- ment. He believed they had got a body of directors who went heart and soul into the work, and whose object was that they should go on increasing and spreading, and that They should be successful as a business undertaking, and that they should, as they all desired, do a very good work in the town, and gradually lessen the amount of in- temperance. (Hear, bear.) There was one thing he thought they ought to pay especial attention to, and that was to take care that the drink and food they provided was of first-rate quality. [Mr. Morris: We do.] There was no doubt there was sometimes a tendency to make cocoa and coffee deficient in quality, but that ought to be avoided. They wanted everyone who came there to feel that he would have a good wholesome article, whatever it might be. (Hear, hear.) He I was pleased to be present to support Mr. Morris and the other directors on that occasion.
The public were then supplied with coffee free of charge, and the manager was kept busily engaged until nine o'clock.

Tid PRINCE OF WALES THEATRE, WARRINGTON.—The chief attraction at the theatre during the past week hag been the acting of Miss Adeline Stanhope in the new play "Adventuress," of which the audiences that have assem- bled have frequently testified their approbation. The char- acter of Madame Latour received from her its adequate era pression. She is undoubtedly an actress of great power an& histrionic ability, and was exceedingly touching whilst pleading for pity for her son. The other members of the company also sustained their parts with credit. Mr. Sheridan' enterprise in giving Warringtonixos an opportu- -1 nity of witnessing the:performances of such .ixcellent com- panies is commendable.

_ LATEST NEWS.

Daniel Macken, president of the National. Land League, was arrested yesterday and sent to Dundalk gaeL Last night's Gazette contains orders for Court mourning for the late Royal Highness Mike Greek William Alexander of Wantemburg. The Gazette contains notice of granting of the Rev. Wm. Jno. Knox Little the dignity of Canon in the Cathedral of Worcester, void by the resignation of Dr. Bradley. The Spartan, a new steamer of the Union Company, in- tended for Cape service, made her trial trip on the Clyde . yesterday, and was considerad eminently satisfactory. Mr. Ryan, of Doon, County Limerick, who has undergone a long term of imprisonment under the Coercion Act, was unconditionally released yesterday from Limerick Gaol. A telegram from Vienna of yesterday. says an Imperial decree has been issued to-day which ordains the formatioa of separate Bosnian corps d;armee by recruitment in Bosnia. On Thursday, at Ballinsloe, a tenant farmer named •Murray had his skull fractured by another farmer, named Patrick Dowlan. Murray is in a dying state. Dowlan was arrested.

Rear-Admiral Watson, late Commodore at Hong Kong station, succeeds Rear-Admiral Camie as superintendent of the Devonport dockyard, the latter replacing Rear-Admiral Foley at Portsmouth. Messrs. Kenny and Cantwell, Castlecomer, county Kil- kenny, who have evaded arrest for a week, having notified their arrival from England to the police, were arrested under the Coercion Act and conveyed to Naas, yesterday. The Land League School at Mill-street, county Cork, was suppressed by the police yesterday, this being the third time. Children state they will not attend the national school while a Boycotted teacher is allowed to remain. Considerable excitement was manifested at Kilrush, yes- terday, in Consequence of the Kilmurry harriers baying been prevented hunting the district by late Land Leaguers. One gentleman was specially pointed out for Boycotting. The execution of Wm. Osman, sentenced to death at Chester Assizes (Or wife murder, at Woodley, has been fixed for Monday, 14th inst. A memorial, praying for a commutation of the sentence has been extensively signed in the district.

Shortly after the murder of Peter Doherty three shots were fired into the house of John Doherty, his cousin, joint tenant with the deceased of the farm from which a tenant was evicted. Cauliffe, a former tenant, and a man named Alm, riasy have been arrested. All the constabulary on beat duty in Limerick, on Thurs- day, dispensed with the batons which they ordinarily wear, and carried loaded revolvers by their sides, in addition to the sword bayonets with which every man is armed. The order to carry the revolvers is said to have been received 02. Wednesday from Dublin Castle. The Transvaal Committee, at a meeting in London, terday, passed a resolution condemning the terms of the Convention recently ratified under protest by the Boers as calculated to lead to further difficulties. One of the Com- mittee just returned from the Transvaal stating. the feeling among Boers against the treaty to be as strong as against the original annexation. A telegram from Loughrea states that on Wednesday night a farmer named Doherty was shot dead while entering his own house in Carrigan, about 11 miles from Loughrea. Doherty, it is alleged, had been boycotted for some time, but it is also stated that the cause of the outage was that 'he had paid his rent. The police have succeeded in making two arrests. Mr. F. Byrne, secretary of the National Land League of Great Britain, has received a letter from the secritary of the Blackburn Branch, giving further details respecting the interference of the police with the proposed meeting. He says the Exchange is licensed for stage plays, and opposi- tion has been threatened to a renewal of the license if meet- ings are allowed. The secretary adds that the branch will probably sue far breach of contract if refusal of the hall is persisted In. • EXTENSIVE DEFALCATIONS BY A LIVERPOOL CASHIER. A painful feeling has been excited in the Liverpool Cotton Market by the death, as it appears by his own hand, of the cashier in one of the oldest aful most respect firms in the market. The periodical investigation of the books of the firm has been in progress for a few days, but no suspicion that anything wrong was entertained, and the cashier as- sisted as usual. On Tuesday he was absent, and his body was afterwards discovered is a field in the neighbourhood of Birkenhead, the cause of death being a shot from a revolver, which was found near the body. Up to this time the ex- amination of the firm's affairs appear to reveal a deficiency of X 5,000. THE BRIGHTON MURDER. The trial of Peroy Lefroy Mapleton for the murder of Mr. Frederick Isaac Gold, on the Brighton railway, on the 27th June, commenced yesterday morning at Maidstone, before the Lord Chief Justice, the courthouse being crowded in every part, and a large crowd of persons also waiting outside in the pouring rain. The prisoner, in reply to the usual question, pleaded not guilty. The Attorney General thereupon opened the case for the crown, expressing a hope that the jury would dismiss from their minds any of the excitement or prejudice which the murder of Mr. Gold at the time created. He detailed the whole case against the prisoner, and said there was no trace of the third party, and added if such a person did really exist why bad not the prisoner given up Mr. Gold's property, and assisted in his discovery instead of disappearing altogether. The first witness was Joseph Goldsmith, assistant engineer of the Brighton railway, who put in plans of the line. Mrs. Gold next gave evidence, and was followed by the rdllway servants and others examined on the inquest, no freili evidence being adduced in cross-examination. Trral adjourned shortly before six o'clock.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIAN
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIAN

The fortnightly mPeting was held on Tuesday afternoon, at Dutton Workhouse. The Rev. Canon Barclay occupied the chair, and there were also present :—Messrs. John Ash— ton, Thomas Norman, James Darbyshire, G. S. Hazlehuret, W. Whittaker, W. Wright, Henry Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk).

RTINCORN MATTERS. Mr. Nomara remarked that it had been arranged that a house and shop in Church-street, Runcorn, occupied by Mr. George Ward, should be used as the pay :Ace for the town at an annual rent, of £l4, inclusive of all rates.—The CLERK read a cotnnaunication from Dr. McDougall stating that be should be willing to permit his office to be used as a vacci- nation station, on pay:Rent of a yearly sum of £B.—Mr. NORMAN proposed that the two offers should be accepted and Mr. WarrraKEE seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously.

MR. HAZIHRURST ON VAGRANCY. Mr. HAELEHURST referred to a lithographed communica- tion from Mr. Joseph Everest, clerk to the Atcham Guardians, Shrewsbury, requesting the Board to support them in sending a memorial to the Local Government Board, calling their attention to the great increase of vagrancy during the past few years. In the Atcbam union the number of vagrants had increased from 357 in 1872 to 1,470 in 1881. Mr. Hazlehurst said the increase struck him as being very serious, and he should like to know what was the position of the Runcorn Union as to tramps.—The CLERK, on the application of Mr. Hazlehurst, agreed to pre- pare a return on the fabled.

div.head: INMATES.
div.p: THE INMATES.

The MASTER (Mr. Jones) -reported that there were 190 in- mates in the House against 156 in the corresdonding week of last year. There were 33 boys and 30 girls attending the Workhouse schools, and 14 boys and 19 girls receiving an industrial training.

WARRINGTON POLICE COURT. FUlDAY.—Before Mr. Artingstall (chairman) and Alderman Burgess. BEGGING.—Mary Lynch, who had a baby in her arms, was charged with begging in Bold-street and Egypt-shasete on the previous afternoon, and she was committed to gaol for seven days with hard labour. THE " Susncr."—Rotranna Boardman was remanded from Wednesday on suspicion of having stolen a number of articles of clothing, but nothing could be proved against her and she was discharged. ASSACLT.—Maria Shaw was charged with using language to Elizabeth Baekhouse calculated to provoke a breach of the peace, and Ann Shaw, her daughter, with assaulting her. It appeared that Maria Shaw was indebted to the com- plainant to the amount of 305., and that on Thursday the bailiffs were in the house. On Saturday night whilst the complainant and her husband were on their way home, they were met by the defendants, who used much teut language, and Ann struck her in the face.—This was denied, Ann stating that complainant and her husband were "beastly drunk."—Defendants were each bound over to , keep the peace.

THE BISHOP OF LIVASPOO; AT PRICSOOT.—On Sunday morning last, Bishop 'Lyle preached at Pre.cot Parish Church, from the 27th and 28th verses of xxxiii chapter of Job. In concluding his sermon, which was of an excellent character, the Bishop appealed to the congregatios on behalf of the fund for repairing the bells and tower of the church. He observed that so well known a church as Preipot, whose Spire was a landmark to all the country round, shonld never be allowed to stand a single day in need of repairs. He hoped all who valued the old parish cburch et Presoot and its tower, would not shrink from giving soraethtng towards its Mar that day. At the close of the service a collection was neap which amounted to £25 16s. 4d.

div.p: xetter to the (Ultra. MONARCHY IN RELATION TO THE EMPIRE, die. Sir,—At last liar. Peers has been compelled to descend from the pinnacle of his self-satisfaction, upon which he appeared to have taken his stand, in the vain belief that abundant abuse was alone needed to overwhelm the poor mortal who had had the temerity to try to prove that his opinions were not exactly infallible. But the stones of truth and equal justice and patriotism, though *slung by a stripling, are so potent that even vain-glorious intellectual Goliaths ultimately find that splenetic vituperation is not sufficient to turn them aside. And so Mr. Peers, after covering that his eternal invective is quite powerless against the keen blade of argument, has at last endeavoured to wield that blade himself, though still, alas! the customary quantity of invective is administered therewith. Whilst regretting that he has not cast the latter old, rtisan unknightly weapon entirely aside, though this partial" would be too much to expect from rine who sneesrosmaet chivalry, I must express my satisfaction that, to Lawson extent, at least, he has learnt the lesson Sir Wilfrad La bas been trying to teach Mr. Bright, Le, "that instead of But it is ceiling people fools we should argue with them." tenths ago. ed a pity he did not learn the lesson a couplteet of ra If, when first I inform him of the c argument," he had humbled himself asutffichiently‘ abtousbeeilsienvoe me, the amount of valuable time and apace that would have been saved is astonishing. Peers a thet eapstincioenndeelsc have But "better late than never ;" and it is a comfort to find thatMr to attempt to controvert by argument expressed ; though I cannot say that I enterain any very exalted idea of the success which has attended him in this more legitimate method of warfare. My answer to many of his assertions is embodied in previous letters, whicla it would be impertinent of me to take tip time by reproducing. To the rest I need but briefly refer. As to statement No. 1, then. I may again repeat that I never stated that loyalty to a common sovereign was alone sufficient to keep the empire together, but that it helped materially to do so. And even though a British Republic might not treat our colonies unfairly the chances are that they would object to own it as their head, would say that they were as good as it, and would consequently establish their independence. In the Daily News, if my memory serves me, I read quite , recently that at one time Ireland would have been totally disconnected from the British empire had it not been for the golden link of the Crewn. The Standard seam that to con- sult what are called the sentimental feelings of the colonies is, without doubt, the best and most efficient means that can be employed to retain them, and that if the future ruler of this empire were merely to sojourn for a few months In the Australian colonies he would ensure their attachment , to England for the next fifty years. How strong the bond I of loyalty is in British North America, despite what thel Morning Post calls "the ridicule of a small knot of English- ' men who have little in common with the rest of their countrymen, except their language," the recent tour of the Marquis of Lorne, with its many pleasing incidents, testifies, and according to the Uitenhage Times the people of South Africa, whilst desiring "freedom from the muddlingl and mismanagement ef home politicians" are delighted to offer "a voluntary and cheerful obedience to the finest, the noblest, and the greatest throne the world has ever known." I might multiply indefinitely illustrations in proof of my opinions, but surely these and those I have ad- duced in previous letters will be sufficient to convince the unbiassed reader of the truth of my argument, that loyalty to a common sotereign in an empire like our own is a powerful bond of unity. That they will convince Mr. Peers lam not so sanguine. A few paragraphs of Don Quixote or Robin- son Crusoe, judging by his own style of argument, would perhaps be to him more conclusive; but I appeal from Mr. Peers to those who are candidly open to conviction. As to my statement that our limited monarchical system imparts a permanence to our institutions which is lacking in repab- , lican countries, I may again remind Mr. Peers that since' the establishment of the republic in 1789 France has under- gone no leesthan eight revolutions, and may inform him that the American President has 63,000 offices at his dis- posal, the occupants of which be can expel on his accession to power to make room for his own personal friends and sup- porters, thus throwing " the great republic" into a state of periodic disturbance and disquietude. Interesting instances of republican permanency these, are they not? Nothing of this kind in limited monarchical England. And in face of the perpetual French revolutions and America's bloody civil war and infamous assassins, surely I had some justification for stating that while other countries have been deluged with anarchy, England under her limited monarchy has to a great ex great Well might the Neue Freie Presse say, in commenting on the assassination of the Czar of Russia and the President of America, that it would seem that extreme liberty and extreme despotism are both ill- adapted to suppress political assassination, and in the anti- podes of modern political development popular discontent fads expression in political murder." As to Ireland, per- haps Mr. Peers is not aware that it was under the English republic in Cromwell's time that her land was" covered with thousands of the slain." Your correspondent has entirely misinterpreted arguments number 4,5, and 6. These I may deal with together. On his own admission the voice of the people is often the very reverse of the voice of God; it may be turned any way by a glass of beer or the eloquence of a self-seeking demagogue; that voice being in a republic all-powerful it may elect as its representatives none but self-seeking dernagognies ; these .self-seeking demagogues may pass laws solely in their own interests, regardless of the interests of the rich, and may even sanction commu- nism, whilst the upper classes being in a numerical minority would be powerless to elect their own representatives to oppose these unjust laws; and so their rights might be trampled on and their property stolen. But under our limited monarchical system the aristocratic grade of society —the great property owners of the country—are represented in a separate House of Parliament, and acting in conjunction with the Sovereign, can impose a check upon the revolu- tionary and confiscatory tendencies which an absolute democracy might exhibit. As I pointed out in my second letter, the Irish Land Act would have become law with some A "glaring abuses," tuaremedied, had it not been for the pecu- liarity of our constitutional system, by which one element, in that system was able to eliminate those injustices. The rest of my arguments I have defended in previous letters, and repeated reiteration would be RS wearisome to the reader as it is unnecessary. As regards England's greatness and freedom I cannot agree with Mr. Peers that our form of I government hashed neabing to do with it. But I know that a republican land, with every natural advantage and peopled by the English race, to whom Mr. Peers attributes our national greatness and freedom, is neither so great nor so free as is England, and—to once more allude to France— a•nearly a hundred years ago she commenced a new career • under the blessings of republican rule; since that time her progress has been constantly retarded by regularly recurring convulsions, ana to-day she is in no sense the equal of the England which has had to labour under the disad- vantages of a form of government which Mr. Peers says has been % burden and a .hindereome el/cumbrance to her." How is it that the countries which have been free from this " hindersome encumbrance "'are to-day so far behind us? I need not again urge sentiment upon his consideration. I -agree with the Daily News that to deny its existence and laugh at its claims shows a most imperfect perception of the motives which have animated humanity since time begun. The pages of history teem with illustrations of the influence of sentiment upon individual and national life. In times past thousands have been found to rally round their rareereign from none but a sentimental enotive,—call them foals if you like, but they are fools who at least can fight,— and in considering the propriety of substituting a republican for our limited monarchical form of government we cannot ostrich-like bury our heads in fancied security and cry "peace !" when in all probability war and blood and tumult will be attendant upon the change we advocate. It appears that it has only just dawned upon your correspondent that there are other people in England besides himself that may have a word to say on the subject when the time comes. It dawned upon me long ago that perhaps the tens of thousands who thronged the streets of Liverpool on the recent visit of the heir apparent, to greet him with the most unbounaed enthusiasm, and the millions that throughout the country greet royalty with the warmest welcome and the heartiest professions of loyalty and love were not all hypocrites—that perhaps some of them meant it—and that perhaps if a great constitutional struggle arose not a few of these sentimental individuals might be found banded to- gether on the side of their sovereign. We must consider all these things; we most not in our infatuated devotion tie theories close our eyes to facts. I have approached this subject with no frenzied political prepossessions;l believe neither in the divine right of kings nor in the infallibility of the people; but after a candid, unbiassed consideration e the whole questioa I repeat that I am humbly of opinion that the abolition of the British monarchical system would involve the sacrifice of many important benefits which result therefrom; to abolish that system a bloody revolution might be necessary; the people are as yet unfit • to have the absolute control of the affairs of this great empire; and even if we succeeded in establishing a republic the chances are that we should be much worse governed than we are at present, be less truly free than our limited monarchical system makes us, and might be in constant • danger of revolution; and I therefore contend that under • eresent circumstances it is not Quixotic to defend that system, but politic and above all patriotic. I need say little more. I wish every question to stand upon its own merits. • If an institution be well founded it will haN no cause to fear those "winds of argument" and that earthquake of / popular investigation" of which yeur correspondent speaks; if it be ill-founded, ths sooner they are directed against it the better. What I desire is to see such questions as this • fairly and impartially discussed, not for the sake of snatching • a personal or a party triumph, but to the end that the 'unity, • the real liberty and the trds happiness of this grand old empire of ours mar be permanently secured and gradually perfected. It remains only for me to say that e e Mr. Peers shows signs of continuing his classical (poi rtions and democratic fulminations until doomsday, not - , much for • the purpose of annihilating monarchy—which 1, doubt he has discovered is not so easily annihilated—as of ennibilating me, I must leave him to it. He is at perfect liberty to con- tinue the interesting process until his stock of invective is exhausted. For myself I must apologise for my already too lengthened trespass On your columns and express the hope that in spite of the uncompromising nature of the cod- teoversial attitude which Mr, Peers and I have assumed. personally our relations may be of the friendliest.—l am, &c., ARTHUR BUNNY:TT.

BY A SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE GENTLEMAN. [SPECIAL.] No. XXH. NAZARETH (CommirED). • We returned to our tents through the Mahometan quarter, and, just at the ontskirts of the town, our guide, without any introduction or ceremony, marched us into a Bedouin's house. It was one of the better class, and yet to English eyes, discomfort seemed to reign supreme. Through the tow doorway we stepped upon the mud floor of the barn-like place, which had a mitered roof. At about eight feet from the door was a trough or manger reaching across the house, while behind, on a raised platform level with the top of the trough, squatted an elderly Arab with his two wives,, one close beside him doing some needlework, and the other kneading dough at some distance. This single apartment served for a sitting-room, dining-room, kitchen, stable, and hen-house, and many other purposes in the interests of this respectable old Arab and his belongings. Near to the door outside was one of those fearfully offensive ovens which seem to be an essential of Arab life in the villages. These ovens are small huts five or six feet square and three or four feet high, in the centre of which is a sort of bee-hive, open at the top and capable of receiving a large cake. On depositing the cake the top is covered with a close-fitting lid, after which, manure being• heaped upon it, fire is applied, and so the cake is baked. In time the ashes accumulate, and not only half fill the hut but block up the narrow door, and lie all about, filling the atmosphere with the pungent and sickening dust. To the Arab women and children these surroundings seem rather a luxury than otherwise. You will see the children lying,wit h their heads out of the oven doors (mite comfortable; and it strikes me— such is the power of habit—that the very odour of the ashes may impart a flavour quite agreeable,from long usage, to the Arab taste. Pictures like these, I din quite aware, throw rather a dismal colouring over scenes which the imagination would like to paint with golden tints and purple hues. But the faithful chronicler has no alternative. He must describe things as they present themselves to his eyes, and in this once sacred land we saw things in its social life and physical condition that chilled the heart and made us feel how utterly forsaken and desolate it was. The next day being the Lord's day, we accepted Dr. Zellar's courteous invitation to attend an English service in his church. In the afternoon we paid a visit to the Female Orphan Institution, which is under the care of Miss Dixon. It is situated on the hill behind the town, and is a very neat, substantial, and commodious building. It is capable of accommodating a hundred children but not more than 18 children regular inmates. The lady superintendent of this establishment is a most agreeable and estimable lady, who has devoted 25 of the best years of her life, here and in Jerusalem, to the carrying out of her benevolent enterprise. From the summit of the hill behind the orphanage we had another deeply thrilling view of the whole land—one over which the Divine Saviour must have often gazed with deep yearning in His immeasurable love for the lost sheep of the house of Israel. While we looked around and thought of these things, our attention was auddenly drawn to two Arab boys, who, in that lonely hill were rolling about and grappling each other by the throat, a mode of , fighting indicating a barbarous and bloodthirsty training, quite sufficient to account for the atrocities and abominable cruelties that mark the Mahometan rule and people. Our guide ran forward and used his feet and hands towards them pretty freely, making their ears tingle, I suspect, with the good English boxing he gave them. _

- , NAZARETH TO CARMEL. MormaY, Maims 27.—We were early astir this morning and in the saddle by eight o'clock. Having dropped Haifa out of our programme, with the twofold object of avoiding excessive fatigue and spending the Lord's day in Nazareth, we had partly to retrace our steps in order to take in Kishon and Cannel before proceeding further into Galilee. On leaving Nazareth, instead of passing over, the face of the hill which we found so steep and difficult to climb on Satur- day, we descended by a gentle and easy path down its western slopes. Having reached the plain, we crossed in a south-westerly direction, and soon found ourselves travelling over a beautifully wooded track of country. The richness of the foliage and greenness of the swards made us feel as if we were enjoying a ride through some fine old andestral parks in England on one of our finest of summer days. Of course the trees were all[different from ours. Here was the wide-spreading, ever-green Syrian oak, under whose delight- ful shadow we, ever and anon, paused to seek a temporary shelter from the burning heat. There was also the wild lemon bright with blossom and emerald leaf, contrasting with the dark umbrageous walnut and the no less sombre locust. For some miles we travelled through scenes ail these, the most beautifully wooded in Palestine, and then we emerged upon the narrow valley that forms the apex of Eadmelon's immense plain and lands us by the side of the brook Kishon, and at the base of Mount Carmel, where our tents had been pitched for the night. Kishon is easily fordable at this point and is but a sluggish river. After a Ibrief rest we rode along its sedgy banks towards the eastern point of Carmel and then began to climb its rough.and thickly-wooded sides. The mountain at this point is clothed ' with verdure from base to summit, the thick foliage often concealing from view, as you keep in the well-worn tracks, the edges of almost perpendicular rocks along which you aretravelling. About half way up we came to an old foun- tain, built in the fissure of a rock. Here a young mountain guide offered his services, and was eagerly engaged by our conductor. It was comparatively easy to find our way to the top- the difficulty arose when we got to the top,, to find our way, across ploughed fields on the table land to the one path on the other side of the field ' that led through a labyrinth of trees and shrubs to the high , places we were bound for—the high places .on which the I sun-god, Baal, was worshipped in days long departed, and where Elijah demolished his altars and confounded his priests. By this one beaten but nearly overgrown track, through tangled bushes of broom, honeysuckle, hawthorn, wild lemon, itc., we threaded our way until we reached the rock-hewn seats on the natural terrace that overlooks the magnificent plain below. Behind these seats were hung huge blocks of limestone, supposed by Mr. Porter and others to be the altar of sacrifice around which Elijah and the priests of Baal worshipped. I see no reason to doubt the identity of the place. There is still the appearance of a trench around the outer circle; and strange to say, the action of fire, with some oily matter as an agent, is still visible on the white stone. At about a stone's-throw from this ancient altar, is a large fountain, from which it would be easy to carry,vrater In abundance to fill the trenches. The position is very commanding; it overlooks the whole expanse of Esdraeloa's mighty plain, stretching, without fence or hedge, about 15 miles in front, and 12 miles from north to south, which takes in the whole region between the hills of Samarie and Galilee, while the mountaia ranges of Gilboa and the Little Hermon run in from the far east. We know not how many of the people of Israel witnessed the con- I miming fire that fell from heaven upon Elijah's sacrifice, but it is quite certain that thousands and thousands might have stood on the open plain and seen it flashing down upon the altar, standing out so conspicuously on this battlement of rock. We thought as we went up the rough and stony paths of Carmel what strong and hardy men the prophets and the ancient Israelites must have been to make a moun- tain like this their daily haunt; and as we came down we thought of the thousands of ruthless but faithful men who dragged the 850 prophets trembling down these very paths, not leaving hold of one until they made the brook Kishon to run crimson with their blood. I felt this evening in one of my most sensitive moods the pure and warm sir shad I been lifting me out of a ti:reatened sickness all day, yet leaving me in a state of nervous excitement that made the solemnity of Carmel almost more than I could bear. When we got to the bottom I remember giving my horse rein to follow the others in their short cuts over ploughed fields, and nothing more. All that took place on the tenting ground during that evening and the following morning has faded completely from my memory. Even the yelling of the wolves, hyrenas, and jackals, with which they say Cannel abounds, has not left a single impression or recollection. My senses most have been steeped in oblivion all night, and dreams of Carmel must have driven all things else out of my mind in the morning. Ido not remember recrossing Kishon next morning, but Isemember that we re- traced much of our journey of the preceding day, passing over the park-like undulating elopes that skirt the hills of Galilee, and which, after one or two brisk scrambles, brought us behind the hill of Nazareth, and upon the extensive tract of country, with Sepphoris as the central object, which we had , seen from the heights on Sunday afternoon. It was noon , when we came near to Sepphoris, and we felt the heat more oppressive than we had done since we left home. The olives under which we lunched only seemed by their scanty foliage to break up the beams of the burning sun into sharper points. After lunch we were wandering uneasily about, when we met a blind teacher with a ungiber of Arab ,pupils just leaving school. They interested us very much. ,From their answers to our questions, through an interpreter, we discovered that the boys had had their minds filled with the most absurd and outrageous ideas • respecting Christ ideas quite too horrible to repeat, and leading us to the coo- elusion that from early childhood the Mahometans are taught to despise both Christ and all who bear the name itf "Christian." Yet we were surprised to find that when an Arabic New Testament was offered to them, whether young or old, they eagerly accepted it. Mr. and Mrs. Allen had wisely provided themselvts with a number of copies, and dis- tributed them with great discretion. I shall never forget a picture we, had before us at Nain. In the absence of our dragoman who was an excellent scholar, and who generally undertook' to read the New Testament to the Arabs, Aboo was enlisted as reader for that day. A group of about a read nßedouin New Testament s seat ineacmirecnlet in theircross-leg own gedo;whileAboo d from the language tihreedlbe.awd.s resting I t was isthfrotmhe tinhde eaecdcoaupnitcohfirtehetorasieseintgh eof men ar,u, upon their knees, and with their chins in their hands, listening with rapt attention to Aboo, who himself got so- interested and excited with the narrative that he broke off every now and then to discant upon it, evidently wishing to impress the wonderful story upon the minds of his hearers. One grave and earnest man interjected a word here and there to show his appteciation of certain points, and when inquired of afterwards whether he could read he answered in the negative. Mrs. Allen then wished to know whether he had any friends who could read the New Testament for him; lie censidered for a while, and then said "Yes, he had a friend in Nazareth who would read it for him." On receiving a copy be carefully deposited it in his bosom. On another occasion, as we were passing out of Palestine into Syria, Mrs. Allen

gathered a group of boys around her, anrint one of them to read tifew verses of the New Testament to the rest.. The eager delight with which the boy received a copy and thrust it into his bosom, while all the others surrounded him, begging for a look, was worth almost going to Pales- tine te see. I cannot bet think that in this old land, where the Divine history was wrought out, the simple but sublime story of God's love in Christ as recorded, not in the ritual of the Greek and Roman churches' but in the book itself, ought to win its way over the hearts of thousands and thousands of the people. Will the break-up of the Ottoman Empire pave the way to this glad result? (To be continued next week.)
