STEALING POULTRY AT NE'WTON.—Robert Hornsby was charged with stealing two geese, four hens, and one rabbit, at Newton, on the 25th ult., the property of John Moore; and Ann Hornsby, mother of Robert, was charged with receiving the same, knowing them to have been stolen.— The male prisoner pleaded guilty, but Mrs. Hornsby said she did not know the hens were stolen.—Supt. Jackson said that a complaint had been made to the police of the loss of . _

the hens the prisoners were charged with stealing, and the police went to Mrs. Hornby's house where they found three hens, a goose which had been plucked, and the skin of a rabbit in the yard. One of the constables followed the female prisoner to the house of her daughter, some distance from Newton, and on entering he saw prisoner's daughter plucking a goose. She refused to say where she got it from, but afterwards said her mother had bought it that morning. —The male prisoner said the house was in his name ; he left the hens there, and told his mother he had bought them. He believed his mother did not know they were stolen.—The Bench sent Robert Hornsby to prison for six weeks,. and

. . discharged Ann Hornsby. BOBBERY.—Peter Woods was charged with having, some- time between the 6th and 11th ult., stolen from the shop of Robert Johnson, two pairs of boots, of the value of 15s. He . . . . . .
was committed to the _Quarter Sessions .for trial.—Peter

Woods and Margaret Woods were jointly charged with having stolen, between the Bth and 10th ult., a piece at shirting and a pair of trousers, from the shop of John Cook, draper, Golborne. They were also committed for trial.

FOOTBALL. RUNCORN (21e That) v. Nnyrron HEATH (2ND TEAK). —These clubs met on Saturday afternoon at Runcorn, when a well-contested game was witnessed by a large number of spectators, ending in favour of the home team. The Newton captain having won the toss, decided to play with the wind. Mason set the ball rolling for Runcorn, when the forwards followed well up. Some tight play ensued in Newton 25, and the ball was carried across the line, but Newton touched down. Play was confined some time in neutral ground, when, by a combined effort, Runcorn got the ball again across Newton goal line. Roich, who had been playing up well, fell on it, but it slipped from under him, when W. Townall. however, claimed a try, which Newton disputed, but the Runcorn captain would not give way, and took the place kick, which failed to cross the bar. The visitors, drop- ping out, forced the ball across the Runcorn line, the ball going dead. Mason again started the ball, and some tight scrimmaging took place in Newton:2s, milli half time was called. On changing sides Hogg started the ball for New- ton, and keeping on, got it into the Runcorn territory. At length one of the visitors got possession, and was in the act of touching it down across the line, when Page, equal to the occasion, slipped under the ball. A maul ensued, which ended in favour of Runcorn. Page touched down for the first time, and dropping out, Runcorn again carried the ball opposite the Newton goal posts. A tthis juncture Page looked like scoring, but unfortunately he slipped. A scrimmage again ensued, when Newton quickly relieved their lines, and carried the ball into Runcorn ground, the ball again going deed. Mason started the ball, and, following well up, in went into touch. From a line up Wainwright got possession, and nicely grounded the leather across the line. The place kick, though a splendid attempt, failed. The Newton cap- tain again started the ball, but Roach returned it, the ball going dead. Newton again dropped out, and worked the ball up once more to the Runcorn lines, when Mason, by a fine run and long punt, landed the ball in touch in the Newton 25. No side being called, Runcorn gained the victory by 1 try;l disputed try, 6 minor points, to Newton's 3 minor points. The following were the teams :—Runcorn, Stubbs, full back ; Roach and S. Waulkey, three-quarter; Tickle and Page half-backs; Riley, Mason (captain), Dennison' Dun- bavand, W. Pownall, J. B. Clarke, Whinyates, D. Sherlock, Wainwright, and J. Dean. NeWton, T. Whitehead, full back; Pearson and Hogg, three-quarter; Harrop and Day, half- backs; Dean, Leas, Travis, Martin, Crossland, Marlow, Cox, Scholefield, Lewis', and Butterworth. ST. HELENS RANGERS V. WIDNES TRUE BLUE.--Played at Widnes on Saturday last, and resulted in a victory for the St. Helens Rangers. For some time, after the Blues making the kick off, Wright, one of their three-quarters, was the most prominent player, and gave the visitors plenty of tackling exercise. The Blues were the first to score a major point by Bagley running in a try which was not improved upon. Soon after the drop oat Pervin obtained another try, which Burgess converted into a goal. The next to score was Gee, who obtained a try on behalf of the Rangers; but Borthwick failed to obtain the coveted point. Scion after the drop out Webb got hold and made a rplendid run from the centre flag, and would have gained a try had not H. Bing- ham have pushed him in touch about a yard from the goal line. On the ball being thrown out the home team forced it from,its dangerous position into the visitors 25, and here Bee made a nice, although futil . drop at goal. A few minutes further play, during which aeither team gained any material point, brought half time, ad after a short interval the Rangers' captain set the ball in •notion. For 20 minutes the game went on without either te m adding much to their score, although both goals were n several occasions in danger. Traverse now made a spit lid run from nearly the Blue's 25 flag, and evaded all att mpts to collar him until , he was within a few yards of their "Aid line. A scrummage was then formed, and Everson getting hold carried the ball over the goal line. The Blues disputed this try for some reason or other, but the Rangers' captain eltcided to kick. He took the place, and sent,the ball over the mark, in fine stvd.. Arnold followed next with another try—Borthwick took the place which failed. On the Blue dropping out the visitors ant r s few minutes play were attacking the home team in their 25, and Gregson getting hold made a strong run in. The place was entrusted to Rogers, who did the needful by sending the ball over the bar. Time was now called, the points being as follows :—Rangers f 2 goals (1 kicked from a disputed try), 2 tries, and 2 touchdowns. Blues: 1 goal, 1 try, 1 touch-in-goal, 1 dead ball, and 2 touchdowns. Players—Rangers : Rogers, back: Webb, Gregson, and Traverse, three-quarter backs; Swift and Everson, half backs; Clitherow, Lyon, Roughsedge, Taylor, Gee,,Arnold. Jackson, Griffiths, and Borthwick (captain), fon wards. Blues: H. Bingham, back; Bee, Wright, and Bagley, three-quarter backs; Burgess and Oakes (captain), half backs; Pervin, Whittle, Stokes, Whimpenny, Oilier, Proffit, Upward, Corns, and J. Bingham, forwards]

div.head: NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN.
div.p: NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN.
NEWTON IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONERS.

Mr. F. Crooch presided at a special meeting of the Board held on Tuesday, in the Newton Town Hall. The other members present were Colonel MoCorquodale, Messrs. Win- stanley, Emmett, Pardey, Wood, and Messrs. J. E. Worsley (law clerk), R. Brierley (surveyor) and Watkins (medical officer.)

THE LATE MR. BIRLEY-VOTB OE CONDOLENCE. The CHAIRMAN said since the last Board meeting they had bad to lament the loss of Mr. Birley, who was a very active member of the Board; and be thought he was speak- ing the sentiments of all when he said he was sure his loss would be much felt, not only, as a Commissioner but as a justice of the peace and a kind friend.. He was sure no gentleman would be more missed than Mr. Birley, and he therefore proposed ~hat a letter of condolence be sent to Mrs. Birley and family in their bereavement.—Mr. PARDEE was sure the expression of sympathy that had come from the Chairman must be fully endorsed by all. Mr. Birley was elected a commissioner on the passing of the Act, and he had served the town well during a grreat number of years, and as the Chairman very properly said his loss would be felt not only by the Commissioners but by the whole com- munity. He therefore seconded the proposition.—Mr. WINSTANLEY supported the letter of condolence remarking that he had sat on the Board a good limy years with the late Mr. Birley as a Commissioner, and had always found that whatever opinion Mr. Birley might entertain upon a matter when he came to the Board he was always open to conviction, and always seemed desirous of doing the very best he could for the comMunity.—ColonelblcCoßauomax said they all sympathised with the expressions the Chair- man had so properly made use of in regard to Mr. Birley, who was the first chairman of the Board. He continued to act as chairman for many years, and with the exception of a fow years during which he retired Mr. Birley had been a Commissioner from the formation of the Board to the time of his death. He was sure they would all miss the cheerful and happy manner of Mr. Birley when amongst them. He did not think he ever in his life saw a greater display at a funeral than at Mr. Birlev's funeral,—The letter of condo- lence was unanimously agreed to.

ELECTION-OF A NEW MEMBER. The CTIAIRXAN proposed that Mr. Gillespie be elected a member of the Beard to fill the vacancy caused by the death of Mr. Birley, and remarked that that gentleman would make a very useful member.—Colonel MCCOEQUO- DALE seconded the proposition, and said Mr. Gillispie's partner, Mr. Mason, was a member for many years and ren- dered good service. Mr. Gillispie had been a resident in the district for many years, and he thought he was a suitable person to elect.—Mr. PARDEY supported the proposition, which was carried unanimously.

HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT. Dr. Wevxms reported that in the quarter ending the 30th ult., there were registered 56 male and 33 female births, and 24 male and 23 female deaths, the excess of births over deaths being 42. The binh rate was 33.40, and the death rate 17.63 per 1,000 of the estimated population. The death rate for the three quarters of the year was 17.17 per 1,000. Whilst scarlet fever caused 9 deaths (1914. per cent. of the morality in the quarter) there was an absolute im- munity from every other zymotic disease, the solitary death from diarrhcea being primarily referred to dentition. The death rate of the last quarter and of the three quarters of the year compared unfavourably with that of previous years. This, doubtless, was owing to the continued prevalence of scarlet fever, which in the nine months had caused 31 or 25•32 per cent. of the deaths from all causes. The deaths of 8 persons (4 of them in September) from phthisis, and of 7 others from pulmonary diseases, testifi,d to the comparatively low temperature that pertained through- out the third quarter. It was, however, encouraging, in spite of the epidemic amongst children that had prevailed throughout the year, to observe a dirninishing relative rate of infantile mortality. On the 19th ult. the Sanitary Com- mittee had under their serious deliberation the question of adopting more energetic measures 1.4 cope with the still pre- vailing epidemic of scarlet fever with ,the result that an investigation into the extent of the disease had beeff insti- tuted, and other means organised to deal effectively with it. The mildness of the type of the present epidemic was, he feared, one factor in the wide diffusion of it. He could not conceal the fact that parents were either not sufficiently con-, vinced'of the insidious nature of the disease, its easy con); municability, and the prolonged duration of its infective power, or they were too unmindful of the danger of inter- communication of families in this sickness. He had no hesitation in saying that the effective control of the spread of the disease mainly rested with parents and heads of families, aided as they could .be by the special preventive measures adopted by the Board.—Mr. WINSTANLEY asked if Mr. Brierley could give the result of the house-to-house visitation.—Mr. BRIERLET said the visitation was not yet completed. A HALF-TIMER REFUSED ADMISSION TO A SCHOOL.

The School Attendance Committee held a meeting on the 17th ult., when Mr. Pardey was elected to fill the position of chairman, rendered vacant by the death of the late Mr. J. H. Birley. Mr. Ball, school attendance officer, read his report, which gave for the quarter ending September 31 the num- ber on the books as 2.236, average attendance 1,593, absentees 643; as against 2,175, 1,579, and 596 in the quarter ending June, 1881. ifhe school attendance offieer reported that Wm. Pullen, residing in Cartwright's-yard, had been refused admission as a half-timer to St. Peter's schools, although full school fees would be paid; and it was ordered that the matter be deferred for the opinion of the Law Clerk), or if necessaty that of the Education Department.—Mr. PARDEY moved, and Mr. WINSTANLEY seconded, the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. Wixsrmex,xx enquired as,to the legality of the proceeding of refusing to admit the boy into St. Peter's school.—The LAW CLERK said he wrote to the Education Department to ask "Can a public elementary school receiv- ing a grant refuse admission to children known as half- timers, who, though they attend only half the week are pre- pared to pay, and offer to pay the full week's scbool fees?" Two days afterwards he received this reply :—" I have the honour to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 20th bast. lam directed to state in reply my Lords cannot under- takt to answer a general question without any information as to the circumstances under which it has arisen. Should the School Attendance Committee of Newton-in-Makerfield Urban Sanitary Authority communicate with the Depart- ment through their Clerk with reference to any particular case in which a child has been refused admission to a public elementary school on the ground of his being a half-timer, my Lords will be prepared to give an answer to any enquiry they may wish to make on the subject."—He forwarded a copy of the letter to Mr. Brierley, and asked him to lay it be- fore the committee.—Dr. WATKINS, on behalf of the com- mittee of St. Peter's school, said the boy would be admitted, I but not unconditionally, and the committee reserved to themselves the right to say what the fees would be.—Mr. PanDay.asked if Dr. Watkins would name the conditions.— Dr. WATKINS said the committee would guarantee them- selves against any loss on the boy. This he said having consulted those in authorLy.—Mr. PADDEY said whilst the statement was afiytbing but satisfactory, he would not like any action taken until after the meeting of the committee of the scbool.—The minutes were adopted. THE SCARLET FEVER EPIDEMIC.—ROVSE TO HOSE VISITATION. The Highways, Public Works, and Sanitary Committee held a meeting on tbe 17th October. Dr. Watkins reported, that scarlet fever was spreading in the district and recom- mended that an efficient disinfecter be engaged from Liver- pool and that a house-to-house visitation be made with a view to ascertaining the extent of the disease. It was ordered that the officer of health of Liverpool be commu- nicated with to secure the immediate services of a practical person to fumigate and disinfect premises, and that Mr. Caldwell and Mr. Ball be engaged to make a house-to-house visitation under the direction of Mr. Brierley and Dr. Wat- kins. A letter dated 10th instant was read from Mr. Avelins, agent to the London and North-Western Railway Co., com- plaining of the state of Grant-street and offering to nay their share of draining and paving the same. Complaints were also read from thei; tenants in Grant-street of the smoke emitted from the chimney of the Brated Water Com- pany's premises. It was ordered that Mr. Brierley be instweted to prepare the necessary plans, Sic., for the sewering and paving of Grant-street, and that the necessary notices be served upon the respective property owners in the street calling upon them to pave and flag the same within one month in accordance with section /50, Public Health Act, 1875. Ordered that the Earlestown .rated Water Company be written to requesting an immediate abatement of the smoke nuisance from their boiler chimney. The ar- rangement with the bridge master for the repairs of the road e over the Hundred Bridges was submitted by the Sur- veyor and ordered to be sealed and signed by the Chairman. The following plans were submitted and apProved :-2 cot- cottages in Mercer-street for A. Cartwright ; bakehouse in Sack Bridge-street for S. Bethell ; 4 cottages in Crow-lane for A. Ball; bakehouse in Sefton-street, Crow-lane, for R. Whitfield; additions to house and shop in Houghton-street for Thos. Forster; and two houses in Crow-lane for George Tunstall.—The minutes were confirmed. PUBLIC LAMPS. A meeting of the Gas and Water Committee was held on the 17th' October, when an application was re.ad from Mr. G. Ratcliffe for a public lamp near his property in Nelson-et. Additional lamps were reported by the Surveyor to be neces- sary in other portions of the district,and it was ordered that the Chairman of the Committee with the Surveyor should inspect the places requiring, public lamps and that the Chairman have authority to order the fixing of the same where he considered necessary.—On the motion of Mr, WINSTANLEY, seconded by Mr. Emory, the minutes were agreed to.

FINANCE. At a meeting of the Finance Committee on the 17th ult., accounts amounting to ,2473 7s. id. were examined and cheques signed for payment—Mr. WOOD proposed, and the CHAIRMA_N seconded, the confirmation of the minutes, which was carried.

NEWTON PETTY SESSIONS. SATURIDAY.—Before Colonel MeCorguodale and Messm. Houghton and Pearson. CRUELTY TO A HORSE AT EARLESTOWN.—John Unsworth and William Fyldes were charged with cruelly ilitreating a horse at Earlestown, on the 27th Angust, by working it whilst in an unfit state.—P.C. 226 said be found Fyides working the horse at Earlestown ; the animal was very lame and ap- peared to be suffering a good deal of pain.—The Inspector of the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals stated that the defendant Unsworth promised that he would destroy the horse, and if that had been done be would he content with payment of the costs. Fyldes told

div.head: EX-PARLIAMENTARY SPEECHES.
div.p: EX-PARLIAMENTARY SPEECHES.

Viscoust Emlyb, M.P., speaking at the Carmsrthen Farmers' Club, 011 local taxation, said between 1871 and 1879 education charges increased £1,000,000 per annum, and though Government granted 31 per cent., they might justly claim more. Speaking of protection, he said a fatal objection urged against it was that it taxed food, but he pointed out that heavy rates upon food-producing land also taxed food itself.

Sir M. H. Beach, speaking at an agricultural dinner at Alton on Tuesday, referred to several pending agricultural questions. As to settlements, he was not for locking up the land, but thought a change would net greatly benefit the the farmer. As to the abolition of distress, that was a tenants' question, but he did not think it would prove so advantageous as was expected. Then some wanted provision for the tenant leaving his holding. He wished rather to induce him

to stop there. On Monday, Mr. Henry Richard, MX., accompanied by his colleague, Mr. C. H. James, MX., addressed a large meeting of his supporters at Merthyr. Mr. James delivered an address chiefly dealing with the subject of free trade. He condemned fair trade as only protection in disguise, and said the people would never allow their bread to be taxed. Mr. Richard denounced the wars of the late Government, and said that be held them responsible for the loss of life in Afghanistan, because the conflict was unjust. He alluded to the annexation of the Transvaal as one of the most un- scrupulous and audacious acts of usurpation and spoliation ever known in the history of nations. Mr. Jesse Collings, addressed his constituents at Ipswich, on Tuesday, explained his motion for Government aid to secure to English labourers proprietary rig_hts in land. Labourers in the South even now earned 10s. a week on the average, and no thrift was possible for them. but those who had migrated to towns and had saved some money might be assisted by the State to purchase small holdings. We lent money to. Irish landlords at 1 per cent., why not to English labourers at 4or3i ? He would gladly see the land covered with far- mers who were their own landlords. Messrs. Fawcett and Helms addressed their constituents at Hackney on Wednesday. Mr. Fawcett dwelt on the various improvements recently made in the postal service, especially in the arrangements for promoting thrift and the increased employment of females. He should endeavour to popularise the use of the post-office life assurances and • annuities. As to cheapening telegrams, that rbsted 'with the Chancellor of the Exchequer; but when there was a surplus to distribute, he had no doubt Mr. Gladstone would attribute due importance to the improvement of communication. He regretted that he was not able to announce the establish- ment of a parcels post, but he would spare no effort to give this convenience to the public, if possible. Referring to Ireland, he said the Irish people were what we had made them. The Irish Government needed to exercise patience and firmness, but there was complete unanimity in England as to the necessity of maintaining the union. Sir William Harcourt was present on Tuesday at a Liberal demonstration at Workington, and received an address from the West Cumberland Liberal Association. In answer to it he said that the rnsult of the Liberal legislation during the last 50 years had been most advantageous to the country. Notwithstanding all the Tories had predicted, it could not be said that the throne was less secure than it was half a century ago, or that the country was less prosperous. The Liberals still adhere to their old motto of "Peace, retrench- ment, and reform," and though they had inherited many difficulties, they still hoped to be able to accomplish some- thing under these heads when the great Irish difficulty had been overcome. Judging of the way people were flocking to the Land Courts, he hoped the difficulty was now nearly at an end. The county franchise would be a measure the Liberals must deal with, and if the country continued to back them up, he pledged his word the voice of the people should be heard. Sir Wilfred Lawson accepted an invita- tion to become the second Liberal candidate for West Cam- berland.

Lord Randolph Churchill, M.P. addressing a meeting ix Conservatives, on Tuesday, at Hull, condemned the policy of the Government in regard to Irish affairs, and accused Mr. Gladstone and his colleagues of having abandoned law and order for the purpose of creating a state of things which allowed Mr. Gladstone to come in with the Land Act and ap- pear as the saviour of his country. Contrasting Mr. Glad- stone with Lord Beaconsfield, who was mourned by the Queen and her subjects, he said the Prime Minister set him- self on a throne of green and gold, ran greedily after addresses in gold boxes, and like Herod he imagined that his glory also was immortal. If this Government continued we should be within measurable distance of the day when our empire would end, our power be tottering, our commerce waning, our industry decaying, and when we should be dependent for the necessaries of life on the bounty or cupidity of foreigners, with our flag disgraced, and with the spectres of communism and revolution banging over this once peaceful country; and Mr. Gladstone's name would never be uttered by any patriotic Englishman without deep and bitter con- demnation. Sir William Harcourt left Brayton on Thursday to proceed to Hawarden on a visit to to the Prime Minister. In passing through Carlisle he was presented with an address by the Carlisle Liberal Association, in the County Hall. In reply, he said that in the address they had given some credit to himself and his colleagues, but he thought little credit be- longed to those blessed with the 'conduct of such a party as the Liberal party. In playing the game of whist if one held all the honours it was not any credit to the player (cheers and laughter), and as a united Liberal party placed in the hands of the Government the absolute control of the game. it would be a disgrace to Liberal Government if they could not play the cards put into their hands (cheers). In the last two sessions of Parliament there had been shown a spin' of self-sacrifice and of devotion to the cause of this Libera: party on the side of every member of that party such as he believed had been unequalled in the history of party politics (cheers). No doubt that constituted the despair of 'the', opponents: it was only by sepudting the vertibrw of the Liberal party that they could hope to destroy their foes. They had succeeded in doing that on former occasions, he hoped in future they would fail. But be observed tbzt having failed in dislocating the vertibraa of the Liberal party, within the last two days they had announced that it had lost its head. That, he must say, was a piece of intelligence which had notreached him (laughter). If it were true that Mr. Gladstone (loud cheers) had retired from the lead of the Liberal party, it was a secret which he had kept profoundly concealed from his colleagues.

div.head: ELECTION- INTELLIGENCE. BATH.
div.p: ELECTION- INTELLIGENCE. BATH.
At a meeting of the Bath Conservative Association, on Tuesday, it was announced that Lord Desert had consented to stand as the Conservative candidate for Bath at the next election.

div.head: TIVERTON.
div.p: TIVERTON.

Lord Ebrington, the Liberal candidate for Tiverton, addressed an open-air meeting on Tuesday, and was cor- dially received. No Conservative candidate has yet appeared. Mr. Thomas Buller, of Wellington, Somerset, has issued an address to the Tiverton electors in the Liberal interest. He will support the Government in its efforts to maintain the integrity of the empire, and will vote for any measure calculated to relieve the burdens on land.

div.head: STAFFORD.
div.p: STAFFORD.

Admiral Maxse intends issuing an address to the electors of Stafford in the Liberal interest. Mr. George Howell on Tuesday received an invitation from one of the leading members of the late Mr. Macdonald's committee, asking him to stand for Stafford in the Liberal and working men's interest. Mr. Howell has promised to do so should it be the wish of the constituency. It is stated in Stafford that Mr. Plimsoll is likely to be asked to contest the seat rendered vacant by the death of Mr. Macdonald. Some think that Mr. Joseph Arch would he a likely man, the opinion being that he would tend to unite the various sectione of the party. Nothing definite has yet been arranged.

MINIMS' WAGES IN WEST LANCASTEIRE.—An ad- journed meeting of miners' delegates was held on Monday at the Miners' Hall, 'Wigan, when 60 delegates were present representing the whole of the collieries in West Lancashire. it was resolved that the delegates go back to their respective districts and call meetings in eaeh locality : that the men " play "on Tuesday and Wednesday, and that a deputation , wait upon the employers and press for an advance of 15 per cent. It also decided to hold another meeting at Wigan on Wednesday to receive the reply of the masters. An extremely painful case was heard at Camberland Assizes on Wednesday, before Mr. Justice Kay, Margaret Messenger, who is only 14 years of age, being charged with the murder of a child, six months old, the daughter of Mr. Pallister, farmer, with whom she was nurse. The prisoner was jeft in charge of the deceased and an elder child, and an hour afterwards she told a lad that a tall man had taken , away the baby. Afterwards she was seen bringing the dead body from a well. The girl was found guilty and sentenced to death. The jury recommended her to mercy on account of her youth. div.head: EDDISEURY PETTY SESSIONS..
div.p: EDDISEURY PETTY SESSIONS..

MormaY.—Before Messrs. S. Woodhouse (in the chair), E. A. Wright, W. Forster, J. Tomkinson, and 3. Hickson. NrISANCES —At the instance of the Runcorn Sanitary • Authority,,Mr. Farrington, inspector of nuisances, applied for an order to compel Charles Hulse to abate nuisance ex- isting in connection with certain privies at Five Crosses. Order granted.—The same officer summoned Thomas Ains- worth for improper drainage accommodation and endanger- ing other water supply.—Mr. Farrington said ,the defendant was the owner of several cottages in a line with those referred to in the last case. These premises were xvithout proper drainage accommodation, the consequence being that tbe sewage and liquid of all sorts percolated through a wall built at a great expense, and interfering with the water supply.—Order to abate the nuisance in a month's time. . OVERCROWDED CorreoEs —Henry Remick, Frodsham Lordship, was summoned by Mr. Farrington, nuisance inspector to the Runcorn Sanitary Authority, for having two cataget at Five Crosses in such a dilapidated state as to be unfit for humeri habitation. The proceed.ings, the inspector said, were taken on the strength of the report of the medical officer of health to the Runcorn Sanitary Authority, who pronounced the cottages unfit for human habitation, and he (the inspector) asked that an order of prohibition be granted until the premises were rendered fit for occupation. —Mr. Beswick admitted their not being habitable, but be could not send the tenants out —The Chairman said he had been in a similar position and could not get rid of some tenants.—Mr. Beswick said be felt great difficulty to get the tenants out, and if the Bench would make an order in one case he would make the two cottages into one.—The Bench granted an order to close the cottage occupied by Mary Mercer.

- - THE FRODSHAM VounsrruErts.—Ralph Lloyd and George Edge, two members of the Frodsham volunteers, appeared on an adjourned summons charging them with Committing an assault upon Mr. George Lancelley, who was acting for Mr. Walford, tenant of the property on which the shooting took place.—Mr. Rogers, solicitor, Northwich, appeared for com- plainant. —The case bad been heard at the last Court, when the Bench allowed it to be adjourned in order that an oppor- tunity might be tlfforded to each party to come to some arrangement between them.—lt appeared that eemplainant had resisted the use of the ground for range pin oses, and in consequence of the volunteers declining to accept his authority, he placed himself in front of the target, dared the party to shoot, when they removed him.—Mr. Linaker, Frod- sham, appeared for the volunteers, and urged _that some arrangements must have been made to allow an :icerrodanvhssoheliqupoun, retcnewoit talrtyssi the use of the range, otherwise the War office would not have sanctioned the shooting there.—The Chairman, taking into consideration that the volunteers had used the range for 18 years, was of opinion that there was presumptive evidence in their favour.—The magistrates took the view that it was not a matter in which they could interfeahrmea,med the case was dismissed. A MASTER CHARGED WITH ASSAULTING HIS SERPA roghedn Edwinwi th assßate, assaulting aar, mseerrv, servant gFirroldns charged complainant stated that inasmuch as she did not get up from bed when called by him, he mot into a rage and struck her in the face.—Mr. Linaker, who appeared for the defendant, called another servant, who gave a direct contra- , diction to the complainant's statement, and the case was dismissed.
WARRINGTON POLICE COURT.
face, loOsening two teeth, and also kicked him.—For being drunk and disorderly prisoner was fined 108. and cobts, and

20s. and costs for the assault on the police. WANTox Miscirm—Wm. Noon, a youth 16 years of age, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Rylands- street, and with damaging a box of the value of 75., the pro- perty of Mr. Robert Dobson, draper, Bridge-street.--On Saturday night Mr. Dobson's errand boy was taking a box up Rylands:street, when defendant, who was drunk, de- . . . . .
liberaiely kicked in the bottom.—Mr. Hunt characterised

this conduct as wanton mischief.—P.C. Neill &posed to apprehending the prisoner, who was identified by the errand boy.—Prisoner was fined ss. and costs, and ordered to pay the amount of the damage. RUFFIANISM BY A PUDDLER ON STBIBB.—Peter Lyons was charged with being drunk and disorderly on the previous

night, on 10-20, and assaulting George Hardman' of Widnes. —P.C. Cokely said he heard a disturbance near the Central Station, and, proceeding there, found Hardman lying on the pavement, bleeding very much from the face. Prisoner struck him a blow on the face and ran away, but he was afterwards apprehended by the officer.—Hardman said the

prisoner knocked him to the ground without a word passing between them, and also his friend. They had just emerged from the Central ,Station.—Prisoner said he was a puddler, but had not been at work during last week.—He was fined . . .

40s. and costs, or in default, a inonth's imprisonment. RESISTING POLICE CONSTABLES.—Thomas Bowcock, butcher, Horsemarket-street, was charged with assaulting P.C.'s Bruen, Lawrence, and Cokely, whilst in the execution of their duty.-4--P.C. Bruen, on the night of the 24th October, was taking a drunken man in custody, when defendant went up to him, took hold of his coat collar, and tried to pull him off. He also seized bold of P.C.'s Lawrence and Cokely.— Confirmatory evidence was given by Mr. James Dowd and Staff-Sergeant Hepkins.—Defendant said the man the officers were taking into custody was not drunk, and his wife asked him to get her husband up. He in consequence told the officers to let him go, as he had done nothing.—Mr. Hunt: Are you aware that the man pleaded guilty the following morning? No.—Defendant called a witness named Williams, who said he did not touch the officers.—Defendant was fined 40s. and Mts. ATTEMPT TO DEFRAUD BY A RAILWAY SERVANT.—James Halstead was charged on remand with riding on the London and North-Western Railway Company's lines from Chester to Warrington without paying his fare.—On Thursday night the prisoner, who is a discharged brakesman, was found at Warrington in the luggage van of a train from Chester. He had got in the van at Chester from the wrong side of the train. He was wearing railway clothing, evi- dently with the object of riding about the lines, but he had promised to return them to the company, and they would not charge him with that offence.—Prisoner was fined 20s. and costs.
Before the Mayor and Mr. Z. Armitage. BREACH/CS OF THE ELEMENTARY EDIICATION ACT.— The School Attendance Officer, Mr. Riley, summoned the

following persons for not sending their children regularly to school, and the usual penalties were inflicted :—Ralph Samuel, joiner, Farrell-street; Thomas Robinson, tanner, 23, Lord Nelson-street; Ed. Wilson, tanner, 24, They-street; Henry Frangleton, joiner, 4, Crossley-street; Geo. Higham, porter, School-brow; Julia Kenny, labourer, Stanley-street; Michael Rabbit, labourer, Fennell-street; Thomas Darby- shire, hawker, 85, Winwiclt-street ; John Shepherd, collier, Whalley's-yard ; John Lingley, baker, Whalley's-yard ; Edward Hardman, and Sam Allcock. TunsDAY.—Before Major Cartwright (chairman) and Alderman Webster. LOST His TICKET.—Jghn Holland was charged with travelling from Manchester to Warrington in a third-class compartment on the Cheshire Lines Committee, with intent to defrand.—The prisoner alighted from the train arriving in Warrington at eleven o'clock on the previous night. He was without ticket, and refused to pay his fare.—Prisoner said he took a return ticket from Warrington during the afternoon, and he lost the return half. He offered to go to the clerk for identification, but the ticket collector refused to let him do so. The foreman searched the carriage for the ticket, but could not find it.—The Chairman said crlsoner was responsible 4 and prisoner was ordered to pay his fare, and the costs. THEFT FHONI THE MArigrr.—John Broderick, a little ragged and barefoot urchin, nine years of age, was charged with stealing a Vb. of grapes.—Mr. Place, the market inspector, saw the prisoner steal the grapes from a stall in the Market Shed. He put them in his hat and ran away. After a chase Mr. Place captured him, when he gave him a wrong name and address.—The Bench ordered him to receive six strokes with .the birch rod. WEDNEsney..—Before Alderman Davies, Councillor Fairclongh, and Alderman Chandley. MAKING SURE OF THE FUENITURE.—John Hansbery, an ironworker, was charged with committing an aggravated assault on his wife Sarah.—Mr. F. F. Ayre appeared for the defendant.—Prosecutrix said that on Saturday night last her husband Mused her, because she did not make his tea until he had given her sixpence. On Sunday morning she went away from home without making a fire and stayed at her brother's house until about half-past six In the evening. At that time she returned home, where she found four men sitting round the table playing cards. She asked for " Jack " and they replied that he had gone out. She afterwards met him in the entry, near the house, and he struck her a blow on the nose with his fist. She lost much blood. Cross- examined: She did take drink, but did not often get drunk. Directly her husband was locked up she sold up all the goods in the house.—Mr.Ayre said the prisoner was a steady industrious man, and in one employment for nine years. The wife on the contrary, was frequentry drunk, and had on several occasions been put to bed by her neighbours.— No witnesses were heard on either side, and the prisoner was bound over, in his own recognizances, to keep the peace for six months. Tam' FROM THE Pi:mom—Thomas Prescott, a puddler, was charged with stealing a purse, containing a sovereign and *florin, from the person of Thomas Hines, lodging- house keeper, 8, Hill-street.—Prosecutor and prisoner were sitting together in the lodging-house on the previous night, and sometime afterwards the prosecutor found that his purse had been extracted from his pocket. The prosecutor leaked the door and said he would fetch a policeman if prisoner did not "turn it up." He denied the theft for a short time, but afterwards delivered up the purse and money.—He was committed to gaol for two months with hard labour. A. "SusPEcr."—Rosanna Boardman, a weaver by trade, and a native of Blackburn, was charged on suspicion with stealing a shawl and a score of other small linen articles. The prisoner had cohabited with the last prisoner for some twelve 'months, and had been committed to gaol the one for twelve and the other for six months for a robbery.—The case was adjourned. THURSDAY—Before Mr. E. Milner.

A Itnruniery CONVICT. - Patrick Brady alias Craney, Teddington, and Newton, was brought up in custody for failing to report himself. He was sentenced at the York Assizes in 1879, to two years' imprisonment, and twe years' police supervision. Prisoner was remanded to the police authorities at Manchester.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The forthnightly meeting of this Board was held on Thursday, Mr. S. Marsh presiding. There were also present the Rev. Thomas Chambers, Messrs. W. Tyrer, J. T. Hall, W. A. Meadows, J. Fidler, .1. Leatherbarrow, G. J. Paris, James Fisher, E. Syder, John Lowe, Joseph jackson, James Ranson, W. Swift, T. Dobell and W. Gerrard; with Mr. S. H. Hartley, (clerk). WORKHOUSE MASTER'S REPORT. -

The MASTER (Mr. W. W. H. Bicknell) reported that there were 471 inmates of the house on the last day of this week, as compaied with 431 in the previous week and 474 in the corresponding week of last year. There were 160 boys and girls at Kirkdale Schools. The vagrants relieved during the week numbered 101.

div.head: TIIR VAGRANCY QUESTION,
div.p: TIIR VAGRANCY QUESTION,

The Committee, to inquire into the relief and treatment of vagrants in other unions, reported that they had visited the vagrant wards and inspected the arrangements of the Wigan abd Balton Unions, Liverpool Parish and Manchester Town- ship, for the purpos of ascertaining the task of work exacted most likely to repress vagrancy and entail the smallest amount of loss upon the ratepayers. The committee found that in all places named corn crushing machines were pro- vided, and a male vagrant was required to grind 601 b. of crushed Indian corn. The committee learned that the system of cern crushing was the one most detested by the vagrants, more especially where a separate room is allotted to each man. The Board were already aware the sleeping accomodation at the workhouse for casuals was inadequate, but the committee believed if the system of corn grinding i'as introduced the numbers would decrease to such an ex- tent as to obviate the nucessity for erecting sleeping wards. With a view of testing this belief, and to save any unneces- sary expenditure, the committee unanimously recommended that twelve mills and a corn crushing machine, which could be fixed at a cost of under £5 each, should be placed in what is known as the old" Red barn," and a partition placed between each mill to procure isolation. The committee pointed out the necessity for immediate action being taken, and suggested that they should be empowered to carry out the foregoing recommendation with the least poasible delay. —The Rev. T. CHAMBERS moved that the recommendations be carried out.—The motion was seconded by Mr. RaNsorr. —ln the course of discussion as to the profit and loss if the system was adopted, Mr. MEADOWS remarked, that it was not so much a question of profit, if the adoption of the System would act as a deterrent to vagrants. He did not think they would be gainers by the system of grinding corn, but if it acted as a deterrent and prevented them spending a large sum of money in other ways for accommodation of these vagrants, he thought they would be quite justified in adopting the recommendations.—The CLERK said the matter was one affecting that Union very materially, because it was placed between Liverpool and Manchester, and they got a large number of vagrants.—On being put to the meet- ing the motion was unanimously carried. div.p: RUNCORN PARLIAMENTARY DEBATING SOCIETY. The attendance at this debating class is as yet very small, and unless more members come forward the society will un- doubtAly have to be broken up. It was expected that the iree last Wednesday week would have a tendency to bring so together the old members, and also be an inducement for others to join, but it does not appear as if it had contributed to either result, as far as Tuesday evening's meeting was concerned. It was almost a quarter to nine o'clork when the Speaker took the chair, owing to the late arrival of some of the principal members. The subject for discussion was the adjourned debate on the Queen's Speech. On rising, the member for Guildford drew attention to the fifth clause in the Queen's Speech, where it says "The relations with all the Powers continue to be of peaceful, amicable, and cordial nature," and stated that it was a blot on the present Govern- ment that the state of affairs for the last 18 months should have been allowed to have existed. If the Conservative Government had been returned to office the first thing they would have done would have been to renew the Peace Pre- servation Act ir. Ireland. [At this point the hon. gentleman complained of being unwell, and resumed his seat]—The member for Oxford made his maiden speech, in which he hoped to claim the indulgence of the House. lie supported the policy of the Government in reference to Ireland and the Transvaal, and said that Mr. Gladstone had carried out what he intended to do when the Liberal Government came into office. Oae of the first things he took in band was the Irish Disturbance Bill, but it was eventually thrown out by the House of Lords, and he contended that that action had a good deal to do with the present state of Ireland. The Opposition seemed to have a dislike to any bills introduced by the present Government, and endeavoured to obstruct their passage; and it was principally owing to their actions that the British Crown bad been dragged through the dust and the name of England dishonoured, if it had been. He I expressed confidence in the policy of the Government, and I felt sure that it would endear itself to every right thinging man.—The Leader of the Opposition expressed criticisni on two matters—the most prominent before the public eye— namely, the state of affairs in Ireland and the conduct of the Government in the Transvaal. In commenting upon the 'Queen's Speech, he said it was one of the most peaceful documents they had ever had before them. The hopes the Government there expressed seemed to be apologetic excuses for having nothing more tangible to put before them as regarded the state of results. He had been considerably surprised at the action of Her Majesty's Government in reference to Ireland. It was not the intention of the Opposition in any way to weaken the hands of the Ministry in their endeavour to perform the first duties of a government, but he could not help expressing surprise at the way in which the Govern- ment had suffered agitation to grow during the last eighteen months. He felt that the hands of the police bad been tied as mach as possible, and he thought great praiee was due to them for their forbearance in the difficult tasks they had to perform. He maintained that if the Government had been firm when they came into power the recent unfortunate scenes which had taken place in Dublin would have been averted. It was astonishing to find that our Cabinet could not prove the illegality of the Land League under eighteen months. [A Voice: It only took a day.] This the hon. gentleman said only toads matters worse, when it was looked at in the proper light. The objects of the League were just the same eighteen months ago as they were then, only on a smaller scale. The objects of the League had been of a rebellious character for a long time, and it was height of public feeling which caused such pressure upon the Cabinet to take the steps they had done. Adverting to the Transvaal, he said the hon. member for Chelsea gave a most flattering description of the Boers at the last sitting, and he was sorry some of their delegates were not in the strangers' gallery at the time. He spoke in strong terms of the manner in which the title of Suzerain was obtained, and said he would have preferred being a party to adding the title of Empress of India to those possessed by the Queen than the one which had cost the country so much blood and treasure. He was glad that the Convention spoken of in the Queen's speech had been ratified in the Transvaal. His complaint against the Government was that all this might have been gained had there been some foresight and statesmanship on the part of the Ministry. Three-fourths of the coercive acts and repressive measures had emanated from a Liberal Ministry.—The Home Secre- tary, in a smart and cutting address, said he was glad to find the Queen's Speech contained a lot of things the Con- servatives did not quite agree with. The Opposition had raised questions which it was the intention of the Govern- mentt o answer sooner or later. Speaking of the Disturbance Bill, he stated it was impossible for any Government to carry out a bill without the co-operation of both sides of the House. The principal points which seemed to be under- going criticism seemed to be their action in reference to Ire- land and the Transvaal. Earl Beaconsfield had predicted there were some awful things in store for them, but because he was apparently right he (the speaker) was not going to give him the rank of a prophet. He contradicted the Leader of the Opposition in stating tat agitation had gained ground within the last 18 months. The House of Lords suited the wishes of the majority of the Conservatives in throwing out the Dieturbance Bill, and this had served to strengthen Mr. Parnell's bands; and, he considered, they were directly responsible for the lawlessness which had taken place, It was not until the Land Bill became law that the League became illegal. Before they attempted cceecion they had passed the Landßill. With reference to the Transvaal, he alleged that it was to the country's dis- grace that they ever had a battle with the Boers. But the ll.f:nistry were not responsible for this ! It was Sir George C,lley who went in the face of instructions given by the ' Government. The affair had been most dishonourable from beginning to end. It was an absurdity to talk of fighting the Boers, for they were little if any stronger numerically , than the population of London.—The member for Birken- head said the Queen's Speech appeared to be a document more remarkable for what it did not contain than what it did contain. He referred the hon, members to the fourth paragraph, where they were told that a section of the Queen's subjects in Ireland gave cause for anxiety, yet they were " sanguine " to hope. He was sure they all felt desirous 'of the anticipated result being obtained. but when he looked at the history of Ireland, , for the last eighteen months, and the steps they had taken ' to bring about the present state of matters, he was sure there could be little comfort in the assurance or the hope they ex- pressed in that clause. He was somewhat puzzled to under- stand the expression "I am sanguine to hope." He had referred to three dictionaries, but failed to conceive its meaning. They were also told that the relations with all the powers were peaceful, amicable, and cordial. It was not, however, the result of the action of their Government that this extraordinary state of affairs had been brought about in Europe, but by the united action of the greater powers ided by their Government. The gentleman inferred from this that the principal Powers had brought about the pre- sent state of matters exclusive of England. He spoke very strongly of the policy of the Government with regard to Ireland and the Transvaal, and said it required little pre- paration to form a judgement of what had been done. The Foreign Society approved heartily of ill that had been done in the Transvaal. They had shown an example to the whole world in having determined to do justice, notwith- standing all the derisive remarks made by the country. It was the part of a great man to be modest and of great countries also. The quiet people of Ireland were delighted with the action of the Government, and in a few days, or at least, months, he believed they would see the fruits of their persistent endeavours to do justice. On the motion of the member for Preston, the debate was adjourned.

div.head: GOLBORNE.
div.p: GOLBORNE.

GOLBORNE PARISH Caracn.—There was a service of song at this church on Sunday, entitled "Harvest Home:" The i Vicar, the Rev. C. T. Quirk, was the reader, and the musical portion of the service was performed by the choir, whose rumber was augmented for the occasion by about 20 Sun- day school children. The collections, which were on be- half of the fund for reflagging the church walks, realised .-ElO lie. CONCERT AT GOLBORNE.—A concert in aid of the Widows and Orphan Fund of the Anoint Order of Shepherds, A.U., was given at Mr. Brewis's scoolroom, Golborne, on Tuesday. The Rev. C. T. Quirk, M.A., vicar of Golborne, presided, and a varied programme had been provided. A quartette, "The Minister Bell," was very successfully sung by Messrs. Entwistle and Caunee. and Misses Garton and Burton. Ths same vocalists gays " 0 shepherps tell me," with equal effect, and the song, harmonizing as it did with the object of the entertainment, was heartily applauded. Miss S. Walton sung " Norah darling," very effectively. Dr. Mapel's "Mignonette," was given with great taste and feeling, the slnger's fine tenor voice doing full justice to the pleasing but rather difficult song. Dr. Coombs, of Wigan, gave two s)ngs, which were well rendered and warmly received, and songs were also given by Miss Margeson and others. Several duets on the violin and piano by Mr. and Miss Wallwork (the latter a child only 10 years of age, but dis- playing estraordinarY musical precocity) were given in the course of the evening. There was a good attendance, and t:ie concert was, a very successful one.

ENTEUTAINKTINT AT ASIITON-111-MAKERVIELD.—The first a a series of entertainments was given on Monday night to an appreciative audience at St. Thomas's schools, Heath- line, Ashton. The Rev. H. Siddall, vicar of St. Thomas's, occupied the chair, and explained the object of the enter- tainment. It seems that the St. Thomas's reading-room and lending library has -gTaclually got into debt, and the ‘ommittee had resolved at last to free the institution of this encumbrance, and those artistes on the programme were r dents in Ashton and persons interested in the n e'fare of the society with the exception of Mr. J. of Earlel,. town, who generously volunteered his assis; Ince. The pianoforte soles of Mr. Jameson were well received, but the effect would have been greater if a better instrument had been obtained. The glees were fairly given on the whole, but one of the members sang rather flat occasionally which spoiled the effect. The catch "Oh how Sophia" was creditably given. The two readings of Mr. Holbrook were warmly applauded, but were a little too long. Mr. Mitchell sang his songs in his usual style, and received an ovation. Mrs. Holbrook sang "In the gloaming" and "Take back the heart" with taste and feeling, and was warmly ap- plauded. Mr. Wood sang very creditably and left a fay.-mrable impression. The rendering of Mr. Holbrook's songs, especially "Sweethearts," were capitally given, and he was warmly applauded. The comic songs of Mr. Wil- MMs need no comment, he being the lion of the evening. Tae proceedings closed with the National Anthem.

div.p: sheep which was diseased, as far as the pluck and liver ' went. In most cases it did not follow that the rest of the body was diseased. He bad known the defendant for some time, and had always looked upon him as a respectable man. He did not consider him a likely dealer to offer diseased meat for sale.—ln reply to Mr. Husband, witness said his reason for being of this opinion was that he had seen the kind of meat which defendant had bought for several years, and he was, therefore, able to form a judgment as to its character.—The Chairman said there was only one opinion on the part of the Bench, and that was that the meat had been exposed for sale. It was not even denied that it was unfit for human food. They should impose a fine of 20s. and costs.—Mr. Husband applied for the costs of his wit- nesses, and the magistrates said they would grant them for one day only—The case had been before the court on a pre- vious occasion. LICENSE TRANSFERS.—The following transfer of licenses were made —From Robert Almond, for a beerhouse in Ackers-street, Prescot, to Patrick McLoughlin ; for the Commercial Inn, Widnes, from Edward Roberts to Joseph Graves; beerhouse in Liverpool-road, Huyton, from John Hooton to Frank Richards; beerhouse in Kemble-street, Prescot, from Patrick McLoughlin to Thomas McKeen ; and Legs of Man, Church-street, from Thomas Makin to Richard Roughsedge. James Kane applied for a temporary authority under the license held by Robert Butler, and it was granted. The application of John Clare for a temporary authority under the license held by John Holden, at the Ring of Bells, Farnworth, was adjourned in order that the police might make further enquiries. Thomas Deakin was granted an occasional license, to sell at St. Ambrose's bazaar. THURSDAY.—Before Mr. F. H. Gossage. ALLEGED Coat. STEALING. Ellen Grady, a single woman, was charged with stealing a quantity of coal from a wagon in a siding at West Bank Dock.—P.C. Brown said he saw the prisoner filling a bag which would hold about 112 lbs. from the wagon, and he took her up.—She was re- manded until Wednesday.

WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—BeforeHlaollebsrsoros.kFG. H. I 1 A SAD PAGE Ul A LIFE HISTORY:MIS. Mary Rosell, a eG jsusangre (chairman), and . formerly the wife of the late Dr. Hilles, who was at one time a well known surgeon in Widnes, was charged with stealing two scarves, eleven socks, and three dozen buttons; the pro- perty of Mr. James Birchall, draper, Waterloo-road. Mr. James Thomas Wilding, of Market-street, said he was shop- man to the prosecutor, and about a quarter past eight on Saturday night, the prisoner came to the establishment and asked for some stockings. Another assistant showed her a number, and she purchased a pair. Witness was at the counter serving another customer, but, from something that was said to him, he went outside the premises, and there noticed Mrs. Rosell take the socks out of a box which was close to the counter. He then called a policeman and gave her into custody. The officer found upon her the socks, scarves, and other articles.—ln reply to Mr. Husband, who appeared for the defence, witness said all the stolen articles had his employer's private mark upon them. The woman was drunk, and she might have taken them not knowing what she was doing. The articles could not possibly have fallen out of the parcel of goods which the prisoner bought. —P.C. Murray said that at the time when prisoner was given in charge, she made a motion which caused a parcel of but- tons to fell out of her dress. Witness picked them up, and asked her if she had anything else upon her. She said he could look if he wished. He then opened her jacket, and found underneath the articles she was charged with stealing. —ln answer to the Inspector of Police witness said that he afterwards opened the parcel of goods which the prisoner had bought, and found the bill for them inside. It amounted to 6s. ld.—Mr. Husband contended that the evidence clearly showed that there had been no intention of stealing in this case, for even the leading witness for the prosecution had admitted that he did not think the woman knew what she was doing whoa she took the things. The poor creature was evidently in a lamentable condition, and had passed through a great amount of trouble. A drunken man who took an article not knowing what he did, could not •be convicted of the crime of stealing. Then how ' were they to identify the articles, for probably many other shops in the town sold similar things 7 The Chairman: There was a private mark on them. —Mr. Husband did not wish to press the case upon this point, but the witness Wilding had said, "I don't think she knew whether she bought the things or not." If there was anything at all in the case, it was one of kleptomania, but a person suffering from that painful affliction was not to be held guilty of a crime.—At the request of the Bench P.C. Murray was recalled.—Mr. Gossage : What was the condi- tion of this woman ?—Witness: She was in drink, but not so much so but that she was capable of knowing what she was about.—The Bench decided that there was a prima fade against the prisoner, who elected to be dealt with summarily.—The second charge against the prisoner—that of stealing a woollen shawl, the property of Mr. Tebbut— was then proceeded with.—John Jackson, shopman to Mr. Tebbut, said the shawl produced was the property of his master. On Saturday be bung it up before the door, and about six o'clock it was quite safe. Two hours later he missed it. He did not give information to the police but he believed that they were told of the loss.—P.C. police, said that when he searched the prisoner at the police station on Saturday, he found two shawls in her possession, and the one produced was one of them. He charged her with stealing it from the shop of Mr. Tebbut, and she replied, "I know nothing about it." The last witness identified the shawl at the police station.—By Mr. Husband: Prisoner was in liquor.—By the Clerk: She was not so far gone as to pre- vent her knowing what she was about.—Mr. Husband con- tended that in this case there was no evidence whatever to show that the prisoner bad stolen the shawl. She was not seen in or about Mr. Tebbut's shop, and there was nothing to prove she might have bought the article. The prisoner had had a great deal of trouble, and she had, he believed, always borne a good character.—Mr. Birchall was called by Mr. Husband, and said he had known the prisoner for many years, and during that time had always thought her a respectable person. He believed the shopman Wilding to be reliable and trustworthy.—Mr. Gossage : -Were you present 7—Mr. Birchall : I was not, sir.—By Mr. Husband : He saw the prisoner afterwards.—By the Clerk : He did not know that the prisoner was a drunken person. He had never seen her drunk before.—Mr. Wm Miller, draper, of Waterloo-road, Widnes, stated that he had known the prisoner for some years, and looked upon her as a respectable woman. He heard on Saturday night that she was drunk, and was very much surprised.—Mr. Gossage : We consider the first case proved, and fine the prisoner 20s. and costs, with the alternative of one month's imprisonment with hard labour. We dismiss the second charge.—The tine was paid by the prisoner's father, who was in court uring the hearing of the case.

WARRINGTON RURAL SANITARY ATJTHoIiITY Mr. W. Derbyshire presided at the monthly meeting held yesterday. Present :—The Rev. G. F. Roberts; Messrs. Houghton, Cooper, Garnett, J. C. Sutton (clerk), J. H. Gornall (medical officer), W. Owen (surveyor). THE MAINTENANCE OF FEVER PATIENTS. A letter was read from Mr. Arthur Potter, Market Place, in reference to a demand for L 3 10s. for the maintenance of his little boy in the Infectious Diseases Hospital. He begged to be excused attending the meeting as he had an important engagement. The lad was very slightly ill, but at the request of two doctors be agreed to his removal, with the proviso that he would be treated as a large ratepayer of the borough. The lad had attended school in Warrington, had neatly all his meals in Warrington, and except at night none of them lived at Sankey. Under these conditions he hoped the Authority would not charge him The MEDICAL OFFICER: But they live at Sankey; and he was very desirous of getting the case removed himself. The CLERK said it seemed an extraordinary thing to excuse people at all within the borough when they could pay, because it led to this anomaly when they got just out- side the borough. However, the AutnorLy had nothing to do with that; and if they were called upon by the Corpora- tion, as they might be, to pay this money, they would pursue the usual covrse, and call upon Mr. Potter to repay it. He would reply to Mr. Potter that the remedy was in his own hands. If he did not wish to be charged because be was a large ratepayer of Warrington, he should approach the Corporation on the subject, and endeavour to induce them not to charge. If, however, the Corporation approached the Authority, there was nothing for it but to pay. Mr. PARKINSON, of Penketh, appeared before the Authority in reference to a claim that had been made upon him for the maintenance of his ckild in the Infectious Diseases Hospital. He objected to pay the money inasmuch as he stated he did not consent to the removal of the child. The MEDICAL OFFICER said the removal was entirely voluntary. Mr. GARNETT said it was hardly right that the man should , be liberated from payment or compelled to pay for the isola- tion of his child when he so strongly objected to the re- moval. It was a difficult case. After some discussion, The Cu/immix informed Mr. Parkinson that the Author- ity had come to the conclusion that he would have to pay the account either at once or by instalments, unless he became a pauper and asked the relieving officer to bring the matter before the Board of Guardians. Mr. PARKINSON, in reply to the Chairman, said he was prepared to pay 10s, a month, but he thought it was very bard that he should have to pay. The CHAIRMAN said they all thought it was rather bard, but the only thing he could do was to lay the matter before the township. Mr. PARKINSON : Have they a right to take children away? The cHAIRMA,.7 : The Medical Officer informs us there was no resistance. Replying to Mr. Garnett, Mr. PARKINSON stated that the child was under medical treatment at the time of removal, I and the sent the removal van twice. The CHAIRMAN objected to the subject being reopened. Mr. GARNETT : Can we enforce paymet, Mr. Clerk? The CLERK: Oh, yes. Mr. GARNETT : It was ruled before we could not. MONTHLY REPORT. me MEDICAL OFFICER reported that the number of births during the month ending 31st October was 15 males and 9 females and the death 7 males and 6 females. The excess of births over deaths was 11; the death rate 12 6 ; and tin proportionate mortality from preventable diseases 30 per cent.

THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 5, 1881 RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The fortnightly meeting was held on Tuesday afternoon at the Dutton Workhouse. The Rev. Canon Barclay pre sided, and there were also present Messrs. John Ashton, James Darbyshire, Mr. Henry Linaker (clerk), and M r. W. H Linaker (depu(y clerk.)

_ NEW URBAN POWERS. A letter was read by Mr. W. H. Linaker, from the Local Government Board, forwarding two copies of an order which they had issued under section 276 of the Public Health Act, 1875, declaring certain provisions of that Act to be in force in Frodsharn and Frodsham Lordship districts of the Authority, giving the urban powers which had been adver- tised. The order will come into force on the 7th inst. FRODSHAM DRAINAGE SCHEME. The DEPUTY CLERK read a letter from Messrs. Wrigley and Morecroft, dated the 20th ultimo, which stated that the writers had had a conference with their client, Mr. W. E. Wright, and his surveyor (Mr. G. Heywood) on the subject of the Authority's communication of the 13th ult. They could now only act on the assumption that the Authority adhered to their scheme, and this rendered it necessary that Messrs. Wrigley and Morecroft should be put in a position to send in their client's claim pursuant to the statutory notice given to him on the 19th January, last year, and the plan which accompanied it. A subsequent letter from the Authority on the 7th July, this year, was accompanied by a plan showing that it was intended to construct one lamp- hole, and one man-hole in Mr. Wright's land. This they could not recognize as a notice coming within the provisions of the Act. It was manifest that before Mr. Wright could be in a position to estimate the amount of his claim for compensa- tion, he must know what was the nature and extent of the easement sought to be acquired by the Authority. They, therefore, wished the Authority to define the nature and extent of that easement, and, in particular, to state over what width of land, hlong the line of the sewer, the Authority required way leave, and what right of access there was to be to the sewer within Mr. Wright's land ; and whether there were gates to be provided at all the points of entrance and exit of the sewer to and from Mr. Wright's land ' • and for what purposes, and subject to what restric- tions(after the sewer was constructed) Mr. Wright could make use of the land over and through which the Authority acquired a way leave. It rvas not unlikely that the Authority might have some form of grant, or agreement, adopted in similar cases; and, if so, it might, perhaps, be the most simple mode that they should furnish them with the pro- posed form of grant, or agreement, as the ground work upon which Mr. Wright was to base his claim. The letter further stated that if the Authority could see their way to dispense with any lamp-hole, or man-hole within the limits of Mr. Wright's land, the amount of his claim would be propor- tionately reduced.—The CLERK stated that he had replied to the letter as follows :—" Referring to your letter of the 20th instant, I beg to say that Mr. Bancroft, the Authority's engineer, informs me that the Authority will require an easement of 241 lineal yards over Mr. E. A. Wright's land, for the purpose of laying earthenware sewerage pipes of 12 inches diameter ; and on this length of pipe it is proposed fixing one lamp hole and one man-hole. The maximum width of the easement would be two yards over the whole length. The depth of the intended sewer below the level of the ground will be as follows :—viz., at the fence alongside Chester-road 41t. Gin.; at the lamp hole 4ft. •' at the man. hole 41t. Gin.; and at the sewer adjoining Mr. Dutton's land 10ft. 10in. The servants of the Authority shonld have power at all times to go through the gate leading into Mr. Wright's field to examine and repair the line of sewers, (kn., therein." Mr. Bancroft further says, "I am not aware that it is the intention of the Authority to provide gates at the points of entrance and exit of the sewer to and from Mr. Wright's land. In my opinion, it is not necessary, and it is certainly not customary, to do so." If Mr. Wright should at any time build on or sell this field, for building purposes, Ihe would have the right to connect his sewers with the Authority's main, but laud drain pipes ought not to be so connected. I cannot advise the Authority to dispense with the man-hole and lamp hole on Mr. Wright's land. They are absolutely necessary for ventilation, and for examining the conditions of the pipes from time to time. You are, of course, aware that the Authority or the contractor will be liable for all surface drainage during the construction of the works, or by examination of any repairs that may be neces- sary hereafter. The CLERK trusted that they would be able to send Mr. Wright's claim upon an early day. INSTRUCTION TO PROSECUTE A MEMBER OF THE AUTHORITY. Mr. FARRINGTON, nuisance inspector, stated that a nuisance caused by defective drainage existed on the farm premises owned by Mr. John Highfield, at Sevenoaks. The Inspector said that the. nuisance was one of the most glaring in the Union, and be had spoken to Mr. Highfield about it during a period of two years. He had repeatedly been to that gentleman, and served him with numerous notices. He gave an amusing account of the difficulty which he experienced in getting an interview with Mr. High- field upon going to his house when he paid his last visit. The fact of the gentleman not being proceeded against was causing some scandal. The CHAIRMAN ranarked that there was no wonder the public complained, as they would no doubt have the idea that because Mr. Highfield was a member of the Authority they would take no notice of the nuisance, and thus make fish of one and flesh of another. It was no doubt owing to neglect and carekssness on Mr. Highfield's part that the nuisance continued unabated. It was deoided that a summons should be taken on against Mr. Highfield. A STOCKTON HEATH NUISANCE. A complairq v•ss made of a nuisance being caused by the storage of Ainclicau manure at Stockton wharf, and the inspector was directed to write to the Bridgewater Navigation Co. respecting the matter.

div.head: ST.
div.p: THE ST.

At the Royal Raven Hotel, on Monday, a meeting of colliery owners was held, when it was decided to increase the price of coal is. per ton and to make an advance of 10 per cent, in the wages of their employes from next making- up day. In the evening ot the same day Mr. John Cross addressed a meeting of miners on the Fair Ground, and in the coase of his remarks dealt with a statement made recently by Mr. J. C. Gamble to the effect that only the engineering business felt the effect of improved trade in St. Helens. He did not know what kind of " specs " Mr. Gamble was looking through when he could not see an improve- ment in other trades. In the glass trade for instance the manufacturers had cleared out large stocks, and were now working orders that would last a whole year. He believed all branches of industry were improving; but he could not speak of the chemical trade, because the manufacturers did not put their prices in the paper like other trades. The miners, he contended, ought to be put on the same level as other citizens, and he did not sea anything to prevent them having is. 6d. a day of eight hours instead of 3s. a day of I twelve hours. He must confess that the minerswent against their own interests, for although they had been advised, assisted, and taken by the hand by many intelligent and benevolent men in England they always rebelled against their best friends and neglected, if not refused, to he united. Mr. Cross then went on to speak of the overstocking of the market, and drew a comparison between the coal trade of thirty years ago, and that of to-day. In those days many pro- prietors had £5.000 in their pockets, but at the present day they had more like £lOO,OOO. This large accumulation of capital had been brought about by depriving men of their wages; but if the miners were only united, the men in less than twelve months would be working for 9s. a day instead of the paltry 3s. The miners ought to work lew and have more money as wages. The masters were willing to give an advance of 10 per cent., and it was decided to accept that at Wigan, if offered, but it was not then known that it ,would be offered. Having advised them to drink more sweet milk and less ale, which remark elicited some laughter, Mr. Cross put a resolution which had been passed at Wigan, that they play Tuesday and Wednesday. The resolution WAS carried. At the nrieetirmi above reported, many men volunteered to go round the district as bellman to warn the miners not to work on the days mentioned, and this was done on Monday night. On Tuesday morning, a number of colliers did not resume their usual work, but we ascertained that only about one-fifth of Messrs. Pilkington Bros.' men were playing, the majority being at work. A considerable number of those employed at Sankey Brook, Bournes and Robinsons, and the Victoria colliery at Rainford, did not go to work. The reason alleged for playing on the two days mentioned is that the output of coal may be restricted, which though necessarily increasing the price of coal to consumers, says Mr. Cross, would not be unwelcome on the part of the public, because he believes the public would not object to a " rise " in the price of coal pro. videO the colliers were paid decently. A deputation waited upon Mr. France, the manager for Messrs. Pilkington Brothers, on Tuesday morning, and Mr. France then stated that the masters were willing to grant an advance of ten per cent., and N 1 ,{' lye granted that advance if they had been asked. On Tuesday morning another meeting was held at the George Hotel, George-street, at which Mr. Molyneux, presi- dent of the society, presided.—ln his remarks the Chairman said that in the Manchester district the men had that morn- ing commenced with an advance of 15 per cent. That morning they also had waited upon the masters at St. Helens pressing for the 15 per cent., and the masters had decided to give them ten.—Mr. Cross said that they had given notice to the masters for an advance, and having received no answer they had extended that notice to the end of October. In consequence of that the resolution to " play " Wednesday bad been come to, but that resolution had not heea arrived at in a spirit of wantonness. Mr. France only a few days since had said that the masters would not give an advance, but in less than six hours that gentleman had been made to eat his words. Mr. Cross having spoken on the great de- mand there now was for coal, said that he had no doubt that in less than a month they would have another advance of 5 per cent. —Mr. McKinley addressed the meeting and spoke in high terms of Mr. Macdonald, MX., whose death had taken place the previous day. He charged the masters with playing fast and loose with their men, and said that the Wigan and whiston Coal Company some time ago promised an advance of wages as soon as trade warranted their taking that step; but although that company had made some good contracts, and had increased their price for shipping coal, no advance had been made. The masters it was evident would "shilly shally " with the men so long as the men allowed them to do it.—lt was decided that before the men resume work on Wedneoiday Mr. Cross should go to Wigan and see what was being done there. The miners resumed work on Thursday.
