div.head: PUDDLERS' STRIKE AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: PUDDLERS' STRIKE AT WARRINGTON.

MASS MEETING OF THE MEN. Under the presidency of Mr. John Chalmers, a mass meet- ing of the MCD, who have struck work at Bewsey Forge, was held in the League Hall, Bewsey-street, on Saturday evening. The meeting throughout was of a very enthusiastic character, and the,sentiments of the variofis speakers against returning to work at the proposed terms were heartily approved. The CHAIRMAN said they had met to say something about the dispute that had taken place between the Bewsey puddlers and their employers. Some time ago the manager of the works sent in a kind of fettling, such as they had not had before, and said they must work it. The men said nothing until they heard again from him, when he said they must work it at a reduction of 3d. a ton. The manager said it would be an improvement to the iron; they would be able to make better iron out of the material given them, but they must pay 3d. per ton for it. The men's reply to that was "no," as, considering what they had been reduced in times gone by, and that two years ago they suffered a reduction of 3d. a ton for the kind of fettling sent in, which was being pro- duced at no extra cost to the employers, they felt they were justified in asking that the 3d. a ton should not be taken off as proposed. That took place about the middle of the week, and they were told they could go on until the end of the week. They did so, and they called a meeting at which it was decided they should not work at the reduction. A deputation was sent to the manager to tell him the result of the meeting, but when they arrived at the works, he was not to be found. However, they saw him on Monday afternoon, when he told the men they would have to work this fettling and also suffer the reduction. They said they could do nothing of the kind as they had passed a resolution on the previous Saturday, not to work for less than Ss. a ton for the kind of iron they were working. They therefore gave the manager 14 days' notice, and he said at the expiration of that notice they would have to work at a reduction of 3d. a ton. That notice expired last Saturday, when they called a meeting and sent a deputation to the manager to tell him that they could not accept the terms. He said those who did not accept the terms would have to return to the works on Mon- day to receive what was due to them, and those who accepted them must go in and commence work. But he was happy to say that no one returned to work. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Not an under-band or bye turn had returned to work, although they had been sorely tried during the week—(hear, hear,)—as a certain manager of the works had been to them, and had spoken to them in several parts of the town, but they remained firm and he hoped they would continue to do so. (Hear, hear.) They all knew very well that strikes did not altogether do good. He would have been better pleased if they could have settled the matter without one, but they knew very well things sometimes took place which caused men to do things they really had not thought of doing. This was one of those cases, and it might result in some good in the end. They had sent men to different parts of Lancashire and he was informed two of them had just entered the meeting and they would no doubt have something to say to them. (Hear, hear.) From one or two who had returned he had learned that at other works in Lancashire the prices the men were being paid were higher than at Bewsey Forge for the material used. Under one firm the men were working bar iron for which they received 75.9 d., while at Bewsey they paid 78.6 d (Hear, hear.) Again they found some firms were paying 7s gd. for scraps, for which atßewsey they were paying 7s3d. —("Shame," and applause,)—and at the same time they were using fettling similar to that which had been sent in to them for the last two weeks. 'raking the majority of the works in Lancashire, they found the men were working at a rate not below but in some cases higher than they were asking at present. A rumour was circulated on Monday that the secretary of the association, Mr. Edward Trow, said to a certain manager of the Bewsey works, if the men had been in the Union he would have compelled them to work, and if they had not worked he would have brought union- men to fill their places. That was not true. He was re- ferring to this matter for the purpose of clearing the man. He was seen before he left the town on Monday, and he dis- tinctly told them he said nothing of the kind. What lie said to the manager was that if they had been in the union they would have had to continue work at the same rate at which they left until the question was settled by arbitration. (Hear, bear.) They found the same manager writing to Mr. James Capper, secretary to the operative section of the South Staf- fordshire Wages Board. But how did he write? He wrote in the name of a puddler, while at the same time he was the manager of the works. (Cries of "Shame," and "He did.") That was how he had been gaining information upon certain points regarding the work of the men. Mr. JAMES KILDUFF, of the Dallam works, said he did not see any but Bewsey men upon the platform, and he thought if the other workmen came forward it would show they had sympathy with their fellow workingmen (Applause.) Working at Dallam as he did he could see the state of affairs, and had been dissatisfied with his wages of late. They had not been sufficient to support him and his family. (Hear, hear.) He theeefore considered, if their money went lower, it was time they gave up work. (Hear, hear.) Although he was very temperate he had not a farthing to spend, and he thought it time they got a fair day's wage for . . . •

would give them the statistics. Out of 17,000,000 tens of I iron, which had been the output of the world, England ' alone produced 7,721,833 tons; and yet they would tell them the trade was in a decaying state. Ile admitted it had fallen in price, but they had doubled the production, which had paid for the fall in price. It was monstrous, on the part of the employers, to desire a reduction of 3d. a ton. Let them look at the state of the country, and ses whether it warranted the reduction. Let them look at the works now starting in the country. Masters were actually advertising for men; and yet, in the face of a rising market, their employers wanted to take 21. per cent., or 3d. a ton, off their wages. It was not just to do anything of the kind (Applause.) Mr. GEORGE BROWN said some years ago a man thought himself a beggar if he could not go up street with a sovereign in his pocket—(hear, hear)—on Saturday night, but now he thought himself a gentleman if he had 2s. 6d. It had been asked why should 90 men rule 2,000. It was a simple question. Why should 90 men ruin 2,000? (Hear, hear.) Were 90 men to suffer a reduction that would affect 2,000 men? (Cries of "No.") Were they to be obstinate and refuse, so that it should not affect 2,000? (" Yes.") They were not to be bought and sold. (Applause.) They had got to the lowest price they could be sold at—(hear, hear),—and they would fight the battle out. It was his firm belief victory would be theirs in a short time. Mr. GEORGE POVEY then briefly addressed the meeting; and two representatives from the Whitecross works said the men there were in favour of the Bewsey men, and would give them their best support. The CHAIRMAN said when they had fought this battle, whether they succeeded or not—he believed they would succeed—there was one thing he wished to impress upon them all, and that was to rally round the union and join in (Applause.) A vote of thanks was accorded to the chairman, and the proceedings terminated.

div.head: RUNCORN POLICE COURT.
div.p: RUNCORN POLICE COURT.

MoNDAY.—Before the Rev. E. A. P. Campbell (chairman), and Mr. Thomas. NEW POOR RATE FOR SUTTON.—On the application of the Assistant Overseer, a poor rate of ninepence in the £ was granted for Sutton. THE SCHOOL BOARD AT WORK —The following people were summoned by the Runcorn School Board, for not send- ing their children to school :—Robert Fisher, Cooper-street; Charlotte Done, Mill-brow; Samuel Booth, Spring-gardens; John Nash, Cooper-street; William Salkeld, Norton-street; Thomas Webb, Brunswicliotreet : John Owen, King-street; Edwin Lewis, Spring-gardens; Peter Crogan, Nelson's-row; James Chambers, Wellington-street; Peter Johnson, Shaw- street; Thomas Walley, Shaw-street; and John Hillige, Granville-street. The cases were proved by Mr. Bowyer, school attendance officer, and in each of them an order was made for ss. to be paid, inclusive of costs. About half a dozen of the defendants said they were unable to pay and would go to gaol. One of them named Webb, on being asked if he had any goods upon which distraint could be made said he had nothing but what he "stood up in." ONE WHO REFUSES TO MAINTAIN BIS OWN FAMILY—A healthy, able-bodied man named Patrick Baxter, about 38 years of age, was summoned by Mr. Thomas Houghton, collector to the Runcorn Board of Guardians, for neglecting to maintain his wife and family, who were now chargeable to the common fund of the Union.—Mr. Houghton said the prisoner's wife and children had been chargeable since the 30th of April last, and during all the time no money had been received on their account. In 1879 the family were in the workhouse, and £ll 18s. was spent in keeping them, of which the prisoner only paid 175. 6d. The total amount owing by him now was £24.—Baxter said his difficulties had I been brought about by his wife drinking. He was committed to Knutsford one month, with hard labour. I A YOUNG MAN WITH A FOUL MOUTH.—John Dyer, was summoned under the Runcorn Improvement Act, 1852, for having used abusive language.—P.C. Noden stated that about half-past ten, on the night of the 14th ult., Dyer was in Mersey-street, using language of a most awful des- cription, and wanting to fight.—Defendant was fined 10s. and 9s. 6d. costs, or, in default, 14 days' imprisonment, with hard labour. A NORTHWICH MAN CONVICTED OF CRUELTY.—James Malom was summoned for having caused a horse to be cruelly illtreated by allowing ill to be worked when in an un- fit state, and George Wilkinson, a youth in his service, was charged with driving it whilst in that state.—P. C. Cooper said that about ten minutes to eleven im the 26th ult., he and P.C. Egerton were on the bank of the river Weaver at Aston- by-Sutton, when he met Wilkinson driving a brown mare, which was drawing a flat. They stopped the mare, and found on the right shoulder a raw wound about four inches in length, from which matter was oozing. Ho asked the boy if his master knew that the animal was in that state, and be replied that he saw the horse when he was bringing it out, and "told him to be careful" with it. The collar was wet from the matter which had run upon it, and the wounds appeared to be old ones.—P. C. Egerton gave corroborative evidence.—The Bench fined the lad ss. and 17s. 6d. costs, and his master 20s. and 18s. 6d. costs.
